properties.name: Gökçeada (Imbros)
properties.desc: Turkey's largest island, 90 minutes off Kabatepe, with abandoned Greek hill villages — Zeytinli, Tepeköy, Dereköy — that refill every August with returning families. It was the country's first cittaslow and runs largely on organic farming. Aydıncık's shallow salt lake is the windsurf spot; Kefalos and Laz Koyu are where you actually swim.
properties.season: Jun and Sep — the meltem blows hard all August and ferries stop in winter storms
properties.tip: The Greek villages sit 300 m up and are cold after dark even in August, and the last ferry back leaves early — day-tripping from Çanakkale is a wasted day.
properties.rev: Visitors praise the emptiness, the goat cheese and the wild coast, and warn that public transport is minimal, half the villages are ghost towns, and vehicle ferry places sell out weeks ahead in August.
properties.onward: İstanbul (IST) then 4.5 h to Kabatepe pier via the 1915 bridge, and a 90-min ferry; there is a small seasonal airstrip

properties.name: Bozcaada
properties.desc: Ancient Tenedos: a small island of vineyards, poppies and constant wind, with a Venetian-Genoese fortress guarding a harbour of Greek stone houses in faded blue and ochre. Ayazma and Sulubahçe face south into clear water. A dozen working wineries press Çavuş and Kuntra grapes grown in quantity almost nowhere else.
properties.season: Jun and Sep — August is a booked-out crush and winter ferries cancel in northerlies
properties.tip: Leave the car at Geyikli and rent a scooter; the island is 40 km² and the ferry vehicle queue in summer eats more time than the whole island takes to cross.
properties.rev: Repeat visitors love the wine, the cobbled quarter and the light; complaints are August prices, a ferry that strands people in bad weather, and a harbour that is now mostly boutique hotels.
properties.onward: İstanbul (IST) then 5.5 h by road to Geyikli-Yükyeri iskele, and a 35-min ferry; foot passengers can also sail from Çanakkale in summer

properties.name: Enez (Ainos)
properties.desc: Ancient Ainos at the mouth of the Meriç, where Thrace runs out into Greece. A Genoese-Byzantine castle stands over the village with the roofless church of Hagia Sophia inside it, and below runs a dozen kilometres of empty Saros Gulf sand with water clean enough that the Aegean crowd would ruin it if they knew.
properties.season: Jun–Sep for swimming — Saros water stays cold and clear later than the Aegean
properties.tip: Drive past the castle to Sultaniçe or Erikli for the sand, and stop at the Gala Lake hides on the way back for pelicans, flamingos and spoonbills.
properties.rev: People are startled by how empty and clean the beaches are and by the scale of the castle; the complaints are almost no infrastructure, mosquitoes off the delta and a long drive from anywhere.
properties.onward: İstanbul (IST) then 4 h by road via Keşan; buses reach Keşan and a dolmuş covers the last 24 km

properties.name: Troy
properties.desc: Nine cities stacked in one mound above the Trojan plain, with the Bronze Age walls and the sloping ramp of Troy VI still standing well enough to read. Alone it is a confusing pile of old trenches; with the Troy Museum's rust-coloured cube down the road, the sequence finally makes sense. The wooden horse in the car park is a prop.
properties.season: Apr–May and Sep–Oct — there is no shade on the mound in July and August
properties.tip: Do the museum in Tevfikiye first, then the mound, and walk the boardwalk anticlockwise so the layers arrive in chronological order.
properties.rev: Half of visitors call it the most atmospheric heap of stones they have walked, the other half find it underwhelming without a guide; everyone agrees the museum rescues the visit.
properties.entry: ≈€15 · Troy Museum ticketed separately ≈€12 · both covered by Museum Pass Türkiye
properties.onward: Çanakkale (CKZ) has thin flight links; most come from İstanbul (IST) over the 1915 bridge, then 30 km south from Çanakkale by dolmuş or car

properties.name: Anzac Cove
properties.desc: A 600-metre shingle beach under crumbling ochre cliffs, where the landing of 25 April 1915 went wrong before breakfast. It is smaller than every photograph suggests — seven minutes to walk end to end — and the ground rises immediately into the gullies that decided the campaign. Ari Burnu cemetery sits on the headland at the north end.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — Anzac Day itself needs a permit and a very early start
properties.tip: Come at first light before the buses roll down from Beach Cemetery; the cove is a war grave, and swimming here is discouraged even though nobody stops you.
properties.rev: Almost everyone is struck by how tiny and hemmed-in the beach is; complaints centre on coach convoys, litter in high season and a road that has been eroding into the sea for years.
properties.onward: Eceabat by ferry from Çanakkale, then 12 km north by car or tour minibus; no public bus goes to the cove

properties.name: Assos (Behramkale)
properties.desc: A Doric temple of Athena on a 230 m volcanic crag with Lesbos filling the horizon, and a stone village clinging to the slope below. Aristotle taught here for three years and married the ruler's niece. The old harbour at the bottom is a single row of stone buildings turned into small hotels, with water deep enough to swim straight off the rocks.
properties.season: May–Jun and Sep — August fills the harbour hotels and the one road down
properties.tip: Sleep at the harbour but see the temple at sunset from the top; the descent to the harbour is a 1-in-5 cobbled hairpin that punishes a loaded car.
properties.rev: The view and the swimming get near-universal praise; the standard gripes are cramped harbour rooms at Aegean prices, the brutal access road, and touts on the village lane.
properties.entry: Acropolis ≈₺200 (≈€5) · covered by Museum Pass Türkiye
properties.onward: İstanbul (IST) then 5 h by road, or Edremit Koca Seyit (EDO) 1 h away; the last 3 km down to the harbour is steep and narrow

properties.name: Gallipoli Battlefields
properties.desc: Pine and scrub across 33,000 hectares of ridge above the Dardanelles, with trench lines, cemeteries and monuments left roughly where the fighting stopped in 1915. At Lone Pine and Chunuk Bair the opposing trenches are eight metres apart. The Turkish 57th Regiment memorial and the Anzac sites share one hillside and are visited very differently.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — 25 April is Anzac Day, when the peninsula is sealed and full
properties.tip: Hire a car or a licensed guide from Eceabat instead of a coach tour out of Çanakkale; the sites are 40 km apart and the buses give you eight minutes at each.
properties.rev: Visitors describe it as unexpectedly moving and beautifully kept, while warning that rushed group tours, loudspeaker commentary and midsummer heat can flatten the experience entirely.
properties.onward: İstanbul (IST), 4 h by road to Eceabat via the 1915 bridge, or the Çanakkale–Eceabat car ferry across the strait

properties.name: Kilitbahir Castle
properties.desc: Mehmed II's clover-leaf fortress on the European bank at the narrowest point of the Dardanelles, 1,200 m across from its twin in Çanakkale. The three-lobed keep is unlike anything else the Ottomans built, and from the tower you look straight down on tankers passing at what feels like walking distance. Reopened after years behind scaffolding.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — the strait funnels wind hard in winter
properties.tip: Take the small Çanakkale–Kilitbahir ferry rather than the Eceabat one; it lands at the castle gate and runs roughly hourly.
properties.rev: Visitors call the keep the most interesting castle interior on the strait and the ferry crossing half the pleasure; the complaints are steep unlit stairs and erratic winter opening hours.
properties.onward: Çanakkale waterfront, then the small vehicle ferry across the strait (about 15 min) which lands beside the castle

properties.name: Adatepe and Yeşilyurt
properties.desc: Two stone villages on the southern skirt of Kaz Dağları, rescued from collapse by architects and now the most self-consciously handsome places in the Troad. Adatepe has an olive-oil museum in the old mill and the Zeus Altar on the rock above, where the gods supposedly watched the Trojan War. Yeşilyurt is steeper, quieter and less restored.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — the villages are cool when the coast below is not
properties.tip: Climb to the Zeus Altar at first light: the whole Gulf of Edremit and Lesbos lift out of the haze, and by ten the minibuses arrive from Assos.
properties.rev: People find the stonework and the view genuinely lovely, then note that both villages have become boutique-hotel and gift-shop economies with almost no local life left outside the season.
properties.onward: Edremit Koca Seyit (EDO) 45 min away, or İstanbul (IST) and 5 h by road; signposted off the Küçükkuyu–Ayvacık road

properties.name: Bayezid II Complex and Health Museum
properties.desc: A 1488 hospital on the bank of the Tunca where the mental ward was treated with running water, scent and music — musicians played three days a week — three centuries before European asylums stopped using chains. The hexagonal domed ward is now a museum with slightly eerie mannequins, and the mosque, medrese and soup kitchen around it are intact.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — the riverside floods and turns to mud after winter rain
properties.tip: It is a 20-minute walk out past Sarayiçi or a cheap taxi, and it is run by Trakya University, so the Museum Pass Türkiye does not work here.
properties.rev: Most people call it the most memorable museum in Thrace and the mannequin dioramas either charming or unintentionally funny; the complaints are the walk from town and thin English labelling.
properties.entry: ≈₺200 (≈€5) — university-run, not on the Museum Pass Türkiye
properties.onward: İstanbul (IST) then 2.5 h by bus to Edirne, then a taxi across the Tunca; walkable from the centre in half an hour

properties.name: Kırkpınar Oil Wrestling and Sarayiçi
properties.desc: On an island in the Tunca where the sultans kept their Edirne palace, two thousand men in leather kispet trousers pour olive oil over each other and wrestle for three days each summer — a contest running since 1362. Out of season it is meadow, storks, an empty stadium, and the surviving palace kitchens and Justice Pavilion in the grass.
properties.season: Late Jun–early Jul for the festival; otherwise Apr–Oct for the ruins and the storks
properties.tip: Festival week fills every bed in Edirne and across the Bulgarian border, so book two months out or take the early bus from İstanbul and return the same night.
properties.rev: Those who make it for the festival call it the strangest and best sporting event in Turkey; the standard warnings are brutal heat with no shade, packed stands and touts reselling seats.
properties.onward: İstanbul (IST), 2.5 h by bus to Edirne, then 3 km north-west along the Tunca by taxi or on foot

properties.name: Edirne
properties.desc: Ottoman capital for ninety years and still built like one: three imperial mosques inside a kilometre, a covered bazaar by Sinan, and a plain west of town where three rivers meet under long Ottoman bridges. The food is its own argument — calf's liver fried paper-thin, and almond marzipan. Greece and Bulgaria are each twenty minutes away.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — the Thracian plain is baking in July and grey in January
properties.tip: Eat tava ciğeri somewhere that fries to order off Saraçlar Caddesi, then walk out over the Meriç bridge at dusk to the riverside beer gardens in Karaağaç.
properties.rev: Day-trippers from İstanbul consistently wish they had stayed the night; the usual complaints are a scruffy modern centre, aggressive bazaar hawkers and buses that dump you far from the monuments.
properties.onward: İstanbul (IST), then 2.5 h on the O-3 motorway by bus; long-distance trains no longer run usefully to Edirne

properties.name: Selimiye Mosque
properties.desc: Sinan's verdict on his own career, finished at 86: a single 31.2 m dome on eight piers, lifted so the interior is one uninterrupted volume of light. Four 70 m minarets carry three balconies each, and a muezzin's platform stands in the dead centre with a fountain running underneath it. It reads far larger inside than out.
properties.season: Year-round — winter mornings give the emptiest interior
properties.tip: Come half an hour before sunset prayer and sit under the central platform; the upside-down tulip carved into one of its marble bases is the detail everybody hunts for.
properties.rev: Architects and casual visitors alike call it the finest Ottoman interior anywhere; complaints are restoration scaffolding that has come and gone for years and coach groups that arrive all at once at midday.
properties.entry: Free (mosque); Foundation Museum in the medrese ≈₺100 (≈€3)
properties.onward: İstanbul (IST), then 2.5 h by motorway bus to Edirne otogar and a short taxi; Edirne has no airport

properties.name: 1915 Çanakkale Bridge
properties.desc: The longest suspension span in the world, 2,023 m between red-and-white towers, jumping the Dardanelles between Lapseki and Gelibolu. The crossing takes four minutes and replaces a ferry queue that could run to three hours in August. The best view is not from the deck but from the shore roads below, where the towers stand clear of the strait.
properties.season: Year-round — strong northerlies occasionally close it to high-sided vehicles
properties.tip: The toll is HGS electronic only; confirm your hire car has a working transponder before you cross or the fine arrives by post weeks later.
properties.rev: Drivers are unanimous that it turned a half-day ferry ordeal into a coffee break, while locals on both banks complain the ferry towns lost their trade and the toll is steep for a short hop.
properties.entry: Toll ≈₺500 (≈€12) per car, HGS electronic only
properties.onward: İstanbul (IST) then the O-6 and O-5 motorways across Thrace; this is the direct road from Europe to Troy and the northern Aegean

properties.name: Kaz Dağları (Mount Ida)
properties.desc: Homer's Ida, a 1,774 m ridge of endemic Kazdağı fir and black pine between the Troad and the Gulf of Edremit, cut by streams that stay cold through August. The Çanakkale side above Bayramiç is the quiet one: forest roads, plateau hamlets, and a summit view that takes in Bozcaada, Lesbos and the Trojan plain at once.
properties.season: May–Jun for flowers and water, Sep–Oct for the ridge — snow on top Dec–Mar
properties.tip: Approach from Bayramiç and Yassıçalı for empty forest roads; the popular southern waterfalls run a daily vehicle quota that is gone by mid-morning all summer.
properties.rev: Walkers rate the forest and the water highly and grumble about unsigned trails, the quota system on the Edremit side, and mining and quarry disputes that have scarred parts of the range.
properties.entry: Free on the Çanakkale forest roads; national park entry from the south ≈₺100 (≈€2.50)
properties.onward: Edremit Koca Seyit (EDO) for the southern side, or Çanakkale and 70 km east to Bayramiç for the northern forest roads

properties.name: Şarköy and the Ganos Hills
properties.desc: The Ganos ridge drops straight into the Marmara here, and the slope between is one of Turkey's oldest continuous vineyard belts — Thracian, then Byzantine, then Greek, and now a dozen small wineries that will pour for you without an appointment. Şarköy itself is a plain beach town; the reason to come is the road and the vines above it.
properties.season: May–Jun and Sep–Oct — harvest is September, and August is a domestic-holiday crush
properties.tip: Drive the ridge road from Mürefte to Uçmakdere rather than the coast road, and stop at Hoşköy for the small producers who still sell by the demijohn.
properties.rev: Wine travellers rate the producers well above the region's reputation; the complaints are that Şarköy's own seafront is over-built, the beaches are average and several wineries close on Mondays.
properties.onward: İstanbul (IST) or Çorlu (TEQ), then 2.5 h by road via Tekirdağ; a car is the only sensible way to reach the vineyards

properties.name: Uçmakdere
properties.desc: A single-track road falls 700 m off the Ganos escarpment in a run of hairpins to a fishing hamlet with one grocery and a stone jetty. Paragliders launch from the top most weekends because the sea breeze funnels reliably up the slope. Cyclists climb it as a test piece, and the view down the Marmara from halfway is the payoff.
properties.season: May–Oct — the road is greasy and sometimes blocked by rockfall after winter rain
properties.tip: Go down in low gear and be back up before dusk: there is no lighting, no barrier, and nowhere for a large vehicle to turn around.
properties.rev: Paraglider pilots and cyclists call it one of the best descents near İstanbul; drivers report a genuinely frightening road surface and locals complain that weekend traffic now blocks the hamlet.
properties.onward: İstanbul (IST), 2 h to Tekirdağ then west on the coastal road; the turn-off is signposted between Kumbağ and Mürefte

properties.name: Avşa Island
properties.desc: The Marmara's holiday island: two long sandy beaches, vineyards that still supply a drinkable local wine, and a summer population that multiplies roughly twentyfold. In June and September it is a pleasant, slightly shabby seaside town with clean water and cheap fish. In August it is a ferry queue set to loud music.
properties.season: June and September — August is chaos and winter has almost no sailings
properties.tip: Stay on the Yiğitler side rather than Türkeli if you want to sleep, and buy the return ferry ticket the day you arrive, because Sunday sailings sell out.
properties.rev: Turkish holidaymakers come back every year for the sand and the price; the constant complaints are August noise, overbooked pensions, litter on the main beach and brutal Sunday ferry queues.
properties.onward: İstanbul Yenikapı fast ferry (about 3 h) or the shorter crossing from Tekirdağ; the island is walkable and scooters are for hire at the pier

properties.name: Tekirdağ
properties.desc: A Marmara port town known for two things: köfte bound with rice and cumin, and rakı distilled here since the 1930s. The Rákóczi House is a Hungarian prince's exile home turned museum, restored down to the panelling and furnished by Budapest. The seafront promenade runs for kilometres and fills every summer evening with families.
properties.season: May–Jun and Sep — August is hot, crowded and the sea inside the bay is not the cleanest
properties.tip: Eat the köfte at a charcoal grill near the old bazaar; the motorway service-station versions trading on the name are a different and much worse food.
properties.rev: People come for the köfte and leave content, while noting the town itself is largely concrete, the beaches are poor and the port dominates the view.
properties.onward: İstanbul (IST) or Çorlu (TEQ), then 1.5 h by the coastal road or motorway; frequent buses from İstanbul Esenler

properties.name: Dupnisa Cave
properties.desc: Three linked caves under the Strandja forest, some 3,200 m long, with a river in the lower gallery loud enough to drown conversation. Lit walkways pass columns, curtains and rimstone pools, and the temperature holds at about 13 °C all year. Five bat species winter here, which is why the cave shuts for half the year.
properties.season: May–Sep only — closed to visitors through the bat hibernation months
properties.tip: Take a fleece even in August, and confirm it is open before you drive: the last 12 km from Sarpdere is forest road and there is nothing else out there.
properties.rev: Visitors call it far bigger and wetter than expected and the forest drive worth it alone; the complaints are slippery steps, patchy lighting and people arriving in winter to find the gate locked.
properties.onward: İstanbul (IST), 3 h by road to Demirköy, then 12 km of forest road; no public transport goes to the cave

properties.name: Yıldız Mountains (Strandja)
properties.desc: A low, wet, oak-and-beech massif along the Bulgarian border — the last stand of Euro-Siberian forest in Turkey, and empty in a way nothing else within three hours of İstanbul is. Villages like Sarpdere, Balaban and Armutveren are timber-framed with vine porches and one tea house. The roads are single-track, unsigned and slow.
properties.season: May–Jun and Sep–Oct — winter fog and mud make the forest roads miserable
properties.tip: There is almost no fuel between Demirköy and Kırklareli, so fill up before you turn off, and download the map because there is no phone signal in the valleys.
properties.rev: Those who go describe genuine emptiness and good forest; the honest warnings are that there is nothing to eat, nowhere to stay outside Demirköy, and logging trucks own the roads on weekdays.
properties.onward: İstanbul (IST), then 2.5 h to Kırklareli and north on the Demirköy road; a car is essential

properties.name: Marmara Island
properties.desc: The Proconnesus of antiquity, source of the white-and-grey veined marble in half the Byzantine buildings of İstanbul. The quarries still work, and there are abandoned faces above Saraylar you can walk straight into. Beaches at Çınarlı and Asmalı, an interior of bare hills and dry-stone walls, and a fraction of Avşa's crowds.
properties.season: Jun–Sep — ferries thin out from October and cancel outright in bad weather
properties.tip: Saraylar's open-air marble museum, a field of ancient sarcophagi and column drums beside the harbour, is free and empty; the island bus meets the ferry and runs about three times a day.
properties.rev: Visitors like the quiet and the strange marble landscape, and warn that quarry dust and lorries dominate Saraylar, accommodation is basic, and getting between villages without a scooter is slow.
properties.onward: İstanbul Yenikapı fast ferry (about 4 h with island stops), or shorter crossings from Tekirdağ and Erdek

properties.name: Vize
properties.desc: A Thracian hill town with a Roman theatre excavated below the citadel and a 6th-century church, Little Hagia Sophia, still standing under its original dome and now used as a mosque. Bronze Age dolmens and burial mounds sit in the fields around. Almost nobody stops on the way to the Black Sea, which is the whole appeal.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — the plateau is windy and bleak in winter
properties.tip: The theatre is behind the municipality building and unfenced; if the church door is locked, ask at the tea house on the square and somebody will fetch the key.
properties.rev: Visitors are surprised by how intact the church is and how deserted the theatre feels; the complaints are erratic opening, no signage in any language and nowhere decent to eat.
properties.onward: İstanbul (IST), 2 h by road on the Saray highway; regular buses from Kırklareli and İstanbul Esenler

properties.name: Erdek
properties.desc: A Marmara resort at the neck of the Kapıdağ peninsula, with a plane-shaded promenade, a working fishing harbour and small islands offshore twenty minutes away by boat. Turkish families have come here for generations, the fish restaurants are cheap by Aegean standards, and the sunsets look straight down the gulf towards Bandırma.
properties.season: Jun–Sep — half-shut and grey from November to March
properties.tip: Take the day boat out to Zeytinli or Fener island rather than swimming from the town beach, which is crowded and not the best water on the peninsula.
properties.rev: Regulars praise the value and the boat trips; the recurring complaints are jellyfish in some Augusts, a town beach that gets murky, and holiday-block sprawl along the shore road.
properties.onward: İstanbul, then the fast ferry to Bandırma (about 2 h) and 20 min by dolmuş to Erdek

properties.name: Kapıdağ Peninsula
properties.desc: An island tied to the mainland by two sandbars, a thousand metres high in the middle and forested with chestnut and pine, ringed by a road that passes coves most drivers never stop at. Ocaklar and Narlı face west into the sunset; the northern side towards Ilhanköy is cliffs and empty water. From the ridge the Marmara looks like a lake.
properties.season: May–Jun and Sep–Oct for the loop drive, Jul–Aug for swimming
properties.tip: Drive the loop anticlockwise from Erdek so the sea stays on your right, and take the unsigned tracks down to the north-coast coves, which have no facilities and almost nobody on them.
properties.rev: Drivers and cyclists rate the loop and the empty north side highly; the warnings are potholed sections, no fuel outside Erdek, and coves that need a high car or a walk down.
properties.onward: İstanbul, fast ferry to Bandırma, then 20 min to Erdek where the peninsula road starts; a car or scooter is essential

properties.name: Cyzicus
properties.desc: One of the great cities of the Propontis, whose Temple of Hadrian Byzantine writers ranked among the wonders of the world. What is left is a field of tumbled marble, a vast amphitheatre split down the middle by a stream, and stretches of wall lost in the maquis. It is unfenced, unlabelled, usually deserted, and only recently back under excavation.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — by midsummer the site is chest-high in thistle
properties.tip: The amphitheatre is the piece worth finding, signposted off the Erdek road near Hamamlı; wear long trousers and boots because of the thorns and the ticks.
properties.rev: Ruin hunters find the scale astonishing and the solitude complete; everyone else reports no signage, no path, no shade and a real risk of walking past the main monument without noticing it.
properties.onward: İstanbul, fast ferry to Bandırma, then 15 km north on the Erdek road; the turnings are poorly signed, so use a map pin

properties.name: İğneada Floodplain Forests
properties.desc: Longoz: alder, ash and oak standing in seasonal freshwater between Black Sea dunes and the Strandja hills, one of very few floodplain forests left in Europe. Boardwalks run out over Mert and Erikli lakes, and in spring the water sits knee-deep among the trunks, loud with frogs and warblers. Bulgaria is seven kilometres north.
properties.season: Apr–Jun for flooded forest and birds, Sep–Oct for colour — mosquitoes are serious Jul–Aug
properties.tip: Bring repellent and boots, and use the Mert Lake boardwalk reached from the road south of İğneada village rather than the one by the main park sign.
properties.rev: Birders and photographers rate it very highly; others report mosquitoes in clouds, boardwalks in poor repair after winter, and a village with only a handful of basic pensions.
properties.onward: İstanbul (IST), then 3.5 h by road via Vize and Demirköy; buses reach Kırklareli and a dolmuş covers the rest

properties.name: Bird Paradise National Park (Lake Manyas)
properties.desc: A shallow lake on the migration corridor between Europe and Africa, where some 260 species have been recorded and Dalmatian pelicans breed in flooded willows. A short boardwalk leads to an observation tower above the colony. The park is small and the lake's health has swung with agricultural runoff, so set expectations before you arrive.
properties.season: Mar–May and Sep–Oct for migration — the pelicans are on nests from March
properties.tip: Bring your own binoculars, because the tower stands 200 m off the colony and the park lends none; early morning before the wind gets up is the only worthwhile hour.
properties.rev: Birders say the spring passage is genuinely good; the widespread complaints are a tiny walkable area, a tower too far from the birds, and water quality that has visibly declined.
properties.onward: İstanbul, fast ferry to Bandırma (about 2 h) then 20 min by road; Balıkesir Koca Seyit (EDO) is 1.5 h to the south

properties.name: Kıyıköy
properties.desc: A fishing village walled in by Byzantine ramparts on a headland between two river mouths on the Black Sea. Below the walls, the Aya Nikola monastery is carved entirely from the rock — nave, columns, baptistery, all of it — and usually empty. Small boats run up the Pabuçdere into forest that comes down to the waterline.
properties.season: Jun–Sep — the sea here is cold, and Nov–Mar is grey, wet and largely shut
properties.tip: The rock monastery sits at the end of a signposted path from the lower gate and is unlocked; go before the İstanbul day-trippers arrive around noon at weekends.
properties.rev: Weekenders like the monastery and the river trips and the cheap fish; the recurring complaints are basic pensions, litter on the beach in August and a sea too cold for many.
properties.onward: İstanbul (IST), 2.5 h by road via Saray; dolmuş from Vize a few times a day

properties.name: Gölyazı
properties.desc: An island village on Lake Uluabat joined to the shore by a causeway, built over ancient Apollonia — column drums do duty as doorsteps and a sarcophagus as a horse trough. Fishermen mend nets under a plane tree said to be 700 years old, and pelicans and herons work the reed beds a hundred metres off.
properties.season: Mar–May for pelicans and blossom, Sep–Oct for still water
properties.tip: A fisherman will take you out for an hour for the price of a modest lunch — arrange it at the causeway in the morning, not by phone.
properties.rev: Photographers rave about the light and the storks; others report a village that is visibly poor and half-abandoned, with litter on the shoreline and very little to eat beyond one or two fish shacks.
properties.onward: Bursa, then 40 km west on the İzmir road and a signposted turn at Uluabat; occasional dolmuş from Bursa's Nilüfer terminal

properties.name: Trilye (Zeytinbağı)
properties.desc: A Byzantine-Greek olive village 12 km west of Mudanya, its stone houses with wooden oriels dropping in terraces to a small harbour. The Fatih Mosque was the 8th-century church of Hagios Stephanos and still shows the brickwork; the roofless Taş Mektep schoolhouse stands above the lanes. Everything smells of olive oil, fig and woodsmoke.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — the November olive harvest is the moment to buy oil
properties.tip: Come on a weekday: on summer weekends Bursa empties into the two harbour restaurants and parking on the single lane down is hopeless.
properties.rev: Reviewers call it the prettiest thing on the south Marmara shore and then warn about weekend gridlock, restaurant prices that jumped once it was discovered, and steep unforgiving cobbles.
properties.onward: İstanbul fast ferry to Mudanya, then 20 min west by dolmuş; from Bursa it is 45 min by car

properties.name: Mudanya
properties.desc: Bursa's Marmara port, and the town where the armistice ending the Turkish War of Independence was signed in a seafront house that is now a museum, furnished as it was in 1922. Behind the promenade the old quarter is Greek-era stone and timber, gently restored. The promenade itself is a kilometre of fish tables facing the sunset.
properties.season: May–Jun and Sep–Oct — August fills every table with Bursa weekenders
properties.tip: The İstanbul fast ferry lands here rather than in Bursa; the connecting bus leaves from the terminal door and costs a fraction of the taxi everyone else takes.
properties.rev: People like it as a low-key ferry town with good fish and a genuinely interesting museum; the common complaints are limited swimming, weekend traffic and a seafront that gets loud after dark.
properties.onward: İstanbul Yenikapı fast ferry direct to Mudanya (about 2 h), then 30 min by bus to Bursa

properties.name: Theodosian Land Walls
properties.desc: Six and a half kilometres of fifth-century triple fortification from the Sea of Marmara to the Golden Horn: outer wall, inner wall of ninety-six towers, and a moat now planted with market gardens. Sections are restored, sections are rubble with fig trees growing out of them, and the ruined stretches are the ones worth walking.
properties.season: Apr–May and Oct — high summer means no shade and hard light on the brick
properties.tip: Walk the stretch from Silivrikapı north to Edirnekapı in the morning and stay outside the wall on the moat side; the inside is a building site of car repair yards.
properties.rev: Those who walk a full section find it the most atmospheric thing in the city; everyone warns that some stretches are unlit, dogs roam the moat, restoration quality is patchy and it is best not done alone after dark.
properties.onward: Istanbul Airport (IST) then M1 metro to Topkapı-Ulubatlı or the T4 tram to Edirnekapı; walk the wall in one direction and take a bus back

properties.name: Yedikule Fortress
properties.desc: Mehmed II bolted a five-towered Ottoman keep onto the Golden Gate of the Theodosian walls, creating a courtyard treasury and later a prison where an eighteen-year-old sultan was strangled. The marble Golden Gate, once faced in gold, is bricked up but still there. Reopened after restoration with walkways along the ramparts.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — the courtyard is bare and hot in midsummer
properties.tip: Walk out of the north gate afterwards to the Yedikule bostans, the walled market gardens that have grown lettuce in the same soil since Byzantine times.
properties.rev: Visitors like the emptiness and the rampart views over the Marmara, while noting the restoration has been over-tidy, the labelling is minimal and the surrounding district gives little reason to linger.
properties.entry: Small fee — check locally · usually covered by Museum Pass Türkiye
properties.onward: Istanbul Airport (IST) then Marmaray suburban rail to Kazlıçeşme and a 10-min walk, or the T1 tram to Zeytinburnu and a short taxi

properties.name: Samatya
properties.desc: A Marmara-shore quarter of Armenian and Greek descent that tourists almost never reach, built around a square of meyhanes where the meze trolley still comes to the table and the rakı is cheap. Surp Kevork church anchors one side; behind it, low houses, a Sunday fish market, and the Byzantine Studios monastery ruin ten minutes west.
properties.season: Year-round; Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct for square tables outdoors
properties.tip: Come on a Friday or Saturday evening when the meyhane square fills and a fasıl band works the tables — midweek it is half asleep.
properties.rev: Those who find it call it the last unposed neighbourhood on the peninsula, though the meyhanes are hit and miss, English is rare and the Studios ruin is often locked behind its fence.
properties.onward: Istanbul Airport (IST) then Marmaray suburban rail to Kocamustafapaşa, which is a five-minute walk from the square

properties.name: Eyüp Sultan Mosque
properties.desc: The holiest Ottoman site in the city, built over the grave of the Prophet's standard-bearer who died besieging Constantinople. The courtyard has plane trees, storks of pilgrims in white, and boys in sequinned circumcision costume being photographed. The tomb chamber opposite is lined in İznik blue and the queue to it never really stops.
properties.season: Year-round; Ramadan evenings are extraordinary but jammed
properties.tip: Come on a weekday morning rather than a Friday, and buy a paper cone of pilgrim sweets from the stalls on the approach — the boiled candy shops here are the original ones.
properties.rev: Visitors call the atmosphere the most genuinely religious in Istanbul and worth the trip up the Horn, while noting the crush at the tomb, strict dress enforcement and a commercial approach street thick with stalls.
properties.entry: Free · conservative dress expected, this is a pilgrimage site
properties.onward: Istanbul Airport (IST) then M7 metro to Eyüpsultan, or the Golden Horn ferry from Eminönü straight to Eyüp pier

properties.name: Pierre Loti Hill
properties.desc: A café terrace at the top of the Eyüp cemetery, looking straight down the Golden Horn with the water bending away towards Galata. The walk up through the graveyard is the real attraction: cypresses, turbaned Ottoman headstones tilting at all angles, cats, and almost total silence a few minutes above a busy shrine.
properties.season: Sep–Nov for clear air; hazy and hot Jul–Aug, muddy Jan–Feb
properties.tip: Walk up through the cemetery and take the cable car down, not the other way round — and skip the terrace café, which trades on the view.
properties.rev: The view earns the trip and the cemetery walk surprises people, but the café is widely called overpriced and mediocre, the terrace is packed at weekends and the cable car queue can run past thirty minutes.
properties.entry: Free · cable car a few lira each way
properties.onward: Istanbul Airport (IST) then M7 metro to Eyüpsultan, or the Golden Horn ferry from Eminönü to Eyüp and the TF2 cable car

properties.name: Chora Church (Kariye Mosque)
properties.desc: The finest late-Byzantine mosaics anywhere, packed into two small narthexes: the life of the Virgin, the Journey to Bethlehem, faces with real weight and modelling. The side chapel holds the Anastasis fresco, Christ hauling Adam and Eve out of their tombs by the wrists. It reopened as a working mosque in 2024 after long restoration.
properties.season: Year-round — closed Wednesdays in some seasons; check before travelling out
properties.tip: The mosaic narthexes stay visible but the nave is now carpeted and screened, so go mid-morning on a weekday and give the Anastasis chapel at the south end the time it deserves.
properties.rev: The mosaics are almost universally called the best in the city, but visitors report confusion over the post-2024 mosque arrangement, curtains covering part of the nave, restricted hours around prayers and a long ride out to Edirnekapı for a small building.
properties.entry: ≈€20 for foreign visitors · arrangements changed with the 2024 reopening, check on the day
properties.onward: Istanbul Airport (IST) then M2 to Vezneciler and bus 87, or the T4 tram to Edirnekapı and a 10-min walk downhill

properties.name: Balat
properties.desc: The old Jewish quarter on the Golden Horn, a grid of steep lanes with painted timber houses, the Ahrida Synagogue with its boat-shaped bimah, and old-iron shops that have become antique cafés. Kiremit Caddesi and Vodina Caddesi carry the colour; one street back it is still laundry lines and men playing okey.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct; Sunday mornings are quietest
properties.tip: The synagogues need advance permission through the Chief Rabbinate, so arrange that days ahead — turning up at the door will not get you in.
properties.rev: Charming and photogenic by consensus, but locals and visitors alike now complain about influencer queues at the painted-stair corner, café prices out of step with the neighbourhood, and residents tired of cameras.
properties.entry: Free · synagogue visits by prior arrangement only
properties.onward: Istanbul Airport (IST) then metro to Haliç and bus, or the Golden Horn ferry from Eminönü to Ayvansaray/Balat pier

properties.name: Mağlova Aqueduct
properties.desc: Sinan's finest piece of engineering, a two-tier limestone aqueduct 257 metres long striding across the Alibey valley north of the city, built in the 1560s to carry Belgrad Forest water to Istanbul. It stands almost alone in scrubland above a reservoir, with buttresses shaped like ships' prows to split the current when the valley floods.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct; the track in is impassable mud after heavy rain
properties.tip: The final approach is an unsurfaced track off the Cebeci road and there is no sign — set the coordinates before you leave, and do not attempt it in a low car after rain.
properties.rev: Those who find it call it the most impressive Ottoman structure nobody visits; the complaints are all about access — no public transport, an unmarked dirt track, rubbish dumped at the approach and rising reservoir water at times.
properties.onward: Istanbul Airport (IST) then a hire car; it is roughly 25 km north-west of the centre via Cebeci, with the last 2 km on a rough track

properties.name: Bulgarian St Stephen Church
properties.desc: A neo-Gothic church cast entirely in iron in Vienna in 1893, shipped down the Danube and Black Sea in sections and bolted together on the Golden Horn shore. Every pilaster, gallery and rosette is metal, painted to look like stone. Restored in 2018, it now gleams cream and gold in a small waterside garden.
properties.season: Year-round; morning light comes off the water onto the façade
properties.tip: Rap on the caretaker's door if the church looks shut — it usually opens on request outside services, and the ironwork detail only reads from inside the galleries.
properties.rev: People are consistently surprised by how convincing the fake stone is and how empty the place is, though the interior is small, opening hours are erratic and the traffic on the shore road spoils the setting.
properties.onward: Istanbul Airport (IST) then metro to Haliç and a bus along the shore, or the Golden Horn ferry to Fener pier and a two-minute walk

properties.name: Belgrad Forest
properties.desc: Five thousand hectares of oak and beech north of the city that supplied Istanbul's water for four centuries, still holding Ottoman reservoirs, dams and stone aqueducts among the trees. Neşetsuyu and Bentler have marked trails and running loops; on autumn mornings mist sits between the trunks and the city is completely gone.
properties.season: Apr–Jun for green and Oct–Nov for colour; winter is muddy but atmospheric
properties.tip: Enter at Neşetsuyu on a weekday for the quiet trails; the Bentler entrance on a Sunday is a mangal picnic ground with smoke and speakers, not a forest walk.
properties.rev: Istanbullus treat it as the city's lung and praise the trails, while complaining about weekend barbecue crowds, litter around the picnic areas, and entrance fees per person and per car that have risen sharply.
properties.entry: Small entrance fee per person and per car — check locally · Arboretum ticketed separately
properties.onward: Istanbul Airport (IST) then M11 to Hacıosman and bus 42 to Bahçeköy; a car is much easier for reaching the far entrances

properties.name: Fener
properties.desc: Balat's Greek neighbour, dominated by the red-brick Phanar Greek College standing on the hill like a Victorian asylum. Below it, the Ecumenical Patriarchate keeps a courtyard, a modest cathedral and a gate welded shut since a patriarch was hanged from it in 1821. Steep cobbled lanes, a few surviving Greek families, and cats everywhere.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct; the lanes are treacherous in winter rain
properties.tip: Inside the Patriarchate church, look for the column of the flagellation and the mosaic-covered patriarchal throne — and note the sealed Orta Kapı as you leave.
properties.rev: Visitors find the Patriarchate quietly moving and the hill walk rewarding, while complaining that the Greek College cannot be entered, the streets are steep and poorly lit, and several churches keep unpredictable hours.
properties.entry: Free · Patriarchate open most mornings, modest dress
properties.onward: Istanbul Airport (IST) then metro to Haliç and a short bus, or the Golden Horn ferry from Eminönü to Fener pier

properties.name: Zeyrek Mosque (Pantokrator Monastery)
properties.desc: Three twelfth-century Byzantine churches joined into one brick mass, once the imperial monastery of the Pantokrator and burial place of the Comneni. Restoration finished in 2023 revealed the opus sectile floor of coloured marble under the south church. Around it, the last streets of leaning Ottoman timber houses in Fatih.
properties.season: Year-round — the sloping lanes are slippery in winter rain
properties.tip: Ask the caretaker to lift the protective boarding over the marble floor of the south church; he usually will if you come outside prayer times and ask politely.
properties.rev: Visitors who make the climb call it the best Byzantine building nobody visits, but note the confusing opening hours, the fenced-off north church and a neighbourhood that feels shabby and unsignposted.
properties.entry: Free · working mosque, closed to visitors around prayer times
properties.onward: Istanbul Airport (IST) then M2 metro to Vezneciler and a 15-min walk down through Zeyrek, or the Golden Horn ferry to Unkapanı and a steep climb

properties.name: The Golden Horn
properties.desc: A seven-kilometre drowned valley cutting into the European side, once the imperial harbour, then an industrial sewer, now cleaned enough that cormorants fish it. Small ferries thread from Eminönü up to Eyüp past shipyards, the iron Bulgarian church, and the wooden houses of Balat, with the Süleymaniye on the ridge above.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — winter southerlies make the small ferries choppy
properties.tip: Take the Haliç ferry line rather than a tour boat: it costs a couple of lira with an İstanbulkart, stops where you actually want to get off, and locals use it.
properties.rev: People rate the cheap ferry as the best value in the city, though the water still smells in still August weather, the shoreline path is broken by roads, and the Hasköy and Kasımpaşa banks remain scruffy.
properties.entry: Free · ferry fare a few lira with an İstanbulkart
properties.onward: Istanbul Airport (IST) then metro to Haliç or Eminönü; the Haliç ferry line runs roughly hourly from Eminönü

properties.name: Süleymaniye Mosque
properties.desc: Sinan's best building in the city, sitting on the third hill with a terrace that drops straight to the Golden Horn. Inside it is plain by Ottoman standards — white walls, red-and-white voussoirs, one band of İznik around the mihrab — and it works better for that. The tombs of Süleyman and Roxelana stand in the garden behind.
properties.season: Year-round; late afternoon in Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct for the terrace light
properties.tip: Come out of the north gate to the terrace wall at sunset, then eat kuru fasulye at one of the bean shops on Şifahane Sokak behind the complex.
properties.rev: Regularly called more moving than the Blue Mosque and much less crowded; complaints are about the steep cobbled approach, closures at prayer times and student crowds from the university filling the terrace at dusk.
properties.onward: Istanbul Airport (IST) then metro to Vezneciler (M2) and a 10-min walk uphill, or the T1 tram to Eminönü and a stiff climb

properties.name: Grand Bazaar
properties.desc: Sixty-one covered streets and around four thousand shops under painted vaults, laid out by trade since the fifteenth century. The tourist arteries sell the same lamps and evil eyes; two turns off them you find the gold casters, the bead sellers, and the İç Bedesten, the oldest stone core, where antique dealers work.
properties.season: Year-round · closed Sundays and public holidays
properties.tip: Go in through the Nuruosmaniye gate and head straight to the İç Bedesten, then out to the Sahaflar book market by the Beyazıt gate — that route skips most of the hustle.
properties.rev: Most enjoy an hour of it and find the architecture better than the goods; the persistent complaints are aggressive touting, tourist pricing on everything from carpets to tea, and getting lost with no useful signage.
properties.onward: Istanbul Airport (IST) then metro and the T1 tram to Beyazıt-Kapalıçarşı or Çemberlitaş, both gates a minute away

properties.name: Rüstem Pasha Mosque
properties.desc: Hidden above the hardware shops of the Eminönü bazaar streets and reached by an unmarked stair, this small Sinan mosque carries the densest İznik tilework in Istanbul — tomato-red tulips and carnations covering the piers, the mihrab wall and even the outer porch. The 2021 restoration brought the reds back to full strength.
properties.season: Year-round; late morning light on the porch tiles is best
properties.tip: The entrance is a dark doorway between shops on Hasırcılar Caddesi with a small brass plate — look for the stair, not for a courtyard.
properties.rev: Repeatedly called the best tiles in Turkey outside a museum, with the usual caveats: hard to find, tiny inside, closed at prayer times and increasingly full of photographers since it reopened.
properties.onward: Istanbul Airport (IST) then metro and T1 tram to Eminönü; it is three minutes uphill behind the Spice Bazaar

properties.name: Spice Bazaar and Eminönü
properties.desc: An L-shaped seventeenth-century hall that smells of cumin and dried rose, built to fund the New Mosque next door. The real market is outside it: the streets behind sell cheese, olives, coffee roasted at Kurukahveci Mehmet Efendi, live pigeons and fishing tackle, and prices there are half what they are inside.
properties.season: Year-round; mornings before eleven for the food streets
properties.tip: Buy your saffron and pistachios in the outer streets, not the covered hall, and queue at Mehmet Efendi on the corner for coffee ground while you wait.
properties.rev: Loved for the smell and the food streets around it, criticised for hard-sell inside the hall, inflated prices on saffron and Turkish delight, and a crush at the doors that makes pickpocketing a genuine risk.
properties.onward: Istanbul Airport (IST) then metro and the T1 tram to Eminönü, or any Bosphorus ferry to Eminönü pier

properties.name: Karaköy
properties.desc: The old Genoese port quarter under Galata, now the best eating in the city: chandlers and ship-fitters on one street, third-wave coffee and mezes on the next. Karaköy Güllüoğlu still cuts baklava behind glass at the ferry end, and the fish restaurants under the bridge grill hamsi in winter.
properties.season: Year-round; May–Jun and Sep–Oct for outdoor tables
properties.tip: Eat pistachio baklava standing at Güllüoğlu's counter, then take the Tünel — the 1875 funicular, second-oldest underground railway in the world — up to Beyoğlu instead of walking the hill.
properties.rev: Widely called the best place to eat in Istanbul, though regulars complain gentrification has pushed prices to European levels, the waterfront is a permanent construction site and the cruise terminal has changed the mood.
properties.onward: Istanbul Airport (IST) then M11+M2 to Şişhane and downhill, or any ferry to Karaköy pier; the T1 tram stops on the bridge

properties.name: Hippodrome of Constantinople
properties.desc: A long park where a chariot track used to be, with three survivors standing in a line down the old spine: an Egyptian obelisk of Thutmose III on a carved Byzantine base, the bronze Serpent Column looted from Delphi, and a stripped masonry pillar. The ground level of the track sits several metres below the modern paving.
properties.season: Year-round — best in spring evenings when locals take over the benches
properties.tip: Walk down to the obelisk base and read the relief of Theodosius watching the races; it shows the monument being raised, and almost nobody stops for it.
properties.rev: People are often underwhelmed until they read the base reliefs, and complaints run to carpet-shop touts working the square, no shade and no explanatory signage worth the name.
properties.onward: Istanbul Airport (IST) then M11+M2 and the T1 tram to Sultanahmet, which stops at the north end of the square

properties.name: Blue Mosque (Sultan Ahmed Mosque)
properties.desc: Six minarets, a cascade of half-domes, and inside more than twenty thousand İznik tiles that read blue-green only in strong light. The courtyard is the better half of the building: a rectangle of grey stone and pigeons with the dome rising behind the arcade. It is a working mosque, closed to visitors five times a day.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — the courtyard is a furnace in August afternoons
properties.tip: Go about 30 minutes after the dawn or the late-evening prayer, when the tour groups are absent and the chandeliers are lit low over the carpet.
properties.rev: Visitors love the courtyard and the free entry, then note that the tourist rope keeps you at the back third of the hall, that the interior is dimmer than the photographs suggest, and that touts on the approach are relentless.
properties.entry: Free · modest dress required, headscarves lent at the door
properties.onward: Istanbul Airport (IST) then M11+M2 and the T1 tram to Sultanahmet; the mosque is a two-minute walk from the stop

properties.name: Basilica Cistern
properties.desc: Three hundred and thirty-six columns in shallow water under the street, cool and echoing even in August. Two Medusa heads reused as column bases sit in the far corner, one sideways, one upside down, for reasons nobody has settled. The 2022 restoration added coloured lighting and contemporary sculptures that divide opinion sharply.
properties.season: Year-round — the single reliable cool refuge in July and August
properties.tip: Book the first slot of the day online; from mid-morning the walkways are single file and the reflections are ruined by phone torches.
properties.rev: Everyone agrees the space is remarkable and cool; complaints are consistent about the new coloured lighting and installed artworks, the queue outside, and a foreigner price that has roughly tripled since 2021.
properties.entry: ≈€25–30 day ticket, night ticket dearer · not covered by the Museum Pass
properties.onward: Istanbul Airport (IST) then metro and the T1 tram to Sultanahmet; the entrance is 100 m north of Hagia Sophia

properties.name: Hagia Sophia
properties.desc: The dome floats on forty windows and the light coming through them is the whole point; nothing built for another nine hundred years came close to the span. Since it returned to use as a mosque the ground floor is carpeted and the Deesis mosaic is seen from the upper gallery, reached by a stone ramp worn into grooves.
properties.season: Nov–Mar for the light and the short queues — May and September mean two-hour lines
properties.tip: Foreigners now enter through the north side and go straight up to the gallery; the 09:00 opening buys you twenty quiet minutes before the tour groups reach the ramp.
properties.rev: Nearly everyone calls the interior overwhelming, then complains that the carpet and the ground-floor screens cut off the great floor, that the audio guide is compulsory in the foreigner ticket, and that the queue outside has no shade.
properties.entry: ≈€25 for foreign visitors, upper gallery route · not covered by the Museum Pass
properties.onward: Istanbul Airport (IST) then M11+M2+T1 tram, or Sabiha Gökçen (SAW) then the ferry from Kadıköy to Eminönü and one tram stop

properties.name: Topkapı Palace
properties.desc: Not one building but four courtyards that get progressively quieter, ending at a marble terrace looking down on the Bosphorus where the sultans sat. The Harem is a separate warren of tiled rooms and cold corridors. The treasury holds the Topkapı dagger and an eighty-six carat diamond, and the queue for them moves slowly.
properties.season: Apr–May and Oct — closed Tuesdays; July courtyards have almost no shade
properties.tip: Buy the Harem supplement and do the Harem first thing, before the coaches arrive around 10:30 and turn its narrow corridors into a shuffle.
properties.rev: Most agree the terrace views and the Harem justify the day, while complaints centre on the treasury bottleneck, the sharply raised foreigner price, sections shut for restoration without warning, and thin labelling in English.
properties.entry: ≈€45 including the Harem · covered by Museum Pass Türkiye · closed Tuesdays
properties.onward: Istanbul Airport (IST) then metro and the T1 tram to Gülhane or Sultanahmet; the Gülhane gate is the quieter entrance

properties.name: Dolmabahçe Palace
properties.desc: Six hundred metres of white marble along the Bosphorus, built in the 1850s when the empire could not afford it. The ceremonial hall carries a four-and-a-half-tonne Bohemian chandelier under a thirty-six-metre dome, and there is a crystal staircase with banisters of Baccarat glass. Atatürk died here; every clock reads 09:05.
properties.season: Year-round · closed Mondays; the seaside garden is best in May
properties.tip: Tickets are timed and the palace often sells out by noon in summer — book online, and take the Harem supplement only if you have two hours, since the tour is walked at a set pace.
properties.rev: Impressive to almost everyone and gaudy to some, with steady complaints about compulsory guided groups moved along briskly, no photography inside, long queues at the gate and a price that does not include the Harem.
properties.entry: ≈€40 combined Selamlık and Harem · National Palaces ticket, not on the Museum Pass · closed Mondays
properties.onward: Istanbul Airport (IST) then M11+M2 to Şişhane and the T1 tram to Kabataş, a five-minute walk along the shore

properties.name: Karacaahmet Cemetery
properties.desc: One of the largest Islamic burial grounds in the world, seven hundred years old and covering more than seven hundred acres of Üsküdar under black cypresses. The older sections have marble headstones carved with turbans that indicate the dead man's rank, and women's stones cut with flowers. Traffic noise disappears fifty metres in.
properties.season: Year-round; Oct–Nov light through the cypresses is the best of it
properties.tip: Enter from the Nuh Kuyusu gate on the south side and head for the oldest section near the Miskinler tekke, where the turbaned stones stand thickest.
properties.rev: Those who go find it silent and extraordinary, though there are no maps or paths marked, funerals are frequent and visitors are asked to be discreet, and much of the modern part is ordinary municipal cemetery.
properties.entry: Free · a working cemetery, dress and behave accordingly
properties.onward: Sabiha Gökçen (SAW) then M4 to Üsküdar; the cemetery starts a 10-minute walk inland from the ferry pier

properties.name: Kuzguncuk
properties.desc: One street, İcadiye Caddesi, running up a valley from the Bosphorus, lined with painted wooden houses in ochre, lilac and green. A mosque and a synagogue stand on the same corner and a Greek and an Armenian church a hundred metres apart. Halfway up there is a market garden that residents fought developers to keep.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — spring wisteria on the house fronts
properties.tip: Come on a weekday morning; on Sunday the one street is a slow parade of photo shoots and the breakfast places have hour-long waits.
properties.rev: Charming and genuinely lived-in by most accounts, though weekend crowds, café prices well above the Asian-side average and residents' visible irritation at cameras come up again and again.
properties.onward: Sabiha Gökçen (SAW) then M4 to Üsküdar and bus 15 north, or a ferry to Üsküdar and a 20-min walk along the shore

properties.name: Kadıköy
properties.desc: The Asian side's centre and where Istanbul actually eats and drinks. The fish market grid around Güneşlibahçe Sokak has pickle shops, pastırma counters and a hundred meyhane tables; Moda a few streets on is bookshops, tea gardens on the seawall and a coast path where the whole neighbourhood walks at dusk.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — Moda's seafront is bleak in a February northerly
properties.tip: Cross by the Eminönü–Kadıköy ferry rather than the Marmaray tunnel, sit on the right for the Topkapı profile, and eat at the market before eight when it fills.
properties.rev: Repeat visitors say this is where they would live, but note that the market streets are shoulder-to-shoulder on weekend evenings, prices have climbed steeply, and the bar zone gets loud until very late.
properties.onward: Sabiha Gökçen (SAW) then the M4 metro straight to Kadıköy; from the European side take the ferry from Eminönü or Karaköy

properties.name: Kilyos
properties.desc: The European side's Black Sea beach, thirty-five kilometres north of the city past Sarıyer: a broad arc of grey-gold sand with real waves, backed by dunes and beach clubs that run day beds, music and volleyball through the summer. A Genoese tower stands on the hill behind and the water is noticeably colder than the Marmara.
properties.season: Jun–early Sep only; out of season the clubs shut and the wind is raw
properties.tip: The undertow here kills people every summer — stay between the flags at a lifeguarded club, and go on a weekday because Saturday turns the road from Sarıyer into a car park.
properties.rev: Convenient and genuinely sandy for a city beach, but reviews are consistent about strong rip currents, club entry fees that feel steep for what you get, loud music, and litter after busy weekends.
properties.entry: Beach club day entry roughly ₺500–1500 (≈€11–33) depending on the club and the day
properties.onward: Istanbul Airport (IST) then M11 to Hacıosman and bus 151 from Sarıyer, about 40 minutes; parking at the clubs in summer is difficult

properties.name: Beylerbeyi Palace
properties.desc: The sultans' summer place on the Asian shore, directly under the first Bosphorus bridge, with a marble pool and fountain inside the entrance hall to cool the air. Empress Eugénie stayed and copied its windows for the Tuileries. Outside, two seaside kiosks and a terrace where the current runs fast and green past the wall.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct · closed Mondays
properties.tip: Combine it with a walk south along the shore into Beylerbeyi village for tea by the mosque; the ferry pier there is a working local one, not a tourist stop.
properties.rev: Far quieter than Dolmabahçe and rated better value, though visits are guided and brisk, photography is restricted, and the bridge roaring overhead is louder than the photographs prepare you for.
properties.entry: ≈€15 · National Palaces ticket, not on the Museum Pass · closed Mondays
properties.onward: Sabiha Gökçen (SAW) then M4 to Üsküdar and bus 15 along the shore, or a ferry to Üsküdar and a 10-min taxi

properties.name: Arnavutköy
properties.desc: A row of nineteenth-century timber houses standing directly in the water on the European shore, bay windows overhanging the current. Behind them a couple of steep streets, an Ottoman-Greek church, and fish restaurants on the Akıntı Burnu point where the Bosphorus runs hardest. Bebek's expensive cafés are a fifteen-minute walk south.
properties.season: May–Jun and Sep–Oct; the point is windswept from November
properties.tip: Walk the shore path from Bebek to Arnavutköy at dusk and eat at one of the small back-street fish places rather than the waterfront ones charging for the view.
properties.rev: Consistently called the prettiest street of wooden houses left on the Bosphorus, with the caveats that the coast road runs right behind them, parking is impossible and the waterfront restaurants are priced for Bebek.
properties.onward: Istanbul Airport (IST) then M11+M2 to Levent and bus down to the shore, or the T1 tram to Kabataş and bus 22/25E along the Bosphorus

properties.name: Muradiye Complex
properties.desc: Twelve small tombs in a walled garden of cypress and rose, holding the sultans, princes and mothers who lost Ottoman succession fights — including Cem Sultan, who died in Italian exile. Each türbe is different inside: painted vaults, İznik panels, bare whitewash. It is the quietest important place in Bursa and almost nobody is in it.
properties.season: Apr–Jun for the garden, Oct for the plane leaves
properties.tip: One caretaker unlocks the tombs in rotation with a big key ring; walk the loop slowly and point, and he will open whichever ones you ask for.
properties.rev: Visitors describe it as the calmest hour they spent in Bursa; the recurring complaints are that several tombs stay locked and there is almost no English labelling.
properties.onward: Bursa city centre, then a 15-min walk west from Ulu Cami or a short taxi

properties.name: Kınalıada
properties.desc: The nearest island, forty minutes out, red-earthed and almost treeless where the others are pine — the name means henna island, from the iron in the rock. Largely Armenian in population, with a modern church shaped like a wedge and a shoreline of flat rocks that locals swim from all summer. Byzantine emperors were exiled here.
properties.season: Jun–Sep for swimming; bare and windswept the rest of the year
properties.tip: It is the fastest island escape from the city for a swim after work — the rock platforms on the western shore beyond the mosque are free, unlike the beach clubs by the pier.
properties.rev: Praised as the quickest way out of Istanbul into the sea, but honestly reported as the plainest island: little shade, no forest, limited food, and beach clubs that charge disproportionately for a sunbed.
properties.entry: Free · ferry a few lira with an İstanbulkart · beach clubs charge separately
properties.onward: Sabiha Gökçen (SAW) then M4 to Bostancı and the island ferry; from Europe the Kabataş boat reaches it first

properties.name: Rumeli Hisarı
properties.desc: Mehmed II built this fortress in four months in 1452 at the narrowest point of the strait to cut Constantinople off from the Black Sea. Three huge towers and a curtain wall run straight up a steep slope, so the walk inside is all steps. Below it, a village of fish restaurants and a cemetery of Ottoman headstones.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — the slope inside is punishing in July heat
properties.tip: Climb the north tower for the shot straight down the Bosphorus at the Fatih bridge, then eat waffles or fish in the village below rather than inside the tourist strip.
properties.rev: The views are almost universally praised, but the site is steep with uneven steps and no railings in places, parts are periodically closed for restoration, and there is little shade or interpretation inside.
properties.entry: ≈€10 · covered by Museum Pass Türkiye · closed Wednesdays in some seasons
properties.onward: Istanbul Airport (IST) then M11+M2 to Levent and bus, or bus 25E/22 up the Bosphorus shore road from Kabataş

properties.name: Grand Mosque of Bursa
properties.desc: Twenty domes on twelve piers, paid for out of the ransom of a battle and finished in 1399. A fountain still runs under the open oculus in the middle of the prayer hall, and the walls carry 192 panels of monumental calligraphy painted straight onto plaster. It is dim, cool and unusually unfussy for an imperial mosque.
properties.season: Year-round — coldest and emptiest on January mornings
properties.tip: Come between prayers on a weekday and sit by the şadırvan; the calligraphy reads best from the side galleries under the oculus.
properties.rev: Almost everyone finds the fountain-inside-a-mosque arrangement startling and the atmosphere better than İstanbul's big mosques; the complaint is the shoe-rack scrum and tour groups talking over prayers.
properties.onward: İstanbul Sabiha Gökçen (SAW) then 2.5 h by road, or the Mudanya fast ferry; it is in the middle of Bursa's pedestrian centre

properties.name: Burgazada
properties.desc: The small island with the strongest Greek residue and the smallest crowd: one hill, one loop road, a domed church at the top and the house of the writer Sait Faik kept exactly as he left it in 1954, down to his fishing tackle. Kalpazankaya on the far shore is a rock cove with a fish restaurant on the terrace above it.
properties.season: Jun–Sep to swim; May and Oct for the loop walk without heat
properties.tip: Walk the ninety minutes round to Kalpazankaya for a late lunch and the sunset over the Marmara, then take the last ferry back rather than the crowded afternoon boats.
properties.rev: Visitors call it the island to choose if you want quiet, with the trade-offs that there is almost nothing to do beyond walking and swimming, few places to eat, and ferry connections are sparser than to the bigger islands.
properties.entry: Free · museum free · ferry a few lira with an İstanbulkart
properties.onward: Sabiha Gökçen (SAW) then M4 to Bostancı and the island ferry; Burgazada is the second stop from the mainland

properties.name: Çengelköy
properties.desc: An Asian-shore village known for its small ridged cucumbers and for the plane tree at Çınaraltı, under which the tea garden has served the same glass of tea for a century. The shore has yalıs, a naval school, and a promenade where families walk with the Bosphorus current a metre away. Beylerbeyi is the next stop south.
properties.season: May–Jun and Sep–Oct; the tea garden works year-round with braziers
properties.tip: Order a Turkish breakfast at Çınaraltı and ask for the local cucumbers with it, then walk the shore north towards Kuleli for the best view of the Rumeli side.
properties.rev: Locals rate the breakfast and the shore walk highly; visitors report weekend queues at Çınaraltı, patchy service, and a coast road that carries a lot of traffic behind the promenade.
properties.onward: Sabiha Gökçen (SAW) then M4 to Üsküdar and bus 15, or the Beşiktaş–Çengelköy ferry which is the pleasant way in

properties.name: Bursa
properties.desc: Ottoman capital before Edirne and İstanbul, stacked on the north slope of Uludağ so every street either climbs or falls. The Hanlar district around Koza Han is still a working silk and textile market, with tea trays carried between mulberry trees in the courtyard. Eat İskender kebab where it was invented, then take the cable car out of the haze.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — the basin traps haze in high summer and drizzle from December
properties.tip: Koza Han's upstairs galleries are where the actual silk sellers work; the ground-floor cafés are for coach parties.
properties.rev: Visitors rate the mosques, the silk hans and the food higher than they expected, then complain about traffic, concrete sprawl and how far apart the good bits are.
properties.entry: Free to walk; mosques free, city museums ≈₺150 (≈€4)
properties.onward: Bursa Yenişehir (YEI) is tiny; most arrive from İstanbul Sabiha Gökçen (SAW) by road, or by fast ferry to Mudanya then 30 min to the centre

properties.name: Küçüksu Pavilion
properties.desc: A small rococo hunting lodge on the Asian shore between two streams, all curls and shells in white marble, with a double staircase running down to a landing stage on the water. Two rooms up, two down — it was built for afternoons, not for living. The meadow behind it was the Ottoman picnic ground called the Sweet Waters of Asia.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct · closed Mondays
properties.tip: Walk five minutes north to the Küçüksu fountain of Mihrişah Sultan and then on to Anadoluhisarı — the whole shore stretch takes half an hour and hardly anyone does it.
properties.rev: Visitors like the scale and the emptiness and call it a good hour, but note it is genuinely small for the ticket, awkward to reach without a car, and the garden is fenced off from the shore road.
properties.entry: ≈€8 · National Palaces ticket, not on the Museum Pass · closed Mondays
properties.onward: Sabiha Gökçen (SAW) then M4 to Üsküdar and bus 15 up the Asian shore; by car, park at Anadoluhisarı and walk

properties.name: Anadolu Hisarı
properties.desc: The older, smaller fortress on the Asian bank, thrown up by Bayezid I in the 1390s and now half-swallowed by a village of wooden houses at the mouth of the Göksu stream. You cannot go in, but the walls run straight through the neighbourhood with washing lines beside them and rowing boats tied under the keep.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct; the stream mouth is best in morning light
properties.tip: Walk under the Fatih bridge from Küçüksu, then take a rowing boat up the Göksu stream from the little landing — it is the old Sweet Waters excursion and costs almost nothing.
properties.rev: People like stumbling on a fourteenth-century castle inside a working village, though the fortress interior has been closed for years, there is no signage, and traffic on the shore road makes photographing it awkward.
properties.entry: Free · fortress interior closed, viewed from outside
properties.onward: Sabiha Gökçen (SAW) then M4 to Üsküdar and bus 15 north, or the Kandilli ferry and a 20-minute shore walk

properties.name: Çamlıca Hill
properties.desc: At 268 metres the highest point in the city, a pine-topped hill on the Asian side with the entire Bosphorus laid out beneath it — three bridges, the Golden Horn, the old peninsula's domes, and the Marmara with the islands beyond. An Ottoman-style tea garden sits under the pines; the vast new mosque occupies the next summit south.
properties.season: Sep–Nov and Mar–May for clear air; summer haze flattens the view
properties.tip: Go two hours before sunset on a day after rain, when the air is washed clean and you can see the islands — and use the Küçük Çamlıca hill next door if the main terrace is full.
properties.rev: The panorama is agreed to be the best in the city, but the hill is often hazy, the tea garden gets very crowded at weekends, the TV masts intrude on photographs and there is no public transport to the summit.
properties.onward: Sabiha Gökçen (SAW) then M5 metro to Bulgurlu and a 15-min uphill walk or short taxi; by car, park below the tea garden

properties.name: Green Mosque and Green Tomb
properties.desc: Mehmed I's mosque and tomb face each other across a lane on the slope above the city. The tomb is sheathed outside in turquoise tile and inside in cuerda seca panels so deep they look wet. The mosque hides a tiled sultan's loge above the entrance that most visitors walk under without ever looking up.
properties.season: Year-round — spring light through the tomb's stained glass is the best of it
properties.tip: Ask the caretaker about the hünkâr mahfili upstairs in the mosque; the finest tilework in Bursa is behind that small door.
properties.rev: Consistently called the best tilework anyone sees outside Topkapı, with grumbles about the souvenir arcade crowding the tomb terrace and shifting opening hours at the museum.
properties.entry: Free (mosque and tomb); museum in the medrese ≈₺100 (≈€3)
properties.onward: Bursa city centre, then the T1 tram to Yeşil or a 10-min taxi uphill

properties.name: The Bosphorus Ferry
properties.desc: The city's best sightseeing is a commuter boat. The full Şehir Hatları run goes from Eminönü to Anadolu Kavağı in about ninety minutes, past Dolmabahçe, the two fortresses, wooden yalı mansions on both banks and under three bridges, with tea sold from a tray and gulls taking simit out of passengers' hands.
properties.season: May–Jun and Sep–Oct; winter crossings are cold and wet on deck but half empty
properties.tip: Take the long tour outbound and come back on the short hop or a bus, or you lose three hours; sit on the right going up for the European yalıs.
properties.rev: Almost everyone rates it the best value in Istanbul, with complaints about deck seats gone twenty minutes before departure, a rushed and touristy lunch stop at the top, and private tour boats overselling the same route.
properties.entry: ≈€8 for the full Şehir Hatları round trip · short hops a few lira with an İstanbulkart
properties.onward: Istanbul Airport (IST) then metro and T1 tram to Eminönü; the long Bosphorus boat leaves from the Boğaz İskelesi pier

properties.name: Anadolu Kavağı and Yoros Castle
properties.desc: The last village before the Black Sea, and the turnaround point of the long Bosphorus ferry. A twenty-minute climb above it stands Yoros, a Byzantine castle on the headland where the strait opens out, with two ruined towers and a marble gate. From the top you see the Black Sea on one side and the whole strait on the other.
properties.season: May–Jun and Sep–Oct; fog and wind off the Black Sea from November
properties.tip: The ferry gives you about three hours ashore — climb to Yoros first and eat afterwards, because the fish restaurants by the pier fill the moment the boat docks.
properties.rev: The castle walk is rated the best part of the Bosphorus trip, while the village itself draws complaints about aggressive restaurant touts, tourist pricing on fish and a scramble back to the boat at departure time.
properties.entry: Free · the castle is open ground with no gate or ticket
properties.onward: Istanbul Airport (IST) then metro and tram to Eminönü for the long Bosphorus ferry; by land, bus 15A from Üsküdar via Beykoz

properties.name: Heybeliada
properties.desc: The second island, greener and calmer than Büyükada, with a naval school on the waterfront and the Halki Greek Orthodox seminary on the north hill, closed since 1971 but visitable in its grounds. A circular road runs round the pine-covered edge; the coves on the far side are quiet enough to swim off the rocks.
properties.season: Jun–Sep for swimming, May and Oct for walking the ring road
properties.tip: Walk or cycle the ring road anticlockwise and stop at Değirmen Burnu on the west side, where there is shade, a small beach and none of the pier crowd.
properties.rev: Regulars prefer it to Büyükada for the quiet and the pines, though the seminary building itself cannot be entered, restaurants near the pier are ordinary and ferries thin out badly out of season.
properties.entry: Free · ferry from Kabataş or Bostancı, a few lira with an İstanbulkart
properties.onward: Sabiha Gökçen (SAW) then M4 to Bostancı and the island ferry, which calls at Heybeliada before Büyükada

properties.name: Büyükada
properties.desc: The largest of the Princes' Islands, an hour and a half out into the Marmara: no private cars, pine woods, and streets of enormous timber mansions with fretwork verandas built by Greek and Armenian merchants. Two hills, each with a monastery — St George's on the southern one, reached by a path where pilgrims tie rags of cloth to the trees.
properties.season: May–Jun and Sep–Oct — July and August are packed; many places shut Nov–Mar
properties.tip: Rent a bicycle or take an electric shuttle to the Lunapark saddle, then walk the last steep kilometre to Aya Yorgi; the phaeton horses were retired in 2020 and the replacements are limited.
properties.rev: The car-free quiet and the mansions win people over, but summer weekends bring ferry queues in both directions, beach clubs charging a full day rate for a sunbed, and a very crowded main street near the pier.
properties.entry: Free · ferry from Kabataş or Bostancı, a few lira with an İstanbulkart
properties.onward: Sabiha Gökçen (SAW) then M4 to Bostancı and the island ferry; from Europe, ferries leave Kabataş and Eminönü

properties.name: Çınarcık and the Yalova Coast
properties.desc: The stretch of Marmara shore west of Yalova where İstanbul keeps its summer houses: pebble coves, pine slopes dropping to the road, and a promenade of tea gardens. The Erikli and Delmece plateaus rise straight behind, with waterfalls in the beech forest and ten degrees of relief. The water is cleaner here than anywhere on the inner Marmara.
properties.season: Jun–Sep for swimming — July and August weekends multiply the population
properties.tip: Skip the town beach and drive west past Koru for the coves, then take the forest road up to Delmece Yaylası where it is cold enough to want a jumper in August.
properties.rev: Weekenders like the water and the quick ferry hop; the complaints are ranks of holiday blocks along the shore, a shortage of parking and jellyfish in some Augusts.
properties.onward: İstanbul Yenikapı–Yalova fast ferry, then 20 min west by dolmuş; by road it is 2 h round the gulf from İstanbul

properties.name: Cumalıkızık
properties.desc: A 700-year-old Ottoman village on Uludağ's skirt, cobbled roughly enough that you watch your feet, with some 270 timber-and-rubble houses in ochre and blue leaning over the lanes. Weekends bring busloads for village breakfast and mulberry juice; midweek mornings it is chickens, woodsmoke and women selling raspberries from doorsteps.
