properties.desc: One of the oldest Lycian cities, stacked on a bluff over the Xanthos valley with an Ottoman governor's fortress on top of the acropolis and rock tombs cut into the cliff below it, including one with Bellerophon riding Pegasus carved beside the door. The theatre below is large, well preserved and faces the mountains.
properties.season: Mar–Jun and Sep–Nov — the valley is very hot in midsummer
properties.tip: Bellerophon's tomb is reached by an unmarked scramble off the left of the fortress path; ask the ticket seller to point out where it starts.
properties.rev: Visitors rate it the best-value ruin in the valley thanks to the setting, while mentioning the steep unmarked scramble to the tombs, thin signage and midday heat with no shade.
properties.onward: Dalaman (DLM), then Fethiye and 35 km southeast via Kemer; usually combined with Saklıkent, 12 km further on

properties.name: Kaklık Cave
properties.desc: An underground Pamukkale: a collapsed cave whose floor is covered in miniature white travertine terraces filled with warm sulphurous water, lit from a hole in the roof. It is about the size of a tennis court, smells strongly of sulphur, and you walk it on a raised boardwalk in fifteen minutes.
properties.season: All year — the cave holds a steady temperature and is a genuine winter option
properties.tip: Bring nothing you mind smelling of sulphur, and combine it with Laodicea on the same morning; the cave is a 20-minute detour off the Denizli–Afyon road.
properties.rev: Called a fair miniature of Pamukkale for a fraction of the price, with regular complaints about the smell, slippery boards, weak lighting and how quickly the visit is over.
properties.entry: Small fee — check locally; municipal ticket, cash only
properties.onward: Denizli Çardak (DNZ) about 30 minutes; on the D320 towards Dinar, 40 km from Denizli centre, no useful public transport

properties.name: Clandras Bridge
properties.desc: A single-arch bridge over the Banaz stream in the Ulubey canyon, built from large dressed blocks and generally dated to the Phrygian or Lydian period, which would make it one of the oldest bridges still standing anywhere. A Roman aqueduct channel runs along the top, and farm traffic still crosses it.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — the river road can flood in late winter
properties.tip: Go down under the arch on the north bank to see the block-work and the aqueduct channel; from the roadway above it looks like an ordinary farm bridge.
properties.rev: Visitors are surprised such an old structure is unfenced and unattended, and report a rough unsigned approach road, no information board and rubbish left by picnickers.
properties.onward: Uşak, then 45 km south via Karahallı; a car is essential and the last few kilometres are gravel

properties.name: Aizanoi
properties.desc: The best-preserved Temple of Zeus in Anatolia stands in a village 60 kilometres from Kütahya, raised over a vaulted underground chamber you can still walk into. Beside it are a combined theatre and stadium, a colonnaded market building carrying Diocletian's price edict, two bath houses and a second-century bridge still taking traffic.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — the plateau is bleak and often snowbound in winter
properties.tip: Go down into the vaulted basement under the temple cella; it is unlit, the entrance on the north side is easy to miss, and it is the oldest part of the building.
properties.rev: Everyone is astonished by how complete the temple is and how few people are there; complaints are excavation fencing that blocks parts of the site, thin signage and nowhere to eat in the village.
properties.onward: Kütahya by train or bus, then 60 km southwest to Çavdarhisar; minibuses run from Kütahya otogar a few times a day

properties.name: Domaniç
properties.desc: Beech and fir forest on the ridges where Ertuğrul Gazi's tribe summered before there was an Ottoman state, with Halime Hatun's tomb in the village. The plateau meadows above fill with mushrooms in autumn, the roads run through tunnels of trees, and the whole district has about one small hotel.
properties.season: May–Oct; heavy snow closes the high roads from December to March
properties.tip: The Domaniç–İnegöl road over the mountain is the reason to come; drive it in the second half of October when the beech turns and mist sits in the valleys.
properties.rev: Turkish visitors rate the forest and the Ottoman associations; foreign visitors report almost no infrastructure, no English anywhere and a long drive from any useful airport.
properties.onward: Bursa (YEI) airport, then about 2 hours south via İnegöl; from Kütahya it is 90 km north over the mountain

properties.name: Murat Dağı
properties.desc: A 2,300-metre massif on the Kütahya–Uşak border with black pine forest, alpine meadows and thermal springs at its foot. There is a small ski area with a couple of lifts that locals use, and in summer the yayla meadows above Gediz fill with sheep, cold springs and families cooking beside the road.
properties.season: Jan–Mar for snow, Jun–Sep for the meadows; the shoulder months are mud
properties.tip: The thermal hotel at the base is open year-round and is the only reliable bed on the mountain — the lifts run only when there is snow and enough demand.
properties.rev: Turkish skiers describe it as cheap and uncrowded with short runs and unreliable lifts; summer walkers praise the meadows and warn there are no marked trails or maps.
properties.entry: Free; ski lift passes are cheap, roughly ₺300 (≈€7) a day
properties.onward: Kütahya or Uşak by rail, then to Gediz and 25 km up the mountain road; there is no public transport to the top

properties.name: Hamam Boğazı, Banaz
properties.desc: A hot spring in a gorge outside Banaz where mineral water around 40 °C fills open pools cut into the rock beside the stream, with a bath building above them. Locals come with towels and food and stay all afternoon; in winter the steam fills the whole gorge and there is snow on the rocks around the pools.
properties.season: Oct–Apr is the point — soaking here in a plateau summer makes no sense
properties.tip: Bathing is single-sex by session, so check the day's timetable at the gate rather than turning up as a couple and being sent away.
properties.rev: Turkish visitors rate the water and the setting, and consistently mention basic changing huts, no lockers, crowded weekends and facilities that have not been updated in decades.
properties.onward: Uşak, then 40 km east to Banaz on the Afyon road; minibuses from Uşak otogar, then a taxi out to the springs

properties.name: Lake Işıklı
properties.desc: A shallow reed lake at the head of the Meander, fed by karst springs so clear you can see the sand boiling at the source. Fishermen work it from flat-bottomed boats for crayfish and carp, pelicans and flamingos use it on passage, and the village of Işıklı sits on a mound above the water with a ruined citadel.
properties.season: Mar–May and Sep–Nov for birds; midsummer is hot, hazy and full of reeds
properties.tip: Ask at the fish co-operative in Işıklı village about going out with a boat at dawn — it costs little and is the only way to see the spring welling up in the middle.
properties.rev: Birdwatchers and anglers rate it, general visitors find the shore muddy, reedy and short on facilities, and everyone notes that water levels and bird numbers vary a lot year to year.
properties.onward: Denizli Çardak (DNZ) about 45 minutes; the lake is beyond Çivril, roughly 1 hr 30 from Denizli centre by car

properties.name: Kütahya
properties.desc: The tile town: potters have worked here since the 14th century and still do, so façades, fountains and the clock tower are covered in blue and white. Below a Byzantine and Germiyanid castle sit lanes of restored Ottoman konaks, the Great Mosque, and workshops where underglaze painting is still done by hand.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — winters are cold, wet and long at 970 metres
properties.tip: Buy from the workshops in the Germiyan Sokak lanes rather than the shops on the main square, and ask whether a piece is hand-painted or transfer-printed, because both are sold.
properties.rev: Visitors like the tiles and the restored lanes, and note that the rest of the city is ordinary, that many souvenir tiles are machine-printed, and that most sights close by five.
properties.entry: Tile Museum ≈₺100 (≈€2.50); the old lanes are free
properties.onward: Kütahya is on the Ankara–İzmir rail line and about 3 hours by road from Bursa; Zafer (KZR) airport 50 km away has limited flights

properties.name: Phrygian Way
properties.desc: A waymarked long-distance trail linking the Phrygian rock monuments across Afyonkarahisar, Kütahya and Eskişehir, through tuff valleys, altar-topped outcrops and villages that still thresh with horses. The Afyon sections around Ayazini and Döğer are the most spectacular and the least walked, marked in the same red and white as the Lycian Way.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — the plateau bakes in July and snows in winter
properties.tip: Villages on this route have no pensions and often no shop, so arrange a bed in advance through the İhsaniye or Döğer muhtar, or carry a tent and your own water.
properties.rev: Walkers praise the emptiness and the monuments, and warn that the logistics are hard: sparse waymarking in places, no accommodation, dogs at village edges and very little English.
properties.onward: Afyonkarahisar or Kütahya by train or bus, then a taxi out to İhsaniye, Ayazini or Döğer for the trailheads

properties.name: Seydiler Fairy Chimneys
properties.desc: A cluster of tuff pinnacles and mushroom rocks on the edge of Seydiler village, with a rock-cut Phrygian shrine and cave dwellings hollowed into the base of the cliffs. Storks nest on the poles above, tractors cross the field in front, and there is not a single souvenir stall anywhere.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — the poppy fields around İhsaniye flower in June
properties.tip: Walk round behind the pinnacles to the cave houses; the front row you see from the road is the least interesting part of the formation.
properties.rev: People arriving from Cappadocia find it modest but genuinely deserted; the recurring notes are no signage, no facilities and a village where asking directions is the only way to find the path.
properties.onward: Afyonkarahisar, then 35 km north via İhsaniye; the Phrygian Valley road links it to Ayazini and Döğer

properties.name: Aslantaş and Yılantaş
properties.desc: Two Phrygian rock-cut tombs in the valley near Döğer. Aslantaş has a pair of lions carved facing each other over the doorway, taller than a person and still crisp after 2,600 years; Yılantaş collapsed long ago and lies broken in the field. They stand alone in farmland with no fence and no ticket office.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — the dirt approach turns to mud after rain
properties.tip: They are fifteen minutes apart on unpaved farm tracks with almost no signs, so pin both locations before you leave mobile coverage in İhsaniye.
properties.rev: The few who find them describe the lions as extraordinary and the experience as entirely unmanaged: no signs, no guard, farm tracks, and livestock grazing around the monuments.
properties.onward: Afyonkarahisar, then 45 km north towards Döğer; a car is essential and the final stretch is farm track

properties.name: Afyonkarahisar Castle
properties.desc: A fortress on a 226-metre plug of black volcanic rock standing in the middle of the city like a fist. Hittite records mention a stronghold here in the 14th century BC; what survives is mostly Byzantine and Seljuk. Around 700 steps climb it, and from the top the Anatolian plateau flattens out in every direction.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — the steps ice over in winter and bake in July
properties.tip: Start the climb an hour before sunset and carry water; there is nothing to buy on the rock and the staircase has no shade at any point.
properties.rev: Locals and visitors agree the view repays the climb, and complain about the sheer number of steps, patchy lighting after dark and almost no interpretation once you are up there.
properties.onward: Afyonkarahisar sits on the Ankara–İzmir rail line with high-speed services nearby; the rock is a 15-minute walk from the old town

properties.name: Afyonkarahisar
properties.desc: A plateau city of Ottoman timber-framed houses climbing towards the castle rock, with a 13th-century Great Mosque whose flat roof rests on forty wooden columns with carved capitals. It is also the country's dairy and sausage capital: clotted cream with poppy-seed bread for breakfast, sucuk everywhere, and Turkish delight sold by the kilo.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — the plateau is cold and grey from December to March
properties.tip: Do the Ulu Cami and the Ottoman lanes below the rock in the morning, then eat kaymak with ekmek kadayıf at one of the old shops on the main avenue.
properties.rev: Travellers stopping between Ankara and İzmir are surprised by the food and the mosque, and note that the modern city is drab, the old quarter only partly restored and English rare.
properties.entry: Free — the Ulu Cami has no charge
properties.onward: İzmir (ADB) or Ankara (ESB) then about 3 hours by road; the Ankara–İzmir trains and the high-speed station make it an easy rail stop

properties.name: Ayazini
properties.desc: A village built into and around soft tuff, with Phrygian rock tombs carrying carved lions, Byzantine cave churches whose domes are cut from the living rock, and fairy chimneys standing in the fields behind the houses. It is Cappadocia's geology at a tenth of the scale and a hundredth of the visitor numbers.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — the plateau is snowy and bleak in midwinter
properties.tip: The best cave church, the one with a carved dome and columns, is behind the village on the far side of the outcrop, not the one signposted from the car park.
properties.rev: Visitors are startled that a site like this is empty and free, and mention loose rock, no barriers above drops, no facilities and almost no explanatory signage.
properties.onward: Afyonkarahisar, then 30 km north on the Eskişehir road via İhsaniye; you need a car, because buses are rare

properties.name: Patara
properties.desc: Lycia's old capital and harbour, half-buried in dunes behind an 12-kilometre beach. The re-erected bouleuterion where the Lycian League voted, a triple-arched gate standing alone in a field, and the oldest known lighthouse in the world, rebuilt block by block from its fallen pieces.
properties.season: Apr–May and Oct — midsummer is shadeless and the sand radiates heat
properties.tip: One ticket covers the ruins and the beach behind them, so do the site first and walk out to the sand rather than driving back.
properties.rev: Praised as the rare ancient city with a beach attached; visitors grumble about the heat, the mosquitoes from the marsh at dusk and how little shade or signage there is between monuments.
properties.entry: €15 for foreigners · covered by Museum Pass Türkiye and the Mediterranean pass
properties.onward: Dalaman (DLM) 1.5 h or Antalya (AYT) 3.5 h, then 4 km down the lane from the D400 through Gelemiş village.

properties.name: Xanthos
properties.desc: The Lycian capital on a bluff above the Eşen river, twice destroyed by its own citizens rather than surrender. Pillar tombs stand at odd angles beside a Roman theatre, and the Harpy Tomb reliefs on site are casts — Charles Fellows shipped the originals to the British Museum in 1842.
properties.season: Mar–May and Oct–Nov — flowering slopes in spring, brutal glare in July
properties.tip: Walk up past the theatre to the acropolis for the view over the whole Xanthos valley; almost every coach group turns back at the pillar tombs.
properties.rev: Archaeology-minded visitors call it the most important Lycian site in Türkiye; others find it bare and are annoyed that the best sculpture is in London and the labelling is thin.
properties.entry: €3 for foreigners · covered by Museum Pass Türkiye
properties.onward: Dalaman (DLM) about 1 h 15, then the D400 to Kınık village; the site is signposted on the main road.

properties.name: Kalkan
properties.desc: An old Greek-built harbour village of steep whitewashed lanes that has quietly turned into a hillside of villas with private pools. The draw is the rooftop restaurants above the bay and the light at dusk on Kalkan's amphitheatre of houses; the flaw is the near-total absence of sand.
properties.season: May–Jun and Sep–Oct — the hill streets are an oven at noon in August
properties.tip: Swim from one of the beach-club platforms below the old town rather than hunting for a beach that does not exist.
properties.rev: Repeat visitors rate the villa comfort and the restaurant standard highly, while first-timers complain about the vertical streets, taxi prices and how British the high season feels.
properties.onward: Dalaman (DLM) airport, then about 2 h on the D400; Antalya (AYT) is 3.5–4 h east.

properties.name: Kaputaş Beach
properties.desc: A wedge of pale gravel at the mouth of a gorge, reached by 180-odd steps down from the Kaş–Kalkan road. The water is an improbable turquoise because cold karst springs surface here, which also makes it noticeably colder than the open sea. Small, photogenic and completely exposed.
properties.season: Jun–Sep for swimming; May and Oct for photographs without the crowd
properties.tip: Come before 10:00 or after 17:00 — midday the stairs, the two sunbed rows and the roadside parking are all full at once.
properties.rev: Everyone agrees the colour is real; the complaints are the stair climb in heat, the shadeless afternoon, the cold undertow and periodic closures after rockfall on the cliff above.
properties.onward: Dalaman (DLM) or Antalya (AYT), then the D400 — the beach is 7 km east of Kalkan with a lay-by on both sides of the road.

properties.name: Kibyra
properties.desc: A city of horse breeders and ironworkers on a ridge above Gölhisar, with a stadium that still seats ten thousand almost intact. The real object is in the odeon: a floor of coloured marble laid as a Medusa head more than five metres across, one of the few of its kind anywhere.
properties.season: May–Jun and Sep–Oct — 1,000 m up, so cold and wet in winter
properties.tip: The Medusa floor is covered over for protection outside the warm months, so confirm it is uncovered before making the drive.
properties.rev: Visitors find the stadium and the mosaic well worth a long detour and usually have the place to themselves; the complaints are the distance from everywhere, no shade, and the mosaic being under its winter cover.
properties.onward: Denizli Çardak (DNZ) airport, then about 1 h 30 via Gölhisar; from Fethiye it is a 1 h 30 climb inland.

properties.name: Kaş
properties.desc: A shelf of white houses and bougainvillea stacked above a harbour that looks straight at the Greek island of Meis. A Hellenistic theatre sits five minutes from the square, a Lycian sarcophagus stands in the middle of a shopping street, and the evenings are meze, grilled fish and jasmine.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Nov — August is hot and the town doubles in size
properties.tip: Hand your passport to the ferry office by the harbour the evening before you sail to Meis, not on the morning itself.
properties.rev: Visitors love the scale, the food and the diving; the recurring gripes are the parking, the steep haul back up from the harbour, and the fact that the town itself has no real beach.
properties.entry: Free — the theatre and the Lion Tomb are open street-side
properties.onward: Antalya (AYT) or Dalaman (DLM) airport, then the D400 coast road — roughly 3.5 h from either, Dalaman usually the easier drive.

properties.name: Gömbe and Yeşil Göl
properties.desc: A highland town at 1,050 metres under Akdağ, where Antalya escapes the August heat: plane-shaded tea gardens, trout ponds and cherry orchards. Above it a rough track climbs to Yeşil Göl, a green glacial tarn at 2,300 metres, and the Uçarsu waterfall drops off the rock wall nearby.
properties.season: Jun–Sep for the high lake — snow blocks the upper track from November to May
properties.tip: The last stretch to Yeşil Göl needs a high-clearance vehicle or a two-hour walk; village drivers in Gömbe run jeeps up for a fixed price.
properties.rev: People rate the cool air and the tarn walk highly; the complaints are the punishing track, weekend picnic litter at the lake and locals grazing right up to the shore.
properties.entry: Free; jeep transfer to the lake around ₺1,200 (≈€27) per vehicle
properties.onward: Antalya (AYT) about 3 h via Elmalı, or 1 h 30 up from Kaş on the D350; a car or a village jeep is the only way to the lake.

properties.name: Lake Salda
properties.desc: A deep crater lake ringed in places by brilliant white hydromagnesite sand, which turns the shallows the colour of a tropical lagoon. NASA studied it as an analogue for Jezero crater on Mars. The water is alkaline, very clear and cold, and the white shore is now fenced and protected after years of being trampled.
properties.season: Jun–Sep for swimming; May and Oct for the colours without the buses
properties.tip: The famous white beach is a protected zone reached by shuttle with no swimming in parts, so go to the eastern public beach if you actually want to get in the water.
properties.rev: Everyone agrees the colour is real and remarkable; the standard complaints are Instagram crowds, restrictions and shuttles introduced to save the shoreline, mud-smearing visitors, and a lake level that keeps dropping.
properties.entry: Public beach around ₺100 (≈€2.30) plus parking; the protected zone runs a shuttle
properties.onward: Denizli Çardak (DNZ) airport, then about 1 h 15, or Isparta (ISE) and 1 h 45; Antalya is 3 h over the mountains.

properties.name: Kaş Diving
properties.desc: The clearest, best-organised diving in Türkiye: twenty-odd sites within twenty minutes of the harbour, thirty-metre visibility and walls that drop straight off the Uluburun cape. There is a sunken passenger plane at eighteen metres, amphora fields, and the reef where the Bronze Age Uluburun wreck was found in 1982.
properties.season: May–Nov — water is 16 °C in March, 27 °C in late August
properties.tip: Book two-tank morning boats: the afternoon wind gets up off Uluburun and the visibility drops with the swell.
properties.rev: Divers rate the schools and the marine-park rules highly; complaints centre on how bare the reefs are of big fish after decades of fishing, and on peak-season boats stacked at the same buoy.
properties.entry: Two-tank day around €70–90 with kit; try-dives from about €55
properties.onward: Antalya (AYT) or Dalaman (DLM), then the D400 to Kaş; all the dive schools are on the harbour front, no car needed.

properties.name: Üçağız (Teimiussa)
properties.desc: A fishing hamlet on a sheltered lagoon where the Lycian necropolis runs right down to the waterline — rock-cut tombs standing among the boats, some with their lids half in the sea. It is the launching point for Kekova and, for two hours after the boats leave, one of the quietest places on the coast.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — dead quiet and half-shut in winter
properties.tip: Walk east ten minutes past the last house to the necropolis at Teimiussa, where nobody goes and the tombs sit in open scrub.
properties.rev: Praised as an easy, unpolished base with good pensions; the standard grumbles are aggressive boat touts on the quay, weak mobile signal and the long unlit road in.
properties.onward: Antalya (AYT) 2.5 h, then 19 km of narrow lane south from the D400 at Çevreli; dolmuşes run from Demre in summer only.

properties.name: Simena (Kaleköy)
properties.desc: A car-free village of thirty houses climbing to a crusader castle, reached only by boat or on foot. Inside the walls is the smallest ancient theatre in Lycia, cut for about three hundred people, and the view takes in the whole Kekova channel and a sarcophagus standing in the water below.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — most pensions shut from November to March
properties.tip: Stay the night: after the last day boat leaves at five the village belongs to about a dozen guests and the goats.
properties.rev: Almost everyone calls the castle view the best on this coast; the complaints are the steep stepped path with luggage, the castle ticket booth and inflated prices at the waterside restaurants.
properties.entry: Castle ₺200 (≈€4.50) · covered by Museum Pass Türkiye
properties.onward: Antalya (AYT) or Dalaman (DLM), then drive to Üçağız and take a 10-minute water taxi; there is no road into the village.

properties.name: Kekova
properties.desc: A long uninhabited island whose northern shore slid into the sea in a second-century earthquake. From a boat you look down on staircases, doorways and cut foundations a metre under clear water, with the odd sarcophagus lid breaking the surface offshore.
properties.season: May–Jun and Sep–Oct — flat mornings, and the day boats thin out after September
properties.tip: Swimming and diving over the sunken city are banned; take a kayak or a small gulet from Üçağız at 09:00 instead of the big Kaş boats that arrive at noon.
properties.rev: Reliably called the best boat day on the Lycian coast, though people are surprised how little is actually visible from a hull, and midday convoys of tour boats spoil the quiet.
properties.entry: Free to look; boat from Üçağız around ₺1,200–1,800 (≈€26–40) for a shared day
properties.onward: Antalya (AYT) 2.5 h or Dalaman (DLM) 3 h, then the lane south from the D400 at Çevreli down to Üçağız harbour.

properties.name: Elmalı
properties.desc: An apple-growing town on a 1,100-metre plateau behind the Lycian mountains, with a bazaar of low wooden shopfronts and the elegant Ömerpaşa Mosque of 1610 tiled in İznik blue. The surrounding tumuli produced the painted Karaburun tomb and the disputed Elmalı hoard of Lycian coins.
properties.season: May–Oct — hard frosts and snow from December, and the apple harvest is in September
properties.tip: Time it for the Thursday market, when growers come down from the plateau villages and the square fills with apples, cheese and wooden tools.
properties.rev: Travellers heading to Gömbe or the cedars find it a genuine working town rather than a sight; complaints are limited food and lodging, and a centre that has lost many old buildings to concrete.
properties.onward: Antalya (AYT) about 1 h 45 via Korkuteli, or an hour up from Finike on the D635; regular buses run from Antalya otogar.

properties.name: Avlan Lake
properties.desc: A shallow plateau lake ringed by cedar-covered hills south of Elmalı, drained for farmland in the 1970s and deliberately refilled decades later after the microclimate collapsed. It now draws coot, grebes and migrating cranes, with picnic tables under the pines and mirror-flat water at dawn.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Nov — levels drop in late summer and the shore turns to mud
properties.tip: Stop on the Elmalı–Gömbe road at the northern picnic area rather than the main viewpoint; the birds are on that shallow end.
properties.rev: A calm, free stop on the way to Gömbe that locals rate highly; visitors note the water level is unreliable, litter accumulates at the picnic areas and there is no infrastructure whatsoever.
properties.onward: Antalya (AYT) about 2 h via Korkuteli and Elmalı; the lake is 12 km south of Elmalı on the Kaş road, best reached by car.

properties.name: Andriake
properties.desc: Myra's port, where St Paul changed ships on the way to Rome. Hadrian's granary still stands almost to roof height with the emperor's portrait bust over the door, and it now houses the Museum of Lycian Civilisations. Beyond it a reed marsh full of herons runs out to Çayağzı beach.
properties.season: Mar–Jun and Sep–Nov — the marsh breeds mosquitoes in high summer
properties.tip: The site ticket includes the museum in the granary, and the boardwalk over the marsh to the sea is the part almost nobody walks.
properties.rev: Visitors find it refreshingly empty next to Myra and rate the museum well; the drawbacks are almost no shade, sparse English labels and a car park that floods after winter rain.
properties.entry: €6 for foreigners · covered by Museum Pass Türkiye
properties.onward: Antalya (AYT) 2 h to Demre, then 5 km down to the harbour road at Çayağzı, where the Kekova boats also leave.

properties.name: Myra
properties.desc: A cliff face honeycombed with house-shaped Lycian tombs above a Roman theatre whose stage blocks are carved with theatrical masks. Recent digs under the greenhouses have uncovered a second, older theatre and painted terracotta figures, so the site keeps growing while you visit.
properties.season: Mar–May and Oct–Nov — the greenhouse plain traps heat in summer
properties.tip: Go first thing: the tombs face south-west, so morning light flattens them and the afternoon is when the cruise buses from Demre arrive.
properties.rev: The tomb façade impresses everyone; complaints are that the site is small for the price, the fence keeps you well back from the cliff, and tour groups fill the theatre in bursts.
properties.entry: €13 for foreigners · covered by Museum Pass Türkiye and the Mediterranean pass
properties.onward: Antalya (AYT) about 2 h on the D400 to Demre, then 2 km up through the tomato greenhouses.

properties.name: Church of St. Nicholas, Demre
properties.desc: The Byzantine church built over the grave of the fourth-century bishop who became Father Christmas, sunk several metres below today's street level. Inside are opus sectile floors, faded frescoes of saints and the broken sarcophagus Italian sailors raided in 1087, all under a protective steel roof.
properties.season: All year — spring and autumn avoid both heat and the Orthodox pilgrimage peaks
properties.tip: Come before 10:00 or after 16:00; Russian and Ukrainian pilgrim coaches fill the nave in the middle of the day and photography becomes hopeless.
properties.rev: Historically extraordinary, say most; the repeated criticisms are the high foreigner ticket, the scaffolding-like shelter overhead and the tat market you walk through to reach the door.
properties.entry: €17 for foreigners · covered by Museum Pass Türkiye
properties.onward: Antalya (AYT) about 2 h by car or the Kaş-bound bus to Demre; the church is in the town centre, five minutes from the otogar.

properties.name: Arycanda
properties.desc: Lycia's best-sited city, built on five terraces against a mountain wall above the Finike–Elmalı road. The bath house still has arched windows framing the valley, the stadium sits on a shelf above the theatre, and you often have the whole slope to yourself with only cowbells for noise.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — snow can reach the upper terraces in winter
properties.tip: Climb to the stadium at the very top before you look at anything else; the drop back down through the theatre is the whole point of the place.
properties.rev: Repeatedly described as the most beautiful ruin in Lycia and almost deserted; the caveats are the steep uneven climb, no café or shade, and a warden who sometimes shuts early out of season.
properties.onward: Antalya (AYT) about 2 h — take the D635 inland from Finike toward Elmalı; the site is signed on the left after 30 km.

properties.name: Lake Burdur
properties.desc: A closed salt lake that winters most of the world's white-headed ducks, along with flamingos and thousands of waders. It is also a case study in disappearance: the shoreline has retreated kilometres since the 1970s as irrigation took the inflow, leaving pale salt flats and stranded jetties behind the birds.
properties.season: Nov–Mar for the wintering ducks; Apr–May for waders on passage
properties.tip: Bring binoculars and go to the northern shore near Karakent early; from the Burdur town side the birds are usually far out on the flats.
properties.rev: Birdwatchers rate the winter duck counts as internationally significant; everyone else notes there is no hide, no visitor centre, a lot of dust, and a shoreline that is bleak rather than beautiful.
properties.onward: Isparta (ISE) airport, then 50 min to Burdur; the north shore tracks need a car and dry weather.

properties.name: Saklıkent Ski Centre
properties.desc: A modest ski area on Bakırlı Dağı at 1,850 to 2,400 metres, fifty kilometres from Antalya, whose selling point is entirely geographic: you can ski a north-facing run in the morning and swim at Konyaaltı in the afternoon. Three lifts, a handful of pistes, and the national observatory on the ridge above.
properties.season: Jan–Mar for reliable snow; the road is fine but the season is short and unpredictable
properties.tip: Go on a weekday — Antalya families fill the two chairlifts at weekends and the queue is longer than the run.
properties.rev: Novelty value is high and the day is cheap; skiers are blunt that the pistes are short, the snow is thin in warm winters and the equipment hire is basic.
properties.entry: Day lift pass around ₺600 (≈€13) with hire extra
properties.onward: Antalya (AYT) about 1 h 15 on the Korkuteli road, then the signed climb up Bakırlı; minibuses run from Antalya at weekends in season.

properties.name: İnsuyu Cave
properties.desc: Turkey's first show cave, opened in 1965: about six hundred metres of walkway past stalactite galleries to a chain of underground lakes, of which the Great Lake is the one people come for. Groundwater extraction in the valley above has dried the lakes out in bad years, and the cave has closed and reopened repeatedly because of it.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Nov — a constant 14 °C inside whatever the season
properties.tip: Ring ahead and ask whether the lakes actually have water in them; without them it is a short walk past dry formations.
properties.rev: When the lakes are full people call it a genuine surprise; reviews from dry years are flat, and there are regular grumbles about slippery steps, weak lighting and long closures for maintenance.
properties.onward: Isparta (ISE) airport, then about 1 h; the cave is 13 km south of Burdur on the Antalya road.

properties.name: Cape Gelidonya Lighthouse
properties.desc: The southern tip of the Teke peninsula, where a small stone lighthouse looks out over the Beşadalar — five bare islets in open sea. The path in from Karaöz is one of the best hours of the Lycian Way, and the seabed off the cape gave up a Bronze Age shipwreck excavated in 1960.
properties.season: Mar–May and Oct–Nov — no shade at all on the cape in summer
properties.tip: Drive to Karaöz and walk the last 4 km; ordinary cars regularly get stuck on the rutted track beyond the last houses.
properties.rev: Hikers call the approach the finest stretch of the whole trail; the warnings are the exposed heat, no water source, an unmarked final section and a lighthouse you cannot go inside.
properties.onward: Antalya (AYT) 1 h 45 to Kumluca, then the Mavikent–Karaöz road; the last stretch to the cape is on foot.

properties.name: Adrasan
properties.desc: A two-kilometre bay closed at both ends by pine ridges, with a shingle beach, a river mouth and low pensions instead of resorts. It is the calmest swimming water on this stretch and the departure point for boats to Suluada and the Ceneviz coves that you cannot reach by road.
properties.season: Jun–Sep for the water; May and Oct for walking the Lycian Way sections above the bay
properties.tip: Take the small local boat to Ceneviz bay rather than the big Antalya day-trip gulets — it leaves at 10:00 from the river-mouth jetty and holds a dozen people.
properties.rev: Regulars value the low-key family feel and the sheltered water; complaints are the stony beach, the mosquitoes near the river and a village that essentially closes between November and April.
properties.onward: Antalya (AYT) about 1 h 30 on the D400, then 12 km down from the Çavuşköy turning past Kumluca.

properties.name: Tahtalı Dağı and the Olympos Cable Car
properties.desc: A 2,365-metre limestone cone that stands almost directly over the sea, with a cable car climbing to the summit in ten minutes from Tekirova. From the top you see the whole Gulf of Antalya, the Beydağları ridgeline and, on clear winter days, snow on the terrace while people swim below.
properties.season: All year — clearest Nov–Apr; summer afternoons haze over completely
properties.tip: Take the earliest car of the day: cloud usually forms on the summit by late morning in summer and the view is gone.
properties.rev: The ride and the view get consistent praise, but the ticket is expensive by Turkish standards, the summit is bitterly windy, and the whole trip is wasted if cloud sets in — check the webcam first.
properties.entry: Around €40 return for foreigners; paragliding tandem from about €120
properties.onward: Antalya (AYT) 45 min on the D400 to the Tekirova base station; shuttles run from Kemer and most Antalya hotels.

properties.name: Yanartaş (Chimaera)
properties.desc: Two dozen flames burning straight out of bare rock on a hillside above Çıralı, fed by methane seeping from the serpentinite and alight for at least two and a half thousand years. Homer's fire-breathing Chimaera was located here, and the ruins of a Hephaestus temple sit just below the vents.
properties.season: All year, best Oct–Apr when the nights are cold enough to make the flames vivid
properties.tip: Go up after dark with a head torch — in daylight the flames are almost invisible and the twenty-minute stone path is the whole disappointment people report.
properties.rev: Magical after dark, say most; the standard complaints are that the flames are smaller than the photos suggest, the rocky climb is harder than advertised, and the car park now charges too.
properties.onward: Antalya (AYT) 1 h 15, then the Çıralı road; the trailhead is 3 km beyond the village, followed by a 20–30 min climb.

properties.name: Termessos
properties.desc: A Pisidian eyrie at 1,050 metres that Alexander looked at and decided not to besiege. The theatre hangs on the edge of a gorge with Güllük Dağı opposite, and the necropolis above is a chaos of sarcophagi thrown around by earthquakes, half-swallowed by pines and wild cyclamen.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — cool at altitude even when Antalya is at 40 °C
properties.tip: Allow three hours and take water; the climb from the car park to the theatre is a solid thirty minutes up a rough stone path with no facilities on top.
properties.rev: Hikers call it the most dramatic ruin in Türkiye; the caveats are constant — a hard climb, no shade or café, vague signage, and mountain goats and snakes among the tombs.
properties.entry: ₺350 (≈€8) including the national park · covered by Museum Pass Türkiye
properties.onward: Antalya (AYT) about 50 min on the Korkuteli road, then 9 km up a park road; no public transport, so drive or join a tour.

properties.name: Suluada
properties.desc: An uninhabited islet off Adrasan with two white sand coves and water so pale it gets called the Turkish Maldives, which for once is not far off. There is nothing on it — no shade, no kiosk, no jetty — so boats anchor offshore and you swim the last twenty metres in.
properties.season: Jun–Sep only; the crossing is cancelled in any real wind
properties.tip: Take the first boat out of Adrasan at 09:30 and you get an hour before the Antalya day-trip fleet turns up and moors six deep.
properties.rev: The colour lives up to the photos; the complaints are relentless — packed boats with loud music, no facilities, no shade and rubbish left by day-trippers on a protected island.
properties.entry: Free island; boat from Adrasan around ₺1,000–1,500 (≈€22–33) per person
properties.onward: Antalya (AYT) 1 h 30 to Adrasan or Çıralı, then a 45-minute boat crossing; there is no scheduled ferry.

properties.name: Lycian Way — Eastern Half
properties.desc: From Finike to the outskirts of Antalya the trail leaves the beach resorts and climbs: Arycanda's terraces, the empty coast to Cape Gelidonya, the Chimaera flames, then the long haul over the shoulder of Tahtalı. Red-and-white flashes on rocks, village pensions, and stretches where you meet nobody for a day.
properties.season: Mar–May and Oct–Nov — summer on this section is dangerous, winter snow blocks the high traverses
properties.tip: Carry four litres and plan around water: the cisterns marked on older maps between Karaöz and Adrasan are often dry by May.
properties.rev: Walkers rate the eastern half as wilder and emptier than the west; complaints are patchy waymarking after forest fires, bulldozed sections replaced by road, and pensions that shut out of season.
properties.onward: Antalya (AYT), then buses down the D400 drop you at Finike, Kumluca, Adrasan junction or Çıralı; taxis cover the last few kilometres.

properties.name: Olympos
properties.desc: A pirate city swallowed by jungle: bay leaves, figs and oleander growing through a temple gate, a Roman bridge abutment and Byzantine walls along a stream bed that runs down to a pebble beach. You walk the whole site inside a green tunnel, which is why it stays bearable in summer.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — the creek dries and the mosquitoes arrive in August
properties.tip: The beach is only reachable through the ruins on the same ticket, and the gate closes at sunset — swim early, not after dinner.
properties.rev: The treehouse-village atmosphere and the overgrown ruins win people over; the complaints are the ticketed beach access, the mosquitoes, and how loud the valley's backpacker bars get in July.
properties.entry: €10 for foreigners · covered by Museum Pass Türkiye and the Mediterranean pass
properties.onward: Antalya (AYT) about 1 h 20 on the D400, then 11 km down a steep switchback lane from the Olympos junction.

properties.name: Çıralı
properties.desc: Three kilometres of pebble backed by orange groves and small family pensions, with building height capped because loggerhead turtles nest on the sand. No hotel blocks, no jet skis, a stream mouth cold enough to make you gasp, and the Chimaera flames burning on the ridge behind.
properties.season: May–Oct for swimming; Apr and Nov for walking, with pensions open most of the year
properties.tip: Between May and October the beach is roped and closed after dark for the nesting turtles — respect it, and never light a fire or a torch on the sand.
properties.rev: People come back yearly for the quiet and the pensions; the honest downsides are the sharp pebbles, the winding access road, limited food choice and shops that close early out of season.
properties.onward: Antalya (AYT) 1 h 15 on the D400, then 7 km down the Ulupınar valley road; buses drop you at the junction and a minibus meets them.

properties.name: Beydağları Coastal National Park
properties.desc: The park that ties this coast together: 700 square kilometres running from Kemer to Adrasan, taking in Phaselis, Olympos, the Chimaera and the whole seaward wall of the Bey mountains. Red pine and cedar to 2,000 metres, wild goats on the ridges, and canyons like Göynük cutting back from the sea.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Nov — fire risk closes forest tracks in high summer
properties.tip: Göynük canyon is the easy way in — the lower gorge is a two-hour wade and gets you the scenery without a full mountain day.
properties.rev: Walkers rate the variety from beach to 2,000 metres in an hour; the recurring problems are unsigned forest junctions, summer fire closures and canyon operators overselling the Göynük trip.
properties.entry: Free to enter; Göynük canyon around ₺350 (≈€8)
properties.onward: Antalya (AYT), then the D400 south — Kemer, Çamyuva and Tekirova are all gateways; a car is essential for the mountain roads.

properties.name: Sagalassos
properties.desc: A Pisidian mountain city at 1,500 metres on the flank of Akdağ, abandoned after earthquakes and never built over. The Antonine nymphaeum has been re-erected and mountain water pours through it again, the theatre leans into the slope with its seats intact, and the whole site looks out over an empty valley.
properties.season: May–Jun and Sep–Oct — snow can close the road from December to March
properties.tip: Go in the morning before the cloud builds on Akdağ, and take a jacket; it is ten degrees colder up here than in Burdur.
properties.rev: Repeatedly described as the most spectacularly sited ruin in Türkiye and better excavated than most; complaints are the steep walking on loose ground, the exposed cold wind and the 7 km of hairpins up from Ağlasun.
properties.onward: Isparta (ISE) airport, then about 1 h via Ağlasun, or 2 h 30 from Antalya (AYT); a car is effectively required.

properties.name: Ağlasun
properties.desc: The small town seven kilometres below Sagalassos, and the reason to stay the night rather than day-trip. Old stone and timber houses run up the valley, plane trees shade the square, water runs in channels along the streets, and the pensions fill each summer with the Belgian archaeologists who dig the site above.
properties.season: May–Oct — quiet and cold once the excavation season ends
properties.tip: Eat at the square in the evening and ask about a lift up to the ruins for opening time; the pensions arrange it far cheaper than a taxi from Burdur.
properties.rev: Travellers value the price, the quiet and the walking access to Sagalassos; they also point out there is almost nothing to do after dark, few rooms, and no alcohol served in most places.
properties.onward: Isparta (ISE) airport, then about 50 min south-west; buses run from Burdur and Isparta a few times a day.

properties.name: Phaselis
properties.desc: Three natural harbours joined by a marble main street, with pines growing out of the paving and Tahtalı's cone rising straight behind. You can swim off the ancient quays where Alexander's fleet anchored, then dry off in a theatre that looks down onto the middle bay.
properties.season: May–Jun and Sep–Oct — swimmable water with a fraction of the August crowd
properties.tip: Arrive at opening, park at the far south harbour rather than the entrance lot, and swim before the Kemer boats unload around 11:00.
properties.rev: The combination of ruins and swimming is what everyone raves about; the complaints are the ticket price for a small site, thin facilities and boat parties that take over the beaches at midday.
properties.entry: €10 for foreigners · covered by Museum Pass Türkiye and the Mediterranean pass
properties.onward: Antalya (AYT) about 50 min on the D400 past Kemer; the site entrance is 2 km off the highway at Tekirova.

properties.name: Isparta Rose Harvest
properties.desc: For about four weeks from late May the plateau around Isparta smells of damask roses. Pickers are in the fields before dawn because the oil evaporates once the sun is up, and sacks of pink petals go straight to the distilleries at Gülbirlik and Gönen, where a tonne of petals yields a few hundred grams of oil.
properties.season: Late May to mid-June only — outside that window there is nothing to see
properties.tip: Be standing in a field between five and seven in the morning; by nine the picking is finished and the roses are gone for the day.
properties.rev: Those who time it right describe the smell as the whole point and worth the early alarm; the frequent disappointment is arriving in July to bare bushes, plus pushy roadside shops selling diluted rose oil.
properties.entry: Free in the fields; distillery tours a small fee
properties.onward: Isparta (ISE) airport, then 20 min, or Antalya (AYT) and 2 h over the Taurus; the rose villages ring the city.

properties.name: Karain Cave
properties.desc: A vast dry cave mouth in a cliff above the Döşemealtı plain, occupied on and off for around 500,000 years — the longest human sequence in Anatolia. Three chambers, a small site museum with flint tools and Neanderthal teeth, and a terrace looking out over the plain that alone justifies the drive.
properties.season: All year — a cool refuge in summer, though the track is slippery after rain
properties.tip: Ask the guardian to unlock the third chamber; without asking you are shown only the first two and out in ten minutes.
properties.rev: Prehistory enthusiasts find it moving and almost empty; others complain the display is dated, the climb is steeper than expected and the finds themselves are mostly in Antalya.
properties.entry: €5 for foreigners · covered by Museum Pass Türkiye
properties.onward: Antalya (AYT) about 40 min — take the Burdur road to Döşemealtı, then the signed lane through Yağca village; no public transport.

properties.name: Konyaaltı Beach
properties.desc: Seven kilometres of grey pebble running west from the Antalya cliffs with the Beydağları rising straight out of the sea at the far end — the best mountain backdrop of any city beach in Türkiye. The water shelves fast and stays clear, and the promenade behind is all cafés and cycle path.
properties.season: Jun–Oct for swimming; the promenade is pleasant all year
properties.tip: Walk west past the Beach Park section: the free stretches nearer the Sarısu end are cleaner and a third of the price for sunbeds.
properties.rev: Locals love the mountain view and the clean water; visitors complain that the pebbles hurt bare feet, that the drop-off is steep for children, and that the beach clubs charge city prices.
properties.entry: Free on the public stretches; sunbed pairs from ₺400 (≈€9)
properties.onward: Antalya (AYT), then the T1 tram or a 25-minute taxi to the western end; the whole beach is walkable from Kaleiçi in 20 minutes.

properties.name: Antalya Archaeological Museum
properties.desc: Türkiye's best provincial collection: the Roman emperors and dancing girls hauled out of Perge's theatre, the Weary Herakles whose upper half came back from Boston in 2011, and a hall of sarcophagi carved with the labours of Hercules. It gives every Pamphylian ruin you visit its missing statuary.
properties.season: All year — the obvious rainy-day plan on this coast
properties.tip: Check before you go: the museum is closed for a full rebuild, and only a small selection is on temporary display elsewhere in the city.
properties.rev: Rated by many as second only to Istanbul's; the dominant issue in 2026 is the long closure for reconstruction, and past visitors also complained about weak lighting and thin English labelling.
properties.entry: €15 for foreigners when open · covered by Museum Pass Türkiye — closed for reconstruction, verify before travelling
properties.onward: Antalya (AYT), then the T1 tram to Müze stop at the western end of Konyaaltı; a 10-minute walk from the cliff park.

properties.name: Kaleiçi (Antalya Old Town)
properties.desc: The walled old town falls in tight lanes of Ottoman wooden houses down to a Roman harbour still used by tour boats. Hadrian's Gate opens it at the top, the fluted Yivli minaret marks the skyline, and the Hıdırlık tower at the cliff edge is where the city goes to watch the sun set behind the Beydağları.
properties.season: Mar–Jun and Sep–Nov — July and August in the lanes are airless
properties.tip: Walk in through Hadrian's Gate but leave by the Karaalioğlu park side, and eat one street back from the marina where prices halve.
properties.rev: The setting and the restored houses charm nearly everyone; the constant complaints are restaurant touts, marina prices, late-night bar noise for anyone sleeping there, and cobbles hostile to wheeled bags.
properties.onward: Antalya (AYT) is 15 km out — the tram from the airport line or a 20-minute taxi drops you at Hadrian's Gate; no cars inside the walls.

properties.name: Mount Davraz
properties.desc: A 2,635-metre Taurus peak with a ski centre on its northern flank, twenty-five kilometres from both Isparta and Eğirdir. From the top of the chairlift you can see Lake Eğirdir on one side and Burdur's salt lake on the other, and in summer the same lifts serve walkers on the summit ridge.
properties.season: Jan–Mar for skiing; Jun–Sep for the ridge walk and the lake views
properties.tip: Stay in Eğirdir rather than at the mountain hotels and drive up for the day; the lake town is cheaper, warmer and far better for eating.
properties.rev: Skiers call it quiet, cheap and surprisingly scenic; the drawbacks reported are inconsistent snow in warm winters, limited lift capacity at weekends and a resort base that is little more than a car park and two hotels.
properties.entry: Day pass around ₺600 (≈€13) with hire extra
properties.onward: Isparta (ISE) airport, then 40 min to the base; Antalya (AYT) is about 2 h 30 by road over the pass.

properties.name: Düden Waterfalls
properties.desc: Two entirely different falls on the same river. Upper Düden drops into a mossy basin with a walkway that takes you behind the curtain into a cave; Lower Düden throws itself forty metres off the travertine cliff straight into the sea at Lara, best seen from a boat or the clifftop park.
properties.season: Mar–Jun after the snowmelt — flow drops sharply by late August
properties.tip: Do the upper falls early on a weekday: at weekends the picnic park is full of Antalya families and the cave path becomes a queue.
properties.rev: An easy, genuinely impressive half-day; the gripes are two separate tickets and car parks, weekend crowds, and how thin the water runs at the end of a dry summer.
properties.onward: Antalya (AYT) 20 min by taxi; city bus KL08 reaches the upper falls, and the lower falls are on the Lara road east of the centre.

properties.name: Lara Beach
properties.desc: The sand side of Antalya: a long golden strip east of the city where the big themed resorts line up behind a public beach park. Shallow, warm and family-friendly, with the lower Düden falls tipping off the cliff at its western end and sand-sculpture festivals on the beach each summer.
properties.season: Jun–Oct — August is hot, packed and expensive
properties.tip: Use the municipal Lara Beach Park entrance rather than a hotel gate; it has proper showers, shade and a fraction of the cost.
properties.rev: Praised for actual sand and calm water; the standard complaints are hotel-monopolised frontage, traffic on the Lara road, seaweed after storms and paying for everything twice in resort areas.
properties.entry: Public beach park around ₺150 (≈€3.50) with a sunbed
properties.onward: Antalya (AYT) is only 15 minutes away by taxi; city buses run the Lara road from the centre in about 30 minutes.

properties.name: Kurşunlu Waterfall
properties.desc: An eighteen-metre fall dropping into a green pool at the head of a small wooded canyon, with seven smaller pools stepping down through pine and laurel below it. It is a nature park rather than a spectacle — terrapins on the rocks, squirrels in the pines, and shade the whole way round the loop.
properties.season: Mar–Jun — the flow is weak by September and the pool goes murky
properties.tip: Take the lower boardwalk loop past the small pools; most visitors photograph the main fall from the viewing terrace and drive away in fifteen minutes.
properties.rev: A calm, shaded break from the coast heat; visitors warn that the fall is modest, that it can be reduced to a trickle in late summer, and that weekends bring coach parties.
properties.entry: ₺150 (≈€3.50) per person plus a small vehicle fee
properties.onward: Antalya (AYT) 15 min — it is 7 km inland from the airport off the Aksu road, easiest with a car or on a Perge–Aspendos tour.

properties.name: Lake Eğirdir and Yeşilada
properties.desc: Türkiye's second-largest freshwater lake, held between bare limestone ridges and turning genuinely turquoise in the shallows. The town sits on a promontory under a Seljuk castle, and a causeway runs out to Yeşilada, an old Greek fishing island of stone houses now full of small pensions and a ruined church.
properties.season: May–Jun and Sep–Oct — swimming is realistic from late June to September
properties.tip: Sleep on Yeşilada, not in the town: the pensions on the island face west and the sunset from their terraces is the reason to come.
properties.rev: Walkers and cyclists rate it as the best-value lake base in Türkiye; the honest complaints are the falling water level, algae blooms in hot summers, concrete on the causeway and a military zone occupying part of the promontory.
properties.onward: Isparta (ISE) airport, then 45 min, or Antalya (AYT) and about 2 h 30 over the Taurus; buses run from Isparta every hour.

properties.name: Perge
properties.desc: The most legible Roman city on this coast: a stadium for twelve thousand, twin Hellenistic gate towers, and a colonnaded street running 300 metres with a water channel still cut down its middle and chariot ruts in the paving. The baths keep their marble floors and the whole grid is easy to read.
properties.season: Mar–May and Oct–Nov — the plain hits 40 °C with zero shade in summer
properties.tip: Start at the far end by the nymphaeum and walk downhill with the water channel; everyone else walks up into the sun and gives up halfway.
properties.rev: Consistently called better value than Ephesus for the space and quiet; the complaints are the total lack of shade, a closed theatre across the road and coach groups arriving mid-morning.
properties.entry: €11 for foreigners · covered by Museum Pass Türkiye and the Mediterranean pass
properties.onward: Antalya (AYT) 15 min — it sits 2 km north of Aksu off the D400; the Antalya–Aksu dolmuş drops you at the junction.

properties.name: Lake Kovada National Park
properties.desc: A small forested lake south of Eğirdir, fed by the canal that drains it, ringed by pine and oak with trails along the shore. It is one of the quietest national parks in the country: no boats, no cafés, a barrier, a fee, and an hour or two of walking with wild boar tracks in the mud.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — mosquitoes in July, and the lake shrinks badly in drought years
properties.tip: Combine it with the drive on to Yazılı canyon; on its own Kovada is a half-day at most and there is nowhere to eat inside the park.
properties.rev: Visitors describe real quiet and clean air and are glad they came; they also report minimal facilities, unmarked side trails, low water in late summer and a fee that feels steep for what is provided.
properties.entry: ₺150 (≈€3.50) per person plus a vehicle fee
properties.onward: Isparta (ISE) airport, then about 1 h 15 via Eğirdir; there is no public transport to the gate.

properties.name: Yazılı Canyon
properties.desc: A cold green gorge in the Taurus above Sütçüler, with plane trees, pools you can swim in and a Greek inscription on the rock that gives the canyon its name. The Roman Via Sebaste ran through here, and the modern St Paul Trail follows the same line along the water.
properties.season: Jun–Sep for swimming; May and Oct for walking without the crowds
properties.tip: Walk beyond the first bridge where the day-trippers stop; the good pools and the inscription are another twenty minutes upstream.
properties.rev: Walkers rate the water and the shade highly in July; the complaints are the winding 80 km approach from Isparta, crowded weekends, litter near the entrance and water cold enough to hurt.
properties.entry: ₺150 (≈€3.50) per person plus a small vehicle fee
properties.onward: Isparta (ISE) airport, then about 1 h 45 south via Sütçüler, or 2 h north from Antalya (AYT).

properties.name: Sillyon
properties.desc: A flat-topped mesa rising out of the Pamphylian plain, fortified since Hellenistic times and never properly excavated. A landslide in 1969 took half the theatre down the slope, but the ramp gate, a Seljuk mosque and a stadium survive up top, along with the longest inscription in the Pamphylian dialect.
properties.season: Mar–May and Oct–Nov — no shade, no water, and the plain bakes in summer
properties.tip: Drive up to the village on the north side rather than attempting the old ramp from the south, and keep clear of the sheepdogs guarding the flocks on the plateau.
properties.rev: For ruin-hunters it is the best empty site near Antalya; everyone warns about the unmarked approach, aggressive dogs, unstable cliff edges and the fact that nothing is signed or fenced.
properties.onward: Antalya (AYT) about 40 min east, then 8 km of farm road north from the D400 near Serik; a car is essential.

properties.name: Selge
properties.desc: A Pisidian city at 1,000 metres above the Köprülü canyon, where the village of Altınkaya has grown into the ruins — goats on the theatre steps, a farmhouse leaning on a temple wall. The approach through eroded limestone pinnacles is as memorable as the site, and a Roman bridge crosses the gorge below.
properties.season: May–Jun and Sep–Oct — the last road is icy and sometimes closed in winter
properties.tip: Village children will offer to guide you and sell you flowers; agree a price first, and take the drive slowly — the final 12 km is single-track with drops.
properties.rev: The setting and the near-total absence of other tourists are what people remember; the complaints are the nerve-testing road, persistent child sellers and almost no interpretation on site.
properties.entry: Free — a small parking donation is usually asked
properties.onward: Antalya (AYT) about 2 h — the Beşkonak road up the Köprüçay, then the narrow climb past Oluk bridge; a car with decent clearance helps.

properties.name: Aspendos
properties.desc: The best-preserved Roman theatre anywhere, built around 160 AD and still roofed by its own stage wall, seating seven thousand under an intact vaulted gallery. Behind it, most visitors miss the acropolis and one of the finest surviving Roman aqueducts, with two pressure towers standing in open fields.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct; the opera and ballet festival runs in September
properties.tip: Walk the fifteen minutes uphill to the aqueduct and basilica behind the theatre — nine out of ten visitors never leave the auditorium.
properties.rev: The acoustics and preservation astonish people; the criticisms are heavy-handed restoration in concrete, souvenir stalls at the gate, and a bare hot site once you step outside the theatre.
properties.entry: €15 for foreigners · covered by Museum Pass Türkiye and the Mediterranean pass
properties.onward: Antalya (AYT) about 45 min east on the D400, then 4 km inland at Serik; every Antalya–Side bus passes the junction.

properties.name: Köprülü Canyon
properties.desc: Fourteen kilometres of gorge cut by the Köprüçay through cypress forest, with water cold enough to take your breath in August. It is Türkiye's rafting centre — grade II–III, wet and cheerful rather than frightening — and a Roman bridge still spans the narrowest point at Oluk.
properties.season: Apr–Oct for rafting; May–Jun has the strongest flow after snowmelt
properties.tip: Book the early morning run: by noon the river is a convoy of rafts and the riverside restaurants have queues an hour long.
properties.rev: A genuinely fun day and cheap by European standards; complaints are conveyor-belt operators, hard-sell photo packages, hour-long transfers and a river far busier than the brochures suggest.
properties.entry: National park ₺100 (≈€2.30) per car; rafting packages €25–40 with transfer
properties.onward: Antalya (AYT) about 1 h 30 via Serik and Beşkonak; almost everyone comes on an operator minibus from Side, Belek or Antalya.

properties.name: Antiochia in Pisidia
properties.desc: A Roman colony on a terrace above Yalvaç where Paul preached the first sermon recorded in Acts. The sanctuary of Augustus sits on a rock platform cut into the hillside, the aqueduct arches still march across the slope, and the basilica of St Paul keeps a mosaic floor naming its donors.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — 1,200 m up, so cold and often snowy from December
properties.tip: See the Yalvaç museum in town first; the fragments of the Latin Res Gestae inscription from the site are there, not on the hill.
properties.rev: Biblical-route travellers find it rewarding and nearly empty; others say the ruins are low and hard to read without a guide, the wind on the terrace is fierce, and the site is a long way from anything else.
properties.onward: Isparta (ISE) airport, then about 1 h 45 round the north end of Lake Eğirdir to Yalvaç.

properties.name: Side
properties.desc: A resort village built inside an ancient city, so a colonnaded street of souvenir shops runs past a 15,000-seat theatre and ends at the Temple of Apollo, whose five re-erected columns stand on the point with the sea behind them. The museum occupies the Roman baths by the agora.
properties.season: May–Jun and Sep–Oct — the peninsula is shoulder-to-shoulder in August
properties.tip: Photograph the Apollo columns twenty minutes before sunset from the western beach side, then eat away from the harbour where the menus are half the price.
properties.rev: The mix of ruins, beach and restaurants sells itself; the complaints are relentless souvenir touting, tourist-menu food, traffic on the peninsula and rubbish around the fringes of the site.
properties.entry: €10 for foreigners covering the ancient city and museum · Museum Pass Türkiye accepted
properties.onward: Antalya (AYT) about 1 h 15 east on the D400 to Manavgat, then 4 km to the peninsula; buses run every 20 min from Manavgat otogar.

properties.name: Titreyengöl
properties.desc: A small lagoon a few hundred metres behind the Sorgun beach, ringed by umbrella pines — the name means the trembling lake, from the marshy ground that shivers underfoot. Storks and terrapins in the reeds at dawn, a walking loop under the trees, and a long sand beach on the far side of the pines.
properties.season: May–Jun and Sep–Oct — the resort strip is saturated in August
properties.tip: Walk the lake loop at first light before the hotel joggers and the pedalos; the far bank is where the herons stand.
properties.rev: Guests of the surrounding all-inclusives rate the quiet and the pine shade; independent visitors complain the lakeshore is effectively hotel property and the water itself is stagnant and green in late summer.
properties.onward: Antalya (AYT) about 1 h 10 east on the D400, then 5 km south at Manavgat toward Sorgun; hotel shuttles serve the whole strip.

properties.name: Manavgat Waterfall
properties.desc: Not high — barely four metres — but wide, and the whole Manavgat river pours over a limestone shelf in a solid white sheet under plane trees. The appeal is the terrace of tea gardens along the bank and the river boats that run down from the town bridge to the sea.
properties.season: Apr–Jun for volume; the river runs lower and warmer by September
properties.tip: Skip the ticketed viewing park and take the river boat from Manavgat bridge instead — you see the same water, plus the delta and the fish restaurants.
properties.rev: Pleasant for an hour with cheap tea; almost every review notes that the fall is far smaller than expected, that the site is packed with coaches and stalls, and that it is not worth a long detour.
properties.onward: Antalya (AYT) about 1 h 15 east on the D400; the falls are 3 km north of Manavgat, and dolmuşes run there from the otogar.

properties.name: Seleukeia (Pamphylia)
properties.desc: A small Roman town lost in dense pine forest on a hill fifteen kilometres above Side, with an agora, baths and a market building whose relief frieze is still in place. Nobody sells tickets, birds are the only noise, and pine needles cover half the paving — the antidote to Side in August.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Nov — pleasant in the forest shade even at midday
properties.tip: Park at Bucakşeyhler village and take the marked path up; navigation apps often send cars onto a forest track that ends nowhere.
properties.rev: Those who find it call it a magical hour alone in the woods; the complaints are that it is genuinely hard to find, overgrown, and that the best reliefs are hidden behind scrub.
properties.onward: Antalya (AYT) about 1 h 20 to Manavgat, then 15 km north through Bucakşeyhler; there is no bus and no signage from the main road.

properties.name: Ormana
properties.desc: A cedar-and-juniper village at 1,000 metres built in düğmeli or buttoned style — horizontal timbers slotted into stone without a nail, so the walls read like woven fabric. Perhaps sixty of the old houses survive, some restored as guesthouses, above a valley of walnut and mulberry trees.
properties.season: May–Oct — snow closes some of the approach roads in midwinter
properties.tip: Ask at the Ormana Antique House to see inside a restored buttoned house; from the street you only see the outer skin of the technique.
properties.rev: Visitors are charmed by the architecture and the silence; the complaints are that a Turkish TV series brought weekend coach crowds, that several houses are derelict, and that food options are minimal.
properties.entry: Free — the Antique House charges a small fee
properties.onward: Antalya (AYT) about 2 h 15 via Manavgat and the İbradı road; hire a car, since buses reach İbradı at best once a day.

properties.name: İbradı
properties.desc: Antalya's smallest district, a stone town of under three thousand people wedged into cedar forest at the top of the Manavgat gorge. The road up from the coast is the real attraction: an hour of switchbacks through the canyon with the river far below, ending in cold mountain air and walnut orchards.
properties.season: May–Oct — winter brings snow and the gorge road ices over
properties.tip: Drive up from Manavgat and come down via Akseki rather than doubling back; the loop takes in the gorge, Ormana and the cedar ridges in one day.
properties.rev: Travellers praise the drive and the temperature drop; the honest downsides are almost nothing to do in the town itself, very few beds and shops that shut at dusk.
properties.onward: Antalya (AYT), then the D400 to Manavgat and 75 km north up the gorge road — about 2 h 15 in total by car.

properties.name: Altınbeşik Cave
properties.desc: Türkiye's largest underground lake, entered by rowing boat from a cliff mouth high above the Manavgat gorge. Two hundred metres of flooded passage, travertine dams glowing under the lamps, and a hall where the guide kills the light and the water goes completely black and silent.
properties.season: Mar–Jun when meltwater fills the lake; boats often stop running by late summer
properties.tip: Ring the national park office at Ürünlü before driving up — when the water level is wrong the boats do not run and the trip is wasted.
properties.rev: Those who catch it right describe it as unforgettable; the recurring complaints are wasted journeys when the boats are not operating, a rough final track and a very short visit for the drive involved.
properties.onward: Antalya (AYT) about 2 h 30 via Manavgat and İbradı, then a steep 7 km down to Ürünlü; a car is essential.

properties.name: Alara Castle and Alarahan
properties.desc: A Seljuk caravanserai of 1232 sits by the Alara river with its courtyard and stables intact, while the castle above is reached by a rock-cut tunnel of some 120 dark steps spiralling inside the crag. At the top: cisterns, a bath and a view down the whole valley to the sea.
properties.season: Mar–Jun and Sep–Nov — the tunnel climb is brutal in midsummer heat
properties.tip: Bring a torch — the tunnel staircase to the castle is genuinely unlit, wet in places and the reason most visitors turn back.
properties.rev: Those who make the climb rate it one of the best small sites in the region; complaints are the pitch-dark slippery tunnel, no railings, and a han partly given over to souvenir stalls.
properties.entry: Free for the han; small fee for the castle path
properties.onward: Gazipaşa (GZP) 1 h or Antalya (AYT) 1 h 30 on the D400, then 9 km inland at the Alara river bridge west of Alanya.

properties.name: Akseki
properties.desc: A Taurus town at 1,000 metres whose surrounding villages — Sarıhacılar, Güçlüköy, Belenalan — keep some of the finest vernacular stone-and-timber architecture in Türkiye, all cantilevered upper floors and flat earth roofs. The Seljuk Ulu Camii sits in the centre and cedar ridges rise on every side.
properties.season: May–Oct — heavy snow between December and March, though the town stays reachable
properties.tip: The town is the base, not the sight: drive out to Sarıhacılar and Güçlüköy, where whole streets of old houses survive unrestored.
properties.rev: Rated highly by anyone interested in vernacular architecture and empty mountain roads; complaints are the long drive from the coast, depopulated villages and very limited accommodation.
properties.onward: Antalya (AYT) about 2 h via Manavgat or 2 h 30 on the inland Konya road; buses run once or twice daily from Manavgat.

properties.name: Alanya Castle
properties.desc: Six kilometres of Seljuk wall wrapping a rock peninsula 250 metres above the sea, built by Alaeddin Keykubad after 1220. Inside are cisterns, a Byzantine chapel and a village of gardens; below stand the octagonal Red Tower and the five-bay dockyard, the only intact Seljuk shipyard left.
properties.season: Mar–Jun and Sep–Nov — the climb in July heat is punishing
properties.tip: Take the cable car up from Iskele and walk down through the Ehmedek quarter; the road up by taxi misses the whole inhabited part of the castle.
properties.rev: The views and the scale impress; complaints are that the inner castle is largely ruins and gardens, the walk is long and shadeless, and the site has separate tickets for tower, shipyard and citadel.
properties.entry: €12 for foreigners for the citadel · covered by Museum Pass Türkiye; cable car around ₺250 (≈€6)
properties.onward: Gazipaşa (GZP) 40 min or Antalya (AYT) 2 h on the D400; in town the cable car station is on the Iskele waterfront.

properties.name: Damlataş Cave
properties.desc: A small stalactite cave found by quarrymen in 1948 under the western cliff of the Alanya peninsula, with a chamber of orange-tinged columns fifteen metres down. Its constant 22 °C, 95 per cent humidity and high carbon dioxide are prescribed for asthma, and patients still sit inside for hours each morning.
properties.season: All year — the cool interior is a relief in July and August
properties.tip: It opens early for asthma treatment before general visiting, so arrive at opening if you want the chamber without a queue behind you.
properties.rev: Cheap, cool and ten minutes long — which is exactly the complaint: many find it too small and too crowded for the queue, and the air is genuinely heavy for anyone claustrophobic.
properties.onward: Gazipaşa (GZP) 40 min or Antalya (AYT) 2 h; the cave is at the foot of the castle rock beside Cleopatra Beach, walkable from central Alanya.

properties.name: Cleopatra Beach
properties.desc: Two kilometres of coarse pale sand on the western side of the Alanya peninsula, with the castle rock closing the view at one end. The grain is unusually large and light, the water deepens gently, and the legend that Mark Antony gave the beach to Cleopatra is repeated on every sign.
properties.season: May–Oct — the water stays swimmable into November
properties.tip: The far western end past the Atatürk statue is the least developed stretch, with the same sand and a fraction of the sunbeds.
properties.rev: Consistently rated the best city beach on this coast for water quality and Blue Flag standards; the complaints are density of sunbeds, loud beach bars and a promenade of identical tourist restaurants.
properties.onward: Gazipaşa (GZP) 40 min or Antalya (AYT) 2 h on the D400; the beach starts a five-minute walk west of central Alanya.

properties.name: Dim Çayı
properties.desc: A cold mountain river fifteen kilometres east of Alanya, where restaurants build wooden platforms straight over the water and you eat trout with your feet in the current. Upstream the valley narrows below the Dim dam, and Dim Cave sits on the slope above with a 400-metre lit gallery.
properties.season: Jun–Sep — the whole point is the cold water when the coast is at 38 °C
properties.tip: Drive past the first cluster of platforms near the mouth: the places 8 km upstream are cheaper, quieter and the water there is properly cold.
properties.rev: A local favourite for escaping the heat; complaints are traffic and parking chaos at weekends, water cold enough to hurt, and platform restaurants that charge per person for the seat.
properties.entry: Free along the river; Dim Cave ₺200 (≈€4.50)
properties.onward: Gazipaşa (GZP) 30 min or Antalya (AYT) 2 h to Alanya, then 15 km inland up the Kestel valley road; dolmuşes run in summer.

properties.name: Sapadere Canyon
properties.desc: A 750-metre boardwalk pinned to the wall of a narrow Taurus gorge above Alanya, ending at a waterfall and a pool that stays around 12 °C in August. Walls rise 400 metres on both sides, the light comes in slabs, and the drive up passes through goat villages and old terraced fields.
properties.season: May–Oct — the walkway closes in winter and after heavy rain
properties.tip: Get there before eleven; from midday the boardwalk becomes single-file with coach groups and the pool is unswimmable for the crowd.
properties.rev: The gorge and the cold water get good reviews; the complaints are a long winding minibus transfer, an entrance fee for a short walk, and rails and concrete that make it feel managed.
properties.onward: Gazipaşa (GZP) 45 min or Antalya (AYT) 2 h to Alanya, then 40 km of mountain road inland; most people come on a half-day tour.

properties.name: Gazipaşa
properties.desc: The last town before the Mersin border, where the Taurus comes down to the sea and the coast turns wild. Banana and avocado terraces, empty shingle beaches at Koru and Kahyalar, the ruins of Selinus where the emperor Trajan died in 117, and none of the resort density of Alanya an hour west.
properties.season: May–Oct for swimming; Mar–Apr for the coast road and the hills in flower
properties.tip: Drive the D400 east from town toward Anamur for half an hour — the cliff corniche past Kaledran is the best coastal driving in the province.
properties.rev: Travellers value the quiet and the prices next to Alanya; the honest downsides are little nightlife, patchy restaurant choice out of season and beaches with a strong undertow after wind.
properties.onward: Gazipaşa–Alanya (GZP) airport is 6 km from the town centre, with Alanya 45 min west on the D400.

properties.name: Anemurium
properties.desc: A Roman and early Byzantine city abandoned on the southernmost cape of Anatolia, its streets running downhill to a grey pebble beach. Three bath complexes still stand vaulted to roof height, and above them spreads a necropolis of some three hundred two-storey tomb houses, several with painted plaster and mosaic floors intact.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Nov — July and August are merciless with zero shade
properties.tip: Arrive two hours before sunset, walk the necropolis while the light is low, and swim off the site's own beach afterwards.
properties.rev: Repeatedly described as the most underrated ruin on the coast and often visitor-free, though people warn about heat, snakes in the tomb rubble, the rough final track and very little interpretation.
properties.onward: Gazipaşa (GZP) airport, then about 2 h 30 east on the D400; from Adana it is a long 5 h drive west.

properties.name: Mamure Castle
properties.desc: A castle standing directly on the beach with thirty-nine towers, a water-filled moat and palm trees growing in the courtyard. Roman in origin, rebuilt by the Karamanids and kept in use by the Ottomans into the nineteenth century, it is one of the few Turkish castles you enter across a proper drawbridge causeway.
