properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Nov — the walls throw no shade at midday
properties.tip: Walk the seaward rampart in the last hour before closing, when the storks are on the towers and the light comes off the water.
properties.rev: Visitors call it the most complete castle on the south coast and cheap for what it is, while grumbling about long restoration closures, missing handrails on the wall walk and the traffic noise from the D400.
properties.onward: Gazipaşa (GZP) airport, then 2 h 15 east on the D400; the castle is 6 km east of Anamur town, on the seaward side of the road.

properties.name: Aydıncık (Kelenderis)
properties.desc: A small town on the emptiest stretch of Turkey's south coast, built over ancient Kelenderis, whose harbour mosaic shows the same bay in the fifth century. The water off Sancak Burnu is clear enough to snorkel from the rocks, and the hotels are family pensions rather than resorts.
properties.season: Jun–Oct for the water; May and Nov for walking the coast
properties.tip: Drive 15 km east to the Gilindire cave, where 250 steps drop from the cliff to an underground lake at sea level with water you can touch.
properties.rev: People come for a coast with no tour buses and cheap fish, and mostly get it, but note the long drive from anywhere, limited food choice out of season and pebble rather than sand beaches.
properties.onward: Gazipaşa (GZP) airport, then 1 h 45 east on the D400, or 3 h west from Mersin; the coast road is slow and winding either way.

properties.name: Silifke
properties.desc: A working river town under a Byzantine castle, built on Hellenistic Seleucia on the Calycadnus. A Roman bridge still crosses the Göksu, the columns of a temple of Jupiter stand in a side street, and a plaque by the water marks where Frederick Barbarossa drowned on crusade in 1190.
properties.season: Mar–Jun and Sep–Nov — the valley is humid and heavy in high summer
properties.tip: Drive up to the castle café for the evening view over the Göksu delta, then eat the local strained yoghurt with the town's own black carrot pickles.
properties.rev: Travellers treat it as a base for Uzuncaburç and the delta and find the castle view better than expected, but say the town centre is traffic-heavy, plain, and short on decent places to sleep.
properties.entry: Castle free; museum ₺150 (≈€3.50) · covered by Museum Pass Türkiye
properties.onward: Çukurova (COV) airport, then 2 h 30 west on the D400; frequent Mersin–Silifke buses take about 1 h 30 from Mersin otogar.

properties.name: Uzuncaburç (Diocaesarea)
properties.desc: A temple city on a 1,200 m plateau where the ruins and the village share the same lanes. The Temple of Zeus Olbios carries some of the earliest Corinthian columns anywhere, thirty of them still standing, and a five-storey Hellenistic watchtower gives the village its name, meaning tall tower.
properties.season: May–Oct — the plateau road can ice over in winter and the site empties
properties.tip: Buy grape pekmez and tarhana from the village women at the temple gate; they are the reason the site is still lived in rather than fenced.
properties.rev: Visitors rate it well above its visitor numbers and love the cool mountain air after the coast, while noting the 28 km of switchbacks from Silifke, the goats in the theatre and the thin explanatory signage.
properties.onward: Çukurova (COV) airport, then 2 h 30 to Silifke and a slow 45-min climb up the mountain road; a few daily minibuses run from Silifke.

properties.name: Heaven and Hell Sinkholes
properties.desc: Two collapsed karst chasms in the limestone above the coast. You take 452 steps down into Heaven to a fifth-century chapel of the Virgin built across the mouth of a cave, where an underground river roars out of the dark. Hell is a sheer unclimbable shaft you can only stare into from a steel platform.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Nov — the climb back out of Heaven in August is punishing
properties.tip: Do the descent first thing in the morning and wear grippy shoes; the last stretch of steps to the cave mouth is wet, polished limestone.
properties.rev: People find the scale genuinely startling and the chapel worth the knees, but complain about the return climb, the slippery final steps, the souvenir stalls at the top and queueing on summer weekends.
properties.entry: ₺200 (≈€4.50) for the site, Asthma Cave a small extra fee
properties.onward: Çukurova (COV) airport, then 2 h west on the D400 and a 2 km climb up from Narlıkuyu; taxis wait at the junction.

properties.name: Narlıkuyu
properties.desc: A cove the size of a courtyard where a karst spring surfaces straight into the sea and fish restaurants stand on stilts over the water. In a one-room building beside them lies the floor of a fourth-century bath house, a mosaic of the Three Graces that survived because a village well sat on top of it.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — lunchtimes in August need booking
properties.tip: The mosaic building often shuts by five and over lunch, so see it before you sit down to eat, not after.
properties.rev: The setting and the fish get consistent praise; the recurring complaints are that the museum is one small room for the price, parking is chaotic and the shoreline is rock, not sand.
properties.entry: Mosaic museum ₺100 (≈€2.30) · covered by Museum Pass Türkiye
properties.onward: Çukurova (COV) airport, then 2 h west on the D400; it is signposted directly off the coast road below the Heaven and Hell turning.

properties.name: Kızkalesi (Maiden's Castle)
properties.desc: A Byzantine sea fort rebuilt by the Armenian kings of Cilicia, sitting on its own islet about 200 metres off a shallow sandy bay. You can swim, pedalo or take a boat out and walk the shell of towers with the water visible through the gateways. The town behind it is plain concrete holiday blocks.
properties.season: May–Jun and Sep–Oct — the beach is wall-to-wall Adana and Konya families in August
properties.tip: Swim out before nine in the morning; after ten the channel fills with pedalos and the boatmen start charging for the same crossing.
properties.rev: Almost everyone rates the swim-to-a-castle novelty highly, then complains that the island interior is rubble with no shade, the town is architecturally grim, and August turns the bay into a car park.
properties.entry: Free beach; boat return around ₺300 (≈€7) per person
properties.onward: Çukurova (COV) airport near Adana, then about 2 h west on the D400 through Mersin; Mersin–Silifke minibuses drop you on the highway.

properties.name: Korykos (Corycus)
properties.desc: The land half of the Kızkalesi pair: a big ruined shore castle facing its island twin across a submerged causeway, with the wreck of a Roman and Byzantine port town spread behind it. The real find is the necropolis on the hill inland, hundreds of rock-cut tombs with carved doors, ploughs and reliefs of the dead.
properties.season: Mar–May and Oct–Nov — the tombs are shadeless and the stone bakes in midsummer
properties.tip: Cross the highway and walk fifteen minutes uphill into the necropolis; ninety percent of visitors never leave the castle by the beach.
properties.rev: Visitors like that it is free, unfenced and empty compared with the beach opposite, but warn about loose masonry, litter in the corners, thorns in the necropolis and no signage in any language.
properties.entry: Free — the land castle is unstaffed
properties.onward: Çukurova (COV) airport, then 2 h west on the D400; it is a five-minute walk from the Kızkalesi beach strip.

properties.name: Kanlıdivane
properties.desc: An ancient town built around the rim of a limestone chasm 60 metres deep and the size of a football pitch. Five ruined basilicas stand at the edge, a Hellenistic tower carries a Greek dedication, and reliefs of a family and an armed soldier are cut into the sheer wall of the pit itself.
properties.season: Mar–May and Oct–Nov — no shade at all, and the plateau wind is welcome
properties.tip: Walk the full rim anticlockwise to find the wall reliefs from above; from the main path they are invisible.
properties.rev: Those who make the detour call it the most atmospheric site on this coast and are surprised to have it to themselves; the gripes are the unmarked turning, the absent guardian and the total lack of railings.
properties.entry: Small fee — check locally; often unstaffed
properties.onward: Çukurova (COV) airport, then 1 h 45 west on the D400 and 3 km inland at the Kumkuyu turning — you need a car.

properties.name: Cehennemdere Valley
properties.desc: A steep gorge in the Taurus behind Erdemli, protected for its Cilician fir and cedar forest. A cold stream drops through a series of small falls between walls of grey limestone, and the temperature falls fifteen degrees in the half-hour drive up from the coastal highway.
properties.season: May–Oct — the forest road is unreliable after heavy winter rain
properties.tip: The strict reserve core needs forestry permission, so aim for the picnic ground and stream below it, which does not.
properties.rev: Day-trippers from Mersin come for the cold water and the shade and rate it highly in July; complaints centre on the unpaved final kilometres, weekend picnic litter and the absence of any marked trail.
properties.entry: Free — a small forestry picnic-ground fee in summer
properties.onward: Çukurova (COV) airport, then 1 h 30 to Erdemli on the D400 and about 40 min up the forest road; a car is essential.

properties.name: The Cilician Gates
properties.desc: The pass that every army between Alexander and the Crusaders used to get from the Anatolian plateau down to the Cilician plain: a cleft in the Taurus where the road, the old caravan track and a Roman rock-cut inscription share one narrow gorge. The motorway now tunnels past it at speed.
properties.season: Apr–Nov — snow and fog close the old road in midwinter
properties.tip: Leave the O-21 at Gülek and take the old road through the village; the actual gorge and the ruined Byzantine castle above it are invisible from the motorway.
properties.rev: History-minded drivers find the sense of the choke point still legible and the climb spectacular, but many arrive expecting a monument and find only rock, guardrails and lorries.
properties.onward: Çukurova (COV) airport, then 45 min north-west on the O-21 towards Niğde; take the Gülek exit for the old road.

properties.name: Tarsus
properties.desc: Saint Paul's home town, layered rather than pretty. Cleopatra's Gate stands at the old harbour road, a stretch of Roman street lies four metres below today's pavement behind glass, and a well in a courtyard is shown as Paul's, complete with a bucket you can drink from. Restored Ottoman houses fill the block around it.
properties.season: Mar–May and Oct–Nov — the Çukurova humidity in July and August is genuinely unpleasant
properties.tip: Walk the excavated Roman road at the end of the day, then drive out to the waterfall for tea and fried fish where the town actually goes.
properties.rev: Pilgrims and history readers rate the concentration of sites in ten walkable blocks; almost everyone mentions the sticky heat, the heavy traffic and how modest Cleopatra's Gate looks in the flesh.
properties.entry: Mostly free; Saint Paul's Well and the museum around ₺100 (≈€2.30) each
properties.onward: Çukurova (COV) airport, then 30 min on the O-51; Adana–Mersin trains stop at Tarsus roughly hourly.

properties.name: Kapıkaya Canyon
properties.desc: A narrow limestone canyon on the Çakıt below Karaisalı, walked on a wooden boardwalk bolted to the rock a couple of metres above cold green water. It is short, maybe an hour there and back, and it pairs naturally with the Varda viaduct twenty minutes away.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — spring meltwater can close the boardwalk
properties.tip: Come on a weekday; at weekends the boardwalk becomes a single-file queue of Adana families with picnic coolers.
properties.rev: Visitors call it a genuine relief from Çukurova heat and good for children, while complaining about weekend crowding, slippery planks, litter at the entrance and a car park attendant with informal pricing.
properties.onward: Çukurova (COV) airport, then 1 h north-west via Karaisalı; the last few kilometres are narrow but paved.

properties.name: Varda Viaduct
properties.desc: A German-built stone arch railway bridge of 1912 on the old Baghdad Railway, 98 metres above the Çakıt gorge near Karaisalı. Trains still cross it. Most people know it as the bridge Bond falls from in the opening of Skyfall, and the regional train from Adana stops at Hacıkırı right beside it.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Nov — the gorge is an oven in high summer
properties.tip: Take the cheap Adana–Karaisalı regional train rather than driving: you cross the viaduct instead of just looking at it, and it costs less than a coffee.
properties.rev: The train ride is the part people rave about; the complaints are that walking out onto the bridge is now fenced off and policed, the timetable is sparse, and the viewpoint involves a dusty scramble.
properties.onward: Çukurova (COV) airport, then 1 h by road to Karaisalı, or take the local train from Adana station to Hacıkırı.

properties.name: Adana Kebap and Şalgam
properties.desc: Hand-minced lamb with tail fat pressed onto a wide flat skewer over oak charcoal, served with sumac onions, grilled long peppers and a glass of şalgam, the salty fermented juice of turnip and black carrot. The city eats liver kebab for breakfast at seven in the morning and treats the whole thing as a licensed ritual.
properties.season: Year-round — Oct–May is more comfortable for eating outdoors
properties.tip: Ask for acılı şalgam and order ciğer at breakfast rather than dinner; that is when the liver is fresh and when the kebapçıs around Kazancılar are full.
properties.rev: Nearly everyone says Adana kebap in Adana is a different dish from Adana kebap elsewhere; the caveats are the fat content, the fierce chilli in the local version and the heat and diesel of the bazaar in summer.
properties.entry: Free — a portion with şalgam and bread around ₺400–600 (≈€9–13)
properties.onward: Çukurova (COV) airport, then 40 min into the centre; the kebap houses cluster around the old bazaar and Kuruköprü.

properties.name: Sabancı Central Mosque
properties.desc: A 1998 mosque of deliberately imperial ambition on the bank of the Seyhan: six minarets, a 54-metre dome and room for tens of thousands, built with Sabancı family money in a classical Ottoman idiom. Seen across the water at dusk with the Stone Bridge in front of it, the theatre works.
properties.season: Year-round — visit in the early morning or after sunset in July and August
properties.tip: Photograph it from the far bank near the Merkez Park footbridge rather than from the forecourt, where you cannot get the minarets in.
properties.rev: Visitors are impressed by the sheer scale and the calm inside, while a good number find it a modern pastiche of Ottoman architecture and note that the tourist entrance and dress rules are enforced strictly.
properties.entry: Free — modest dress, headscarves lent at the door
properties.onward: Çukurova (COV) airport, then 40 min into Adana; it stands beside the Stone Bridge on the west bank.

properties.name: Adana Stone Bridge
properties.desc: A Roman bridge that has carried traffic over the Seyhan for nearly nineteen centuries and now carries only pedestrians. Fourteen of its original twenty-one arches survive, lit at night, linking the old bazaar quarter with the riverside parks where the whole city walks after dark in summer.
properties.season: Year-round — evenings only from June to September, when daytime hits 40 °C
properties.tip: Cross from the Ulu Cami side at dusk so the mosque, the bridge and the river come at you in the right order.
properties.rev: Locals and visitors alike treat the evening crossing as the best free thing in Adana; the usual complaints are heavy-handed restoration, the river's smell in late summer and persistent hawkers at both ends.
properties.onward: Çukurova (COV) airport, then 40 min into the city; the bridge is a 15-min walk from the old bazaar.

properties.name: Yumurtalık
properties.desc: Medieval Ayas, the port Marco Polo sailed from in 1271, now a low-key beach town where Adana empties itself at weekends. A ruined sea tower stands offshore, the fish restaurants are cheap, and the lagoons east of town are a protected reserve with flamingos, pelicans and nesting sea turtles.
properties.season: Jun–Sep for swimming; Nov–Mar for the birds on the lagoons
properties.tip: Skip the town beach and drive to the Yumurtalık lagoon reserve at first light, when the flamingo flocks are still on the near shore.
properties.rev: Weekenders like the prices, the fish and the fact that no one is selling anything; the honest downsides are the oil terminal and İskenderun industry on the skyline, murky water after storms and near-total gridlock on August Sundays.
properties.entry: Free; lagoon reserve free but the tracks need a high car
properties.onward: Çukurova (COV) airport, then about 1 h 15 east via Ceyhan; summer minibuses run from Adana otogar.

properties.name: Yılankale (Snake Castle)
properties.desc: An Armenian castle of about 1200 clamped to a bare rock above the Ceyhan river, its curtain walls following every kink of the crag. Local stories make it the house of Şahmaran, the half-woman half-snake of Cilician folklore. Twenty-five minutes of scrambling puts you on walls with the whole Çukurova underneath.
properties.season: Mar–May and Oct–Nov — the rock reflects heat viciously in summer
properties.tip: Go in the last two hours of daylight and wear proper shoes; the path is loose limestone with no railings and no lighting on the way down.
properties.rev: Rated highly by anyone who likes empty castles with big views, and criticised for exactly what makes it good: no guardrails, no signs, no ticket office, no water and a scramble that is not for small children.
properties.onward: Çukurova (COV) airport, then 45 min east on the O-52 towards Ceyhan; the rock is visible from the motorway.

properties.name: Arsuz
properties.desc: Ancient Rhosus, and the one stretch of Hatay coast people actually swim from: a long shallow bay of coarse sand under the Amanus, a seafront promenade of İskenderun families, and fish restaurants that serve Arab mezze alongside the standard raki table. Quiet and cheap outside July and August.
properties.season: Jun–Sep for swimming; May and Oct for the promenade without crowds
properties.tip: Sit down to eat where the mezze arrive unasked on a tray to choose from; that is the Hatay convention and it is how you find the good tables.
properties.rev: Regulars praise the value and the food and say the sea is cleaner than İskenderun's; the standard complaints are the industrial skyline to the north, unremarkable modern building and a very Turkish rather than international resort feel.
properties.onward: Hatay (HTY) airport, then about 1 h via İskenderun and the coast road south.

properties.name: Musa Dağı
properties.desc: A 1,280-metre limestone ridge dropping straight into the sea, wooded with pine and carob and cut by shepherd tracks. In 1915 the people of six Armenian villages held out on this mountain for forty days until French warships took them off, the episode Franz Werfel turned into a novel. The view runs from the Orontes delta to Syria.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Oct–Nov — summer is too hot for the ascent and winter fog sits on the ridge
properties.tip: There is no waymarked route to the top, so start from Vakıflı and ask in the village; going up blind on forest tracks wastes a day.
properties.rev: Walkers rate the sea views and the emptiness; the honest picture is unmarked paths, no water on the ridge, ticks in spring, sensitivity about the border zone and nothing at all in the way of infrastructure.
properties.onward: Hatay (HTY) airport, then 1 h to Samandağ; drive up through Vakıflı and park where the asphalt ends.

properties.name: Anavarza (Anazarbus)
properties.desc: A Roman city on the cotton plain with a triumphal arch still standing, a colonnaded street running for over two kilometres and mosaics under shelters, all beneath a knife-edge rock ridge carrying an Armenian castle. It was the capital of Cilician Armenia, and the castle walk along the ridge is the best thing in the province.
properties.season: Mar–May and Oct–Nov — the plain routinely passes 40 °C in July and August
properties.tip: Start the castle path from behind the village mosque with two litres of water; it is 45 hot minutes up and there is nothing at the top.
properties.rev: People who make the climb call the ridge castle unforgettable and are astonished to be alone there; the standard warnings are heat, snakes, no shade, no water and a rough track for the last few kilometres.
properties.entry: Small fee — check locally; the village mosaic museum is separate
properties.onward: Çukurova (COV) airport, then about 1 h 15 north-east via Ceyhan and Kozan; there is no useful public transport.

properties.name: Titus Tunnel
properties.desc: A flood-diversion channel nearly 1,400 metres long, cut through solid rock by legionaries and prisoners to stop a mountain torrent silting up the harbour of Seleucia Pieria. You walk through it: open-air trench with walls thirty metres high, then a long roofed section where the chisel marks are still crisp on the rock.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Nov — after heavy rain water runs through the tunnel floor
properties.tip: Climb the path above the tunnel mouth to the Beşikli cave tombs, rock-cut family graves most people miss entirely.
properties.rev: Engineering-minded visitors find it astonishing for the price and love that you can actually walk it; the usual gripes are slippery wet rock, no lighting, uneven steps and thin signposting from the coast road.
properties.onward: Hatay (HTY) airport, then 1 h to Samandağ and 4 km on to Çevlik; the last stretch is signposted from the harbour.

properties.name: Vakıflı
properties.desc: The last Armenian village in Türkiye, about a hundred people on the seaward slope of Musa Dağı among orange and laurel groves. There is one church, Surp Asdvadzadzin, a co-operative selling laurel soap and bitter orange jam, and a dialect of Western Armenian that other Armenians struggle to follow.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Nov — the citrus harvest runs through late autumn
properties.tip: Buy from the village co-operative rather than the roadside stalls below; the laurel soap and the jam are made a hundred metres from where they are sold.
properties.rev: Visitors describe an ordinary, slightly weary farming village rather than a museum, which is the point; some feel intrusive, and post-earthquake damage and a very small ageing population are visible.
properties.onward: Hatay (HTY) airport, then about 1 h via Samandağ and a short climb up the Musa Dağı road.

properties.name: Samandağ
properties.desc: Fourteen kilometres of dark volcanic sand where the Orontes finally reaches the sea, backed by an Arab-Alawite farming district with its own food, dialect and calendar. Green and loggerhead turtles nest along the beach, and the small port of Çevlik at the northern end sits on ancient Seleucia Pieria.
properties.season: May–Jun and Sep–Oct — turtle nesting restricts parts of the beach in high summer
properties.tip: Eat where the signs are in Arabic as well as Turkish, and ask for oruk and the local hummus, which is nothing like the Istanbul version.
properties.rev: People value the emptiness, the food and the lack of resorts, but are blunt about plastic and driftwood along the tideline, the earthquake rubble dumped near the coast after 2023 and the shortage of decent accommodation.
properties.onward: Hatay (HTY) airport, then about 1 h west over the hills from Antakya; minibuses run from Antakya to Samandağ all day.

properties.name: Yayladağı and Kel Dağı
properties.desc: Türkiye's southernmost district, a cool forested upland pressed against the Syrian border. Above it rises Kel Dağı, ancient Mount Casius, holy to Baal Zaphon and later to Zeus, at 1,726 metres the highest thing on this coast. The town below was badly damaged in 2023 and is still rebuilding.
properties.season: May–Oct — winter brings fog, snow and closed forest roads
properties.tip: The summit sits in a military zone and needs permission, so plan for the forest roads and viewpoints below it rather than the top.
properties.rev: Those who go describe genuinely wild country and total absence of tourism; they also report checkpoints, patchy phone signal, earthquake damage in the town and confusion over where you are and are not allowed to walk.
properties.entry: Free — carry your passport for the checkpoints
properties.onward: Hatay (HTY) airport, then about 1 h 15 south of Antakya on a good but winding road.

properties.name: Harbiye (Daphne)
properties.desc: The laurel-shaded ravine eight kilometres south of Antakya that Roman Antioch used as its pleasure suburb. Springs drop through a series of small falls between plane trees, and the mosaics that made the Hatay museum famous were lifted from villas on these slopes. Tea platforms are built out over the water.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — the water is thinnest in late summer
properties.tip: Walk to the upper falls above the café terraces, where the noise drops away and the laurel smell is strongest.
properties.rev: The cool and the noise of water are the draw, especially in July; visitors complain that cafés have colonised almost every viewpoint, that litter builds up at weekends and that the falls are smaller than the photographs suggest.
properties.entry: Free to enter the valley; café terraces expect an order
properties.onward: Hatay (HTY) airport, then 30 min; Antakya–Harbiye dolmuşes leave every few minutes from the city.

properties.name: Hatay Archaeology Museum
properties.desc: One of the largest collections of Roman mosaics anywhere, most of it lifted from the villas of Daphne just up the valley. The Buffet mosaic, Oceanus and Tethys, and the black-humoured Evil Eye panel are laid out at eye level in a purpose-built hall, so you read them as pictures rather than as floors.
properties.season: Year-round — an obvious refuge on a 40 °C afternoon
properties.tip: Start at the far end with the Yakto mosaic's border of everyday Antioch street scenes; it is the single most informative object in the building and most people walk past it.
properties.rev: Mosaic enthusiasts routinely call it world-class and better presented than Zeugma; complaints are thin English labelling, gallery closures for post-earthquake works, and the fact that the city outside gives you nothing else to do.
properties.entry: €9 for foreigners · covered by Museum Pass Türkiye
properties.onward: Hatay (HTY) airport, then 30 min into Antakya; the museum is on the ring road at the edge of the centre.

properties.name: Antakya Old Town
properties.desc: Ancient Antioch, and until February 2023 the finest surviving Arab-Turkish old town in the country: stone courtyard houses, a covered bazaar, and Habib-i Neccar, the oldest mosque in Anatolia. The earthquakes flattened most of it. What you visit now is a reconstruction site with pockets of restored street, and a food culture that refused to die.
properties.season: Mar–May and Oct–Nov — verify what is open before you commit to the trip
properties.tip: Eat first and sightsee second: the künefe and the Antakya breakfast spreads came back long before the buildings did.
properties.rev: Recent visitors describe a city that is half building site and emotionally heavy going, while insisting the food and the hospitality are still the best in Türkiye; almost all advise checking hotel and restaurant status before travelling.
properties.entry: Free to walk; individual monuments vary and several remain closed
properties.onward: Hatay (HTY) airport, back in service since late 2023, then 30 min into town; otherwise Çukurova (COV) and about 3 h by road.

properties.name: Church of Saint Peter
properties.desc: A cave hollowed into the flank of Mount Staurin above Antakya, claimed as one of the earliest Christian meeting places and traditionally linked to Peter himself. Behind the Crusader stone facade the interior is bare rock with a fragment of floor mosaic and a narrow escape tunnel cut into the hillside.
properties.season: Mar–May and Oct–Nov — check the reopening status before you plan around it
properties.tip: The site was damaged in 2023 and access has come and gone since, so telephone the Hatay museum before driving up the hill.
properties.rev: Pilgrims find the austerity moving and the setting on the mountainside striking; secular visitors often say it is one small cave for the ticket price, and everyone flags earthquake-related closures.
properties.entry: €6 for foreigners when open · covered by Museum Pass Türkiye — verify before travelling
properties.onward: Hatay (HTY) airport, then 30 min to Antakya and 3 km up the hill road towards Reyhanlı; a taxi is easiest.

properties.name: Hierapolis Castabala
properties.desc: A colonnaded street of standing columns running straight across a cotton plain, with a medieval castle on the crag behind it. This was the sanctuary of Artemis Perasia, whose priestesses were said to walk barefoot over hot coals. Nothing is fenced, nobody sells tickets, and the columns are usually shared with grazing sheep.
properties.season: Mar–May and Oct–Nov — the plain is 40 °C and shadeless in summer
properties.tip: Go late in the afternoon when the low sun lines up the whole colonnade, and walk up to the castle for the view back down over it.
properties.rev: Visitors are surprised such a photogenic site is empty and free, and equally surprised by the total absence of facilities, shade, signage and any way of getting there without a car.
properties.onward: Çukurova (COV) airport, then about 1 h 30 east on the O-52 and 10 km north of Osmaniye.

properties.name: Belen Pass
properties.desc: The Syrian Gates of antiquity: the road climbs from the Gulf of İskenderun to 750 metres through pine forest and a permanent cold wind, with the whole bay laid out behind you. Cyrus, Alexander and every caravan to Aleppo came this way. At the western foot stands the Pillar of Jonah, where the prophet was supposedly put ashore.
properties.season: Year-round — fog and ice are common on the top in January and February
properties.tip: Take the old road over the pass instead of the motorway tunnel and stop at a roadside grill in Belen town for the local mountain cheese.
properties.rev: Drivers enjoy the temperature drop and the view back over the bay, while noting heavy lorry traffic on the old road, a scruffy strip of development in Belen itself and little to mark the historic pass.
properties.onward: Hatay (HTY) airport, then 45 min north; the pass sits on the old road between İskenderun and Antakya.

properties.name: Karatepe-Aslantaş
properties.desc: A late Hittite hill fort of the eighth century BC in pine woods above a reservoir, where the carved gate slabs are still set where they were found. The banquet scenes, ships and a mother nursing a child under a tree sit alongside the bilingual Phoenician and Luwian inscription that finally allowed hieroglyphic Luwian to be read.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Nov — the site closes early in winter and the woods are wet
properties.tip: The reliefs are shown open-air in situ under shelters on a one-way woodland circuit, so allow an hour rather than the twenty minutes people plan.
properties.rev: Anyone with an interest in the Hittite world rates it among Turkey's most rewarding small sites; the complaints are the long approach road, restricted photography in places and a guardian who moves groups along briskly.
properties.onward: Çukurova (COV) airport, then about 1 h 45 north-east via Kadirli; the last 20 km run through forest with no signage in English.

properties.name: Zorkun Yayla
properties.desc: Osmaniye's summer escape, 1,550 metres up in the pine and juniper of the Nur Mountains, reached by twenty-six kilometres of switchbacks off the hot plain. It is a working yayla of wooden summer houses, cold spring taps, tea gardens and afternoon mist that comes over the ridge like a lid.
properties.season: Jun–Sep — snowbound and largely shuttered from December to March
properties.tip: Come on a weekday and be up there before four, because the fog usually rolls in from the Mediterranean side by late afternoon and takes the view with it.
properties.rev: Turkish visitors love the twenty-degree temperature drop and the pine air; foreign visitors note the ramshackle building, weekend traffic on a narrow road and that there is little to do beyond walking and eating.
properties.onward: Çukurova (COV) airport, then 1 h 30 east to Osmaniye and about 45 min of mountain road; dolmuşes run up in summer.

properties.name: Maraş Ice Cream
properties.desc: Goat milk, sugar and salep root from the mountains above the city, beaten in a churn until it is elastic enough to cut with a knife and eat with a fork. In its home town it is served in slabs on a plate, not in cones, and the theatrical vendor act that tourists know from Istanbul is largely absent.
properties.season: Year-round — the old shops keep going through winter, which is when locals prefer it
properties.tip: Order it kesme, cut in slices on a plate with a knife and fork, and eat it in one of the long-established shops in the centre rather than a chain kiosk.
properties.rev: Almost everyone says the texture is a different product from supermarket ice cream and worth the detour; the criticisms are how sweet and chewy it is, inflated prices in tourist-facing shops and short opening hours.
properties.entry: Free — a plate of kesme dondurma around ₺150 (≈€3.50)
properties.onward: Kahramanmaraş (KCM) airport, then 30 min into the centre; the historic shops are within walking distance of each other.

properties.name: Döngel Caves
properties.desc: A cave system in the hills north of Kahramanmaraş where a stream still runs through the lower galleries and travertine curtains hang in chambers big enough to lose a group in. Above the village a waterfall drops into a pool with trout restaurants on the bank, which is why most people actually come.
properties.season: May–Oct — the access road is unreliable when snow lies on the hills
properties.tip: Bring your own torch; the fixed lighting works only in the developed section and the interesting galleries start where it stops.
properties.rev: Domestic visitors like the combination of cave, waterfall and cheap trout; they warn about the rough last stretch of road, mud underfoot in the cave, weak lighting and weekend crowds at the restaurants.
properties.onward: Kahramanmaraş (KCM) airport, then about 1 h 15 north of the city on progressively narrower roads; a car is essential.

properties.name: Kahramanmaraş Castle
properties.desc: A castle mound in the middle of the city, occupied since Hittite times and rebuilt by Romans, Armenians, Dulkadirs and Ottomans in turn. The famous Maraş lion came off this hill. Since February 2023 it has stood over a city rebuilding itself, and parts of the walls are under restoration scaffolding.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Nov — the summer plain is brutally hot, winter cold and grey
properties.tip: Check with the city museum whether the ramp to the upper walls has reopened before climbing the hill, and combine it with the archaeological museum below.
properties.rev: Visitors value the view and the layered history, but are honest that access has been intermittent since the earthquakes, restoration works block parts of the circuit and the surrounding streets are a construction site.
properties.entry: Free when open; the museum around ₺150 (≈€3.50) · Museum Pass Türkiye accepted
properties.onward: Kahramanmaraş (KCM) airport, then 30 min into town; Çukurova (COV) is about 2 h 30 by road.

properties.name: Germanicia Mosaics
properties.desc: A Roman city found by accident in 2007 when looters dug through a garden in a residential quarter of Kahramanmaraş. Under metal shelters between apartment blocks lie fifth and sixth-century villa floors with hunting scenes, animals and geometric borders in remarkably fresh colour. Excavation continues in gaps between houses.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Nov — the shelters get very hot in midsummer
properties.tip: Ask at the city archaeological museum first; the shelters are locked and a guardian has to come and open them for you.
properties.rev: Those who get inside call the mosaics unexpectedly fine for a site nobody has heard of; the recurring frustration is erratic opening, no signage, no English information and post-earthquake disruption to the district.
properties.entry: Small fee — check locally at the Kahramanmaraş museum
properties.onward: Kahramanmaraş (KCM) airport, then 30 min into the city; the site is inside the Dulkadiroğlu quarter, easiest by taxi.

properties.name: Yedikuyular Ski Centre
properties.desc: A small ski area on Ahır Dağı at around 2,000 to 2,300 metres, twenty-five kilometres above Kahramanmaraş. Two lifts, a handful of pistes and a plateau that looks straight down onto the Çukurova haze. It is a locals' hill: cheap lift passes, families on hired gear, and Maraş ice cream at the base station in the snow.
properties.season: Late Dec–Mar for snow; Jun–Sep for the plateau meadows and paragliding
properties.tip: Go midweek and hire everything at the base; weekend queues at the single chairlift eat most of the skiing day.
properties.rev: Turkish skiers rate it as excellent value with reliable January snow; the caveats are very few runs, one chairlift, patchy snowmaking and a short access road that ices up.
properties.onward: Kahramanmaraş (KCM) airport, then 30 min to the city and about 45 min up the mountain road.

properties.name: Odunpazarı
properties.desc: Eskişehir's Ottoman quarter: narrow cobbled lanes of timber houses painted lilac, mustard and turquoise, climbing a low hill above the modern city. Meerschaum — the soft white stone carved into pipes here for two centuries — is sold in every second shop. The stacked-timber OMM modern art museum at the bottom of the hill is a genuinely good building.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — Eskişehir winters are grey and bitter
properties.tip: Buy meerschaum from a workshop where someone is actually carving; the polished 'antique' pipes in the souvenir shops are mostly pressed dust, not block stone.
properties.rev: Students and weekenders love the colour and the cafés; the recurring gripe is that the restoration has tipped into theme-park, with too many identical gift shops and inflated café prices.
properties.onward: Ankara Esenboğa (ESB) or Istanbul, then the YHT high-speed train to Eskişehir — the station is a 20-minute walk from Odunpazarı.

properties.name: Seyitgazi Complex
properties.desc: A Seljuk and Ottoman complex piled on a rock spur above a small town, built around the tomb of an eighth-century Arab warrior-saint and, beside it, an improbably long sarcophagus said to hold a Byzantine princess who loved him. Dervish cells, a mosque and a cavernous kitchen ring the courtyard, and pilgrims still tie cloth to the window grilles.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — exposed and freezing on the spur in winter
properties.tip: Combine it with Midas City in one loop south from Eskişehir; the two are 30 km apart and both need a car anyway.
properties.rev: Visitors describe an atmospheric, still-functioning shrine rather than a museum, with the caveats that opening hours are erratic, restoration works recur, and English information is essentially absent.
properties.entry: Free · donations expected at the tomb
properties.onward: Eskişehir by YHT train, then 45 km south on the D260; minibuses run from Eskişehir but leave you a walk up to the complex.

properties.name: Midas City & the Phrygian Valley
properties.desc: A 17-metre rock façade carved with a geometric lattice and the name MIDAI stands above a village of poplar trees, and behind it a plateau of tunnelled stairways, rock altars and cult niches. The wider Phrygian Valley runs south through Han and Ihsaniye in tufa canyons and fairy chimneys — Cappadocia's landscape with a thousandth of the traffic.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — snow closes the plateau tracks in winter
properties.tip: Take the dark stepped tunnel down through the rock behind the monument — it is unlit, you need a phone torch, and almost nobody finds it.
properties.rev: Those who make it call the emptiness the whole point, but expect an unstaffed site, patchy signage, a long unpaved approach, and nowhere to buy so much as water.
properties.onward: Eskişehir by YHT train, then 80 km south via Seyitgazi and Han on the D260; there is no useful bus and you need a car.

properties.name: Sakarbaşı Springs
properties.desc: The Sakarya, one of Türkiye's great rivers, starts here as a set of turquoise spring pools bubbling up through white sand in a flat field near Çifteler. The water is startlingly clear and cold, watercress grows in the outflow, and within a few hundred metres it is already a proper river running north.
properties.season: May–Sep — the colour is best in strong overhead light
properties.tip: The pools are on the Çifteler stud farm road and easy to drive past; look for the picnic grove and follow the concrete channel upstream to the boils.
properties.rev: A pleasant, genuinely pretty half-hour that Turkish families rate for picnics, though visitors note litter around the picnic tables and that swimming in the springs is prohibited.
properties.onward: Eskişehir by YHT train, then 60 km southeast via Mahmudiye to Çifteler; minibuses run to Çifteler town but the springs need a taxi or car.

properties.name: Nallıhan Coloured Hills
properties.desc: Bands of red, ochre, violet and pale green run across bare eroded ridges above the Sarıyar reservoir — lignite, clay and iron oxide laid down in an old lake bed and stripped naked by the wind. From the Davutoğlan viewpoint the striping runs for kilometres with the blue reservoir underneath it.
properties.season: Mar–May and Oct–Nov — colour saturates after rain and in low sun
properties.tip: Late afternoon light lifts the reds; at midday the whole ridge goes flat and grey, which is why most people's photos are disappointing.
properties.rev: Photographers travel from Ankara for it and rarely regret the trip, though the tracks up to the best angles are unpaved, unsigned and rutted enough to worry a low hire car.
properties.onward: Ankara Esenboğa (ESB) airport, then 160 km west via Beypazarı; no public transport reaches the viewpoints.

properties.name: Kubad Abad Palace
properties.desc: The lakeside summer palace of Sultan Kayqubad I, built in the 1220s on the southwest shore of Beyşehir with its own island retreat offshore. Only low walls and floor plans survive, but the star-shaped lustre tiles found here — double-headed eagles, peacocks, sirens, and drinking princes — are the finest Seljuk figural ceramics known, now in Konya's Karatay Medrese.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — muddy access in winter
properties.tip: See the Karatay Medrese tile collection in Konya either before or after, otherwise the site is just foundations by a reed bed.
properties.rev: Rewarding for anyone who has seen the tiles first; others describe an unstaffed, weedy enclosure at the end of a rough shore road with almost no interpretation.
properties.onward: Konya (KYA) airport, then to Beyşehir and 35 km along the southwest shore towards Gölyaka; a car is required.

properties.name: Nallıhan Bird Sanctuary
properties.desc: Where the Sarıyar reservoir backs up against bare striped hills, a shallow marsh has become one of inland Anatolia's best bird stops — around 170 species logged, including flamingos, black storks and pygmy cormorants. There is a wooden hide and an observation terrace above the water, and generally nobody else in it.
properties.season: Mar–May and Sep–Nov for migration; the marsh shrinks badly by August
properties.tip: Bring your own binoculars and go at first light — by ten the heat haze off the reservoir wrecks the viewing and the birds are gone from the shallows.
properties.rev: Birders rate it highly in spring passage, but casual visitors often arrive at midday, see distant specks, and find the access track dusty and the facilities minimal.
properties.onward: Ankara Esenboğa (ESB) airport, then 160 km west via Beypazarı to Davutoğlan; a car is essentially required.

properties.name: Balıkdamı Wetland
properties.desc: Where the Sakarya slows and spreads into reed beds south of Sivrihisar, over 200 bird species have been recorded — cranes, glossy ibis, purple heron, and a heavy spring passage of waders. It is flat, wet, mosquito-ridden and completely undeveloped, which is exactly why the birds are there.
properties.season: Mar–May and Sep–Nov — dry and dull by late summer
properties.tip: Go at dawn, wear boots, and bring insect repellent; the tracks between the reed beds flood after rain and there is no hide worth the name.
properties.rev: Serious birders rate it among inland Türkiye's best wetlands; casual visitors find muddy tracks, no facilities, aggressive mosquitoes and shooting pressure in autumn.
properties.onward: Eskişehir or Ankara to Sivrihisar on the D200, then about 25 km south on village roads; a car with some clearance is sensible.

properties.name: Derebucak Caves
properties.desc: Karst country south of Beyşehir riddled with cave systems: Balatini with its lit chambers of stalactites, and Körükini and Suluin, where an underground river runs out of the rock into a wooded gorge. The forest here is cedar and juniper, the water is snowmelt cold, and the whole area sees a fraction of the visitors it merits.
properties.season: May–Oct — the river caves are dangerous or shut in the wet months
properties.tip: Take a jacket even in August; the show cave stays around 12 °C and the river cave mouth is colder still.
properties.rev: Cool, uncrowded and genuinely scenic, but access is on winding forest roads, lighting and walkways are basic, and opening is seasonal and loosely enforced.
properties.onward: Konya (KYA) airport, then 130 km southwest via Beyşehir on the Antalya road; a car is required for the forest approaches.

properties.name: Sivrihisar
properties.desc: A town wedged under jagged quartzite crags with one extraordinary building: the thirteenth-century Ulu Cami, whose flat roof rests on 67 wooden columns with reused Byzantine capitals — one of the wooden hypostyle mosques now on the UNESCO list. Around it are an Armenian church, an Ottoman clock tower, and a statue of Nasreddin Hoca on his donkey, backwards.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — the crags glow at sunset
properties.tip: Ask at the mosque for the light switch; the forest of painted columns is almost invisible until someone turns the interior lights on.
properties.rev: The mosque interior astonishes people who stopped only for lunch on the Ankara road; the town itself is sleepy, with limited food options and a scruffy main street.
properties.onward: Eskişehir or Ankara, then the D200 highway — Sivrihisar sits directly on it, roughly halfway between the two, and all intercity buses stop here.

properties.name: Lake Beyşehir
properties.desc: Türkiye's largest freshwater lake, shallow and pale blue with the Anamas and Dedegöl mountains standing behind it and around thirty islands, some with ruined Byzantine churches. Fishermen sell pike-perch on the quay at Beyşehir town, and the west shore road towards Kubad Abad runs through apple orchards with the water on one side the whole way.
properties.season: May–Sep for the lake; Oct for clear air and empty shores
properties.tip: Hire a boat from Beyşehir quay in the morning to reach Kız Adası and Mada island — afternoon wind gets up and the boatmen stop going out.
properties.rev: Loved for its scale and its fish restaurants, but water levels have dropped badly in dry years, some shoreline is reedy and hard to reach, and the town itself is unremarkable.
properties.entry: Free · boat trips roughly ₺500–1000 (≈€10–20) per boat
properties.onward: Konya (KYA) airport, then 90 km west on the D330; regular buses run Konya–Beyşehir in about ninety minutes.

properties.name: Pessinus
properties.desc: The cult centre of Cybele, from where the black meteorite of the Great Mother was shipped to Rome in 204 BC. What survives in the fields of Ballıhisar village is a stepped theatre-like structure, a canalised stream lined with cut blocks, and a temple platform — plus columns and sarcophagi propped against village walls. Ancient stone lying about in a working farm hamlet.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — mud in spring, stubble and heat in summer
properties.tip: Walk the length of the stone-lined canal through the village; it is the most complete thing on site and nothing directs you to it.
properties.rev: Ancient-history readers find it moving to stand where Cybele's cult began; everyone else reports scattered rubble, no fence, no guide, and a rough 15 km track off the highway.
properties.onward: Eskişehir or Ankara to Sivrihisar on the D200, then 13 km south on a minor road to Ballıhisar; a car is required.

properties.name: Eşrefoğlu Mosque
properties.desc: Forty-eight cedar columns hold up a flat wooden ceiling in near-darkness, lit by a single opening above a sunken snow well in the floor. Built in 1299, it is the largest and best preserved of the wooden hypostyle mosques of medieval Anatolia, with an original carved minbar and a mihrab of turquoise and black tile.
properties.season: Year-round — snow falling through the roof opening in winter is the point
properties.tip: Go in winter if you can: the light shaft over the karlık is designed so snow drops in and melts to humidify the wood, and it is the reason the beams have survived seven centuries.
properties.rev: People repeatedly say it beats far more famous mosques, with the caveats that it is very dark for photography, closed to visitors during prayers, and modest dress is enforced.
properties.entry: Free · donation box at the door
properties.onward: Konya (KYA) airport, then 90 km west to Beyşehir town centre; the mosque is a five-minute walk from the bus station.

properties.name: Seydişehir
properties.desc: An aluminium town with a surprisingly intact Ottoman core of flat-roofed stone-and-timber houses climbing towards the Taurus. It sits at the top of the spectacular road down to Antalya, and above it the Küpe mountain and the Suğla lake basin. The Seyyid Harun Veli mosque and its old quarter are worth the hour before you drive on.
properties.season: May–Oct — the pass to Antalya can close in heavy winter snow
properties.tip: It is the natural coffee stop before the Alacabel pass; fill the tank here, because the descent to Antalya has long stretches with nothing.
properties.rev: Travellers who stop are pleasantly surprised by the old quarter; the town is otherwise dominated by the smelter and the historic houses are patchily maintained.
properties.onward: Konya (KYA) airport, then 90 km southwest on the D695; frequent buses run from Konya, and it is on the Konya–Antalya road.

properties.name: Beypazarı
properties.desc: A weekend town of white Ottoman houses stacked up a hillside, restored before the fashion for it and still half working town. The local trade is silver filigree, carrots, and a many-layered baklava made with 80 sheets of pastry. Above it, the İnözü valley cuts through soft rock full of Byzantine cave chambers.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — weekdays if you want the streets to yourself
properties.tip: Skip the main square restaurants and eat tarhana soup and kuru dolma at a house-restaurant in the back lanes, then drive fifteen minutes into İnözü valley for the caves.
properties.rev: Charming and genuinely well restored, but on Saturdays and Sundays it fills with Ankara coach parties and the historic streets become a queue for photos and carrot juice.
properties.entry: Free (town) · small fee for the Living Museum house
properties.onward: Ankara Esenboğa (ESB) airport, then 100 km northwest on the D140; frequent minibuses run from Ankara AŞTİ, taking about ninety minutes.

properties.name: Gordion
properties.desc: The Phrygian capital where Alexander cut the knot, now a low citadel mound in wheat country with nearly a hundred burial tumuli scattered around it. The Midas Mound is the reason to come: a tunnel drilled through 50 metres of earth ends at the oldest standing wooden building on earth, a juniper and pine chamber sealed around 740 BC.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — the plain is a furnace in July and August
properties.tip: The tumulus tunnel is cool, damp and unlit in places, and the little site museum holds the inlaid furniture found inside — do museum, tumulus, then citadel, in that order.
properties.rev: Newly inscribed by UNESCO and still refreshingly empty, though visitors note the citadel itself is bare stone footings, signage is thin, and there is no shade or café anywhere near.
properties.entry: ₺300 (≈€6) for museum, tumulus and site · covered by Museum Pass Türkiye
properties.onward: Ankara Esenboğa (ESB) airport, then 95 km west via Polatlı; there are buses to Polatlı but the last 18 km to Yassıhöyük really needs a car or taxi.

properties.name: The Porsuk in Eskişehir
properties.desc: A modest brown river that a determined mayor turned into the spine of the city: willow-lined embankments, a string of low bridges, gondolas poled by students, and cafés with their chairs at the water's edge. On a summer evening the whole of Eskişehir is walking along it, and the Adalar strip is one of the most sociable places in inland Türkiye.
properties.season: May–Sep evenings — the gondolas stop running in the cold months
properties.tip: Take the gondola upstream at dusk rather than the daytime run, and eat çiğ börek at a stand-up place off Hamamyolu instead of a riverside terrace.
properties.rev: Turks routinely call Eskişehir the country's most liveable city because of this river, while visitors point out the water itself is murky, the gondola ride is short, and the copycat cafés blur together.
properties.onward: Ankara or Istanbul, then the YHT high-speed train to Eskişehir; the riverfront starts five minutes from the station.

properties.name: Ayaş
properties.desc: A quiet market town of timber-framed houses forty minutes west of Ankara, known for its tomatoes, its vine leaves, and a hot spring in the valley below at Ayaş İçmece. The old quarter around the Ulu Cami has the same bones as Beypazarı with none of the coach parties, and half the konaks are still lived in.
properties.season: May–Oct — the tomato season peaks Aug–Sep and the market is at its best
properties.tip: Come on a Friday for the market and buy Ayaş tomatoes by the crate; they are the reason Ankara households drive out here at all.
properties.rev: Those who make the detour like the total absence of tourism, but there is little restored, few places to eat well, and the thermal facilities are basic municipal ones.
properties.onward: Ankara Esenboğa (ESB) airport, then 60 km west on the D140 towards Beypazarı; minibuses run from Ankara AŞTİ.

properties.name: Sille
properties.desc: A Greek-Orthodox village swallowed by Konya's suburbs but still intact in its gorge: stone houses on both banks of a dry stream, rock-cut chapels in the cliff, and the Aya Elenia church with its painted iconostasis, said to have been founded by Constantine's mother. The Greeks left in 1924; the village kept its bones.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Nov — pretty under snow but slippery
properties.tip: Walk uphill past the last café to the rock-cut chapels above the village, where the frescoes are faint but the graffiti goes back centuries and nobody follows you.
properties.rev: A rewarding half-day from Konya, though the stream bed is dry and concreted, the café strip is aimed squarely at weekenders, and the church keeps unreliable hours.
properties.entry: Small fee for the church — under €2
properties.onward: Konya (KYA) airport or YHT train, then city bus 64 from Konya centre, about 8 km northwest, roughly 25 minutes.

properties.name: Alâeddin Hill
properties.desc: An artificial mound in the middle of Konya, occupied since the Bronze Age, now a park of old plane trees with the Seljuk sultans' mosque on top. The Alâeddin Mosque is a strange, austere hall of mismatched antique columns; beside it stand the ruined arch of the Seljuk palace and a tomb chamber holding eight sultans.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — the plane trees give real shade in summer
properties.tip: Cross the road afterwards to the Karatay Medrese, whose tiled dome of star-and-cross mosaic is the single most beautiful ceiling in the city and takes twenty minutes.
properties.rev: Locals treat it as the city's living room and visitors like that; the mosque interior is often shut outside prayer times and the surviving palace arch is a disappointing sliver under a canopy.
properties.entry: Free (mosque and park) · Karatay Medrese small fee
properties.onward: Konya (KYA) airport or YHT train, then the tram to Alaaddin — the hill is the tram's own loop.

properties.name: Mevlâna Museum
properties.desc: Rumi's tomb under a fluted turquoise-tiled cone, the most recognisable roofline in Konya. Inside, a low-lit hall of sarcophagi wrapped in embroidered cloth, dervish felt hats, illuminated Masnavi manuscripts and a case holding a hair of the Prophet. Visitors move slowly and many are praying; it functions as a shrine that happens to sell tickets.
properties.season: Year-round — 17 December, the Şeb-i Arus, is the annual peak and books out
properties.tip: Arrive at opening, before the coach groups; and if you want to see the sema properly, book the Mevlana Cultural Centre performance rather than the restaurant versions.
properties.rev: Almost universally described as atmospheric and worth the trip, with the usual complaints about shoe-cover queues, dense crowds by 11am, and a strict no-photo rule in the tomb chamber.
properties.onward: Konya (KYA) airport or the YHT high-speed train from Ankara or Istanbul, then the tram along Mevlana Caddesi to the Mevlana stop.

properties.name: Yerköprü Waterfall
properties.desc: The Göksu has cut a deep canyon south of Hadim, and at Yerköprü a tributary drops over travertine terraces into it in a curtain of white water hung with moss and fig roots. A natural rock bridge gives the place its name. The road in switchbacks down into the gorge, and the temperature drops as you descend.
properties.season: Apr–Jun at full flow; Sep–Oct for warm water and low crowds
properties.tip: The descent road is narrow with blind bends and no barrier in places — go slow, and use the lower car park rather than trying to turn round at the falls.
properties.rev: People rate the setting highly, but flow drops sharply by late summer, the access road frightens some drivers, and weekend picnickers leave the riverbank littered.
properties.onward: Konya (KYA) airport, then 130 km south via Bozkır to Hadim, then down into the Göksu gorge; a car is essential.

properties.name: Soğuksu National Park & Kızılcahamam
properties.desc: Black pine and fir forest an hour north of Ankara, cool when the city is at 38 °C, with black vultures nesting on the cliffs and marked trails to the Çamlıdere viewpoints. The spa town of Kızılcahamam sits at its edge, all thermal hotels and mineral water so carbonated that locals bottle it straight from the roadside fountains.
properties.season: May–Oct for the forest; Dec–Feb for snow and a hot pool
properties.tip: Fill a bottle at the maden suyu spring in Kızılcahamam — it is naturally fizzy, faintly metallic, and free — then drive up to Soğuksu before the Sunday picnic crowd arrives.
properties.rev: Ankara's default escape, praised for clean air and cheap thermal hotels; complaints centre on weekend picnic litter, mediocre hotel food, and the park being a park rather than wilderness.
properties.entry: Small vehicle fee for the national park · thermal pools charged separately
properties.onward: Ankara Esenboğa (ESB) airport, then 60 km north on the O-4 / D750; regular buses run from Ankara AŞTİ to Kızılcahamam.

properties.name: Çatalhöyük
properties.desc: A 9,000-year-old town where people entered their mud-brick houses through the roof, buried their dead under the floors and painted bulls on the walls — one of the first places humans lived densely without streets. Two shelters cover the excavation trenches, and a reconstructed house lets you climb down a ladder into a Neolithic room.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — the Konya plain hits 38 °C with no shade in summer
properties.tip: The finds are in Konya and Ankara, not here — read the site panels first, then look at the trench, or it will read as a pit of mud walls.
properties.rev: Archaeology-minded visitors find it genuinely stirring, but many others report a long flat drive, a small visitor centre, and mud-brick trenches that need imagination to read.
properties.onward: Konya (KYA) airport or YHT train, then 50 km southeast via Çumra; buses reach Çumra but the last 10 km needs a taxi.

properties.name: Lake Eymir
properties.desc: A long reedy lake in a fold of steppe on Ankara's southern edge, held by METU university and therefore protected from development. A flat 7-kilometre track runs the shore under poplars, rowing eights train on the water in the evening, and cormorants sit out on the dead trees. It is the closest thing Ankara has to a green lung.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — the poplars turn gold in late October
properties.tip: Enter from the Gölbaşı side and go on a weekday; weekend afternoons the loop fills with cyclists and the car park closes when full.
properties.rev: Ankara's favourite easy walk, though visitors mention restricted entry hours, occasional algal smell in late summer, and the fact that swimming is not allowed.
properties.entry: Free on foot · small charge for cars
properties.onward: Ankara Esenboğa (ESB) airport, then 25 km south past Gölbaşı; city buses run to Gölbaşı and the entrance is a short taxi from there.

properties.name: Anıtkabir
properties.desc: Atatürk's mausoleum crowns a hill above the city, approached along a 262-metre avenue lined with Hittite-style stone lions. The scale is deliberately calm rather than grandiose: pale travertine colonnades, a huge empty ceremonial court, and a guard change performed with unnerving slowness. The museum beneath the terrace covers the War of Independence in real detail.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — the ceremonial court has zero shade in August
properties.tip: Time your walk up the Lion Road for the guard change on the hour, then go underground to the museum almost every day-tripper skips.
properties.rev: Visitors consistently find it more affecting than expected, but complain about the airport-style bag check at the gate and staff turning away anyone in shorts or a hat on the court.
properties.onward: Ankara Esenboğa (ESB) airport, then the Belko Air bus to Kızılay and the M2 metro to Tandoğan, ten minutes uphill on foot.

properties.name: Hacı Bayram Mosque
properties.desc: Ankara's most-visited religious building, a fifteenth-century mosque of brick and Kütahya tile built hard against a Roman temple wall. The square outside is the city's warmest public space: families feeding pigeons, women selling rosaries and boiled corn, and a steady traffic of pilgrims to the tomb of the poet-saint Hacı Bayram Veli.
properties.season: Year-round — Friday midday and religious holidays are packed
properties.tip: Walk around the back of the mosque to where the Ottoman brickwork meets the Roman ashlar; the seam between the two is a metre from your hand.
properties.rev: Visitors find the atmosphere genuinely devotional rather than touristic, though the square is crowded, the surrounding streets are shabby, and modest dress plus headscarves for women are enforced.
properties.onward: Ankara Esenboğa (ESB) airport, then metro to Ulus and five minutes on foot uphill.

properties.name: Temple of Augustus and Rome
properties.desc: The single most important Latin inscription in the world sits in a scruffy yard behind a mosque in Ankara. The Res Gestae Divi Augusti — the emperor's own account of his reign — is carved on the inner cella walls in Latin, with a Greek translation on the outside. Roofless, weathered, and almost entirely ignored by the crowds twenty metres away.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — legible light is better on an overcast day
properties.tip: The Greek text on the exterior south wall is far easier to read than the Latin inside; bring a photo of the translation because there is next to no interpretation on site.
properties.rev: Classicists call it unmissable; everyone else reports a fenced, weedy enclosure with almost no signage and periodic closure for restoration scaffolding.
properties.onward: Ankara Esenboğa (ESB) airport, then metro to Ulus; the temple shares a courtyard with Hacı Bayram Mosque.

properties.name: Museum of Anatolian Civilizations
properties.desc: Two restored Ottoman buildings below the castle hold the best Hittite collection anywhere: the Çatalhöyük wall paintings, the Alacahöyük bronze standards, and orthostat reliefs of gods in pointed hats carried off the walls of Karkamış. It is compact enough to do properly in two hours and rearranged chronologically, so Anatolia's ten thousand years finally line up.
properties.season: Year-round — an obvious refuge on a wet or freezing Ankara day
properties.tip: Do this before Çatalhöyük or Gordion, not after; the finds are all here and the sites themselves are bare earth without them.
properties.rev: Widely rated Türkiye's finest museum, though the foreigner ticket price has climbed steeply and school groups can make the Hittite hall genuinely loud by mid-morning.
properties.onward: Ankara Esenboğa (ESB) airport, then metro to Ulus and a fifteen-minute walk uphill through the Atpazarı copper market.

properties.name: Ankara Castle
properties.desc: Byzantine walls built from recycled Roman marble — column drums and inscribed blocks jammed straight into the masonry — enclose a living quarter of leaning timber houses, laundry lines and cats. Climb to the Şark Kulesi and the whole grey sprawl of Ankara opens out, with the citadel's own tiled roofs directly below.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Nov — the cobbles ice over in winter
properties.tip: Go up an hour before sunset and buy dried fruit and pastırma in the Atpazarı lanes on the way back down, when the spice sellers are still open.
properties.rev: People love the ramshackle village-inside-a-city feel but warn that the summit has no railings in places, the lanes are steep and slippery, and several 'historic' konak restaurants are tourist-priced.
properties.onward: Ankara Esenboğa (ESB) airport, then metro to Ulus; walk uphill through Atpazarı or take a taxi to the Parmak Kapı gate.

properties.name: Ermenek
properties.desc: A town wedged under a vertical limestone wall in the deep Taurus, with a Karamanid mosque of 1302, stepped stone streets, and a castle on the crag above. Below it the Ermenek dam has flooded the Göksu canyon into a long turquoise fjord crossed by one of Türkiye's highest bridges. The drive in from any direction is the attraction.
properties.season: May–Oct — mountain roads in and out are snow-affected in winter
properties.tip: Approach from the Mut or Anamur side rather than Karaman if you can: the canyon road along the reservoir is one of the great drives in southern Anatolia.
properties.rev: Those who go rate the scenery highly, but the roads are long, winding and tiring, accommodation is very limited, and the town closes early.
properties.onward: Konya (KYA) airport, then 110 km to Karaman and 150 km south through the Taurus; also reachable from the Mediterranean coast via Anamur or Mut.

properties.name: Hamamönü
properties.desc: A block of Ottoman Ankara restored back from near-collapse: bay-windowed timber houses in ochre and dusty green, a restored hamam, and courtyards selling handicrafts and mantı. It is frankly a curated version of the past, but the street width, the overhanging upper floors and the smell of woodsmoke in autumn are the real thing.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — Ramadan evenings are the liveliest, and coldest in Jan
properties.tip: Skip the main Hacı Musa street cafés and cut into the side lanes behind the Karacabey hamam, where the restoration stops and the original neighbourhood carries on.
properties.rev: Ankara residents rate it a pleasant evening stroll; travellers who arrive expecting Safranbolu find it small, heavily made-over, and dead on a weekday morning.
properties.onward: Ankara Esenboğa (ESB) airport, then metro to Ulus or Kızılay and a fifteen-minute walk or short taxi to Hacettepe.

properties.name: Binbir Kilise
properties.desc: On the black volcanic slopes of Karadağ, dozens of Byzantine churches and monasteries built from dark basalt stand roofless among the boulders and the sheep — the 'thousand and one churches' surveyed by Gertrude Bell in 1907. Some are barrel-vaulted shells you can walk into; the village of Madenşehri is built among them.
properties.season: May–Jun and Sep–Oct — the mountain track is impassable in snow and mud
properties.tip: Go to Madenşehri first for the concentration of standing churches, and take the higher Değle group only with a high-clearance vehicle or a local driver.
properties.rev: Byzantinists rate it extraordinary and completely unvisited; the practical warnings are consistent — rough unsurfaced tracks, no facilities, sheepdogs, and no interpretation whatsoever.
properties.onward: Konya (KYA) airport, then to Karaman and about 35 km north onto Karadağ via Dinek; a sturdy car and dry weather are needed.

properties.name: Obruk Han & Sinkhole
properties.desc: A thirteenth-century Seljuk caravanserai standing on the empty Konya–Aksaray steppe, deliberately built beside a vast circular sinkhole whose water made the stop possible. The han is a plain fortified block of grey stone; the obruk beside it drops sheer to a dark green disc of water about a hundred metres down, with swallows working the shaft.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — nothing but glare and heat in July and August
properties.tip: It sits right on the old Aksaray road and is easy to miss at speed; look for the village of Obruk itself and the han is directly behind the houses.
properties.rev: A satisfying stop on a long drive, though the han is often locked, the sinkhole rim is unfenced, and there is nothing at all in the village beyond a tea house.
properties.onward: Konya (KYA) airport, then about 90 km northeast on the old Aksaray road via Obruk village; on the route between Konya and Cappadocia.

properties.name: Karaman Old Town
properties.desc: Capital of the Karamanid emirate, the beylik that declared Turkish the language of the state in 1277, and still full of its patrons' buildings: the Hatuniye Medrese with its deep carved marble portal, the Yunus Emre mosque and tomb, the Aktekke, and a squat castle in a park. A serious concentration of fourteenth-century stone in an unshowy town.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — the plain is hot and dusty in high summer
properties.tip: Do the Hatuniye Medrese portal in morning light when the low sun rakes across the carving; by afternoon it is flat and the detail disappears.
properties.rev: A rewarding stop for anyone interested in pre-Ottoman architecture, though several monuments are locked outside prayer times and the modern town around them is plain.
properties.onward: Konya (KYA) airport, then 110 km southeast on the D715; frequent buses and a rail link run from Konya in about ninety minutes.

properties.name: Lake Tuz (Aksaray shore)
properties.desc: Turkey's second-largest lake is barely a lake at all by August — a white salt pan you can walk out onto for a kilometre, water a few centimetres deep, turning pink from Dunaliella algae in high summer. Flamingos breed on the islands, and the Aksaray shore is the quieter side.
properties.season: Jul–Sep for the pink water and salt harvest; in spring it is shallow brine and mud
properties.tip: Walk out barefoot only if you have no cuts — the brine is savage — and rinse your shoes immediately, because dried salt destroys leather.
properties.rev: Photographers love the pink water and mirror reflections; nearly everyone mentions the roadside stops on the Ankara highway are crowded and litter-strewn, the salt cuts feet, and outside July and August the lake can be simply grey mud.
properties.entry: Free · some private shore access points charge ≈₺100 (€2.50) for parking
properties.onward: Nevşehir (NAV) or Ankara (ESB) airport, then the Aksaray–Konya road; the quiet shore is near Eskil, car only

properties.name: Kapulukaya Reservoir
properties.desc: The Kızılırmak backs up behind a dam south of Kırıkkale into a long reservoir between bare ochre hills, with fishermen's shacks, a few tea gardens on the water and almost nothing else. It is not spectacular, but it is the one green line in an otherwise industrial province and the road along it makes a decent break on the Ankara–Kayseri run.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — the hills are scorched brown by July
properties.tip: Stop at one of the fish restaurants on the reservoir road rather than eating in Kırıkkale town, where the options are motorway-grade.
properties.rev: Locals use it for weekend fishing and tea; travellers are honest that it is a pleasant pause rather than a destination, with scruffy shorelines and no real facilities.
properties.onward: Ankara Esenboğa (ESB) airport, then 90 km east on the O-21 / D200 to Kırıkkale and south to the dam; a car is needed.

properties.name: Hirfanlı Reservoir
properties.desc: A 263 km² reservoir on the Kızılırmak, built in 1959 and now the improbable inland sailing and fishing water of central Anatolia. Bare ochre hills drop straight into blue, small boat clubs operate from Kaman and Çiçekdağı, and pike-perch from the lake turns up on menus across the region.
properties.season: May–Sep for swimming and boats; windy and bleak from November to March
properties.tip: The Kırşehir side has the better shore access and the fish restaurants — the Ankara-side road is faster but has almost nowhere to stop at the water.
properties.rev: Locals treat it as their summer sea and the fish is genuinely good, but visitors report scrappy shorelines, litter at the popular access points, water levels that expose mudflats in dry years, and no organised facilities.
properties.onward: Ankara (ESB) airport 150 km, then the Kırşehir road; shore access is easiest from Kaman by car

properties.name: Sultanhanı Caravanserai
properties.desc: The biggest Seljuk caravanserai in Anatolia, built in 1229 and rebuilt after a fire, with a marble portal of interlocking geometry, a vast courtyard and a basilica-like stable hall lit only by a lantern dome. The scale is the point: it sheltered whole caravans crossing the salt plain.
properties.season: Year-round; the courtyard bakes in July and the hall is icy in January
properties.tip: Stand under the central dome of the covered hall and look up — the acoustics and the single shaft of light are what the photographs never get.
properties.rev: Widely rated the best-preserved caravanserai in Turkey and worth the stop on the Konya road; complaints are heavy-handed restoration, a coach-tour rhythm in high season, and a plain highway town outside with little else in it.
properties.onward: Konya (KYA) or Nevşehir (NAV) airport; 45 km west of Aksaray on the Konya highway, right in the village

properties.name: Karapınar Obruks
properties.desc: Sinkholes punched straight down through the flat Konya plain, some old and green with water at the bottom, some collapsed last week in a wheat field. Kızören and Meyil obruks are the classic pair: near-circular shafts sixty to a hundred metres across with vertical walls and a disc of turquoise water far below. Unnerving to stand at the edge of.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — the plain is 38 °C and shadeless in high summer
properties.tip: Stay well back from the lips — the rims are undercut and actively collapsing, and there are no barriers at most of them.
properties.rev: Geologically fascinating and genuinely eerie, though visitors note dirt access tracks, no fencing or signage, and that the newer collapses are on private farmland.
properties.onward: Konya (KYA) airport, then 95 km east to Karapınar on the D330; the obruks are scattered on farm roads and need a car.

properties.name: Manazan Caves
properties.desc: A five-storey Byzantine cave settlement carved into a limestone cliff above the Ayrancı valley, with rooms, chapels and connecting shafts stacked one above the other. The mummified remains found here gave the top floor its name, Kilise Kat. Wind moves through the openings constantly, which is why the bodies dried rather than decayed.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — the valley is fiercely hot in midsummer
properties.tip: The internal stairs and shafts are unlit and worn smooth — take a torch, wear grip, and do not go up alone after rain.
properties.rev: Adventurous visitors call it the best cave site outside Cappadocia; others report no railings, no lighting, no staff, and drops that make it unsuitable for young children.
properties.onward: Konya (KYA) airport, then to Karaman and 40 km east on the Taşkale road; the cliff is signed off the road and needs a car.

properties.name: Taşkale Granaries
properties.desc: A cliff above a village drilled with 250 rock-cut grain stores stacked in tiers, reached by notched footholds and wooden ladders, and still used by families to store wheat. From the road it looks like a honeycomb hanging over the houses. Some chambers are Byzantine rock churches reused; the whole face is one continuous vertical village.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct — the cliff face bakes in July and August
properties.tip: Ask in the village tea house before climbing anything; some ladders are private property and the lower chambers are the only ones safe to enter without help.
properties.rev: Visitors describe it as one of the strangest things in Anatolia and almost unvisited, though there is no signage, no ticket office, and getting inside depends entirely on finding a willing villager.
properties.onward: Konya (KYA) airport, then 110 km southeast to Karaman and 45 km east to Taşkale; minibuses run from Karaman but infrequently.

properties.name: Çankırı Salt Cave
properties.desc: A working rock-salt mine driven into a hill outside Çankırı, part of it opened as galleries of pink and grey salt carved into arches, a mosque and a salt-block dining room. The air is dry, still and around 16 °C, and asthma patients spend hours in the therapy chambers. Salt has been dug here since Hittite times.
properties.season: Year-round — constant temperature makes it a good winter or heatwave stop
properties.tip: Take a jacket and check the mine's visiting hours before driving out; it is an operating mine and public access closes without much warning.
properties.rev: A genuinely unusual hour and popular with families, but reviews mention limited English, a functional rather than scenic mine entrance, and queues on public holidays.
properties.onward: Ankara Esenboğa (ESB) airport, then 130 km northeast on the D765; regular buses run Ankara–Çankırı in about two hours.

properties.name: Meke Crater Lake
