properties.entry: Free to enter; ≈₺75 (€1.60) vehicle fee at the barrier, thermal baths extra
properties.onward: Rize–Artvin (RZV) airport, then 70 km east and inland via Ardeşen and Çamlıhemşin; minibuses run from Ardeşen and Pazar

properties.name: Kaçkar Mountains National Park
properties.desc: Türkiye's only genuinely alpine range outside the far east: glaciated granite to 3,937 m, permanent snowfields, tarns, and a wall of rain forest on the northern flank. Brown bear and chamois are present and occasionally seen. The classic crossing from Ayder over the Çaymakçur pass down to Yusufeli takes three or four days.
properties.season: Mid-Jul–mid Sep for the high passes; snow lies on them until July and returns in October
properties.tip: Hire a local guide in Ayder or Olgunlar for the crossing — the cloud sits on the ridges most afternoons and the cairned routes vanish completely.
properties.rev: Trekkers rate it among the best walking in the country, while warning about persistent afternoon cloud and rain, unmarked routes, aggressive shepherd dogs, and very basic hut accommodation.
properties.entry: Free on foot; vehicle fees at some valley barriers
properties.onward: Rize–Artvin (RZV) airport for the north side via Çamlıhemşin, or Erzurum (ERZ) and Yusufeli for the south; no public transport above the last villages

properties.name: Pokut Plateau
properties.desc: A line of cantilevered timber Hemşin houses on a 2,000 m spur, standing above a valley that fills with cloud most evenings so the huts appear to float. The walk on to Sal and Hazindak along the ridge takes two easy hours. It is the image most people have in mind when they say they want to see the Kaçkars.
properties.season: Late Jun–Sep; the track is snow-covered and impassable Nov–May
properties.tip: The last 10 km from Şalpazarı junction is a rutted dirt road best done in a hired 4x4 or the local minibus — ordinary hire cars regularly ground out and get stuck.
properties.rev: Widely described as the best view in the region, with equally consistent warnings: a punishing dirt access road, rooms that must be booked weeks ahead in August, cold nights, and fog that hides everything for days.
properties.onward: Rize–Artvin (RZV) airport, then Ardeşen and Çamlıhemşin, then 20 km of mountain track — 4x4, local minibus or a two-hour walk up

properties.name: Palovit Waterfall
properties.desc: A wide fifteen-metre curtain of water dropping over a mossy shelf in the forest above Ayder, reached by a rough track and then a ten-minute walk. Spray keeps everything within thirty metres soaked and green. Hydro schemes elsewhere in the valley have taken water off other falls; this one still runs hard.
properties.season: May–Jul at full snowmelt volume; low and disappointing by late September
properties.tip: Go in the morning — the gorge is in deep shade from early afternoon and the fall is unphotographable after about two o'clock.
properties.rev: Visitors find it genuinely powerful in early summer and reduced to a trickle in autumn, and repeatedly warn about a badly rutted access track, slippery steps and no facilities at the parking spot.
properties.onward: Rize–Artvin (RZV) airport, then Çamlıhemşin and the Ayder–Elevit valley road; the last few kilometres need clearance

properties.name: Barhal Church
properties.desc: A tenth-century Georgian basilica in the village of Altıparmak, high-shouldered, blind-arcaded, and in exceptional condition because it has been in continuous use as the village mosque. The stonework of the east end is the finest in the valley. Kaçkar trailheads start twenty minutes further up the road at Yaylalar.
properties.season: May–Oct; the valley road above Yusufeli is difficult in snow Dec–Mar
properties.tip: Ask at the tea house for the key holder — the interior is normally locked outside prayer times and nobody will offer unless you ask.
properties.rev: Travellers rate the preservation and the setting, while noting the interior is often locked, there is no interpretation of any kind, and the 30 km valley road from Yusufeli is slow and narrow.
properties.entry: Free — it is a working mosque; dress modestly
properties.onward: Erzurum (ERZ) airport, then Yusufeli, then 30 km up the Barhal valley; a dolmuş runs from Yusufeli most days in summer

properties.name: Hopa
properties.desc: The last Turkish town before the Georgian border, a working port of tea warehouses, Laz spoken in the market and lorries queuing for Sarp. It rains here more than anywhere else in the country — over 2,000 mm a year. Come for the border-town texture and the fish, not for beaches.
properties.season: May–Sep; it rains hard in every month and October–December is relentless
properties.tip: Eat hamsi in a harbour lokanta between November and February — outside those months the anchovy on the menu is frozen and everyone local knows it.
properties.rev: Travellers describe it as scruffy, genuinely lived-in and useful as a base for Borçka and Macahel, while criticising the noise from border traffic, a grey concrete waterfront and near-constant rain.
properties.onward: Rize–Artvin (RZV) airport, then 80 km east on the coast road; buses continue to Batumi through the Sarp crossing

properties.name: Dörtkilise (Otkhta Eklesia)
properties.desc: A vast tenth-century Georgian monastery church standing roofless in a walnut orchard above Tekkale, far bigger than anything the village around it could ever have needed. Traces of fresco survive high on the apse, and the refectory and chapel ruins are scattered in the trees. Usually you will be the only person there.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct; the orchard track is muddy after rain and snow closes it in winter
properties.tip: Drive past the village of Tekkale to the very end of the track — most people park at the first ruin, which is the small chapel, and never see the big church.
properties.rev: Consistently described as the most impressive and least visited of the Tao-Klarjeti churches, with complaints about the rough unsigned access track, falling masonry, grazing animals inside, and zero facilities.
properties.onward: Erzurum (ERZ) airport, then Yusufeli and 7 km up the Tekkale road, then a rough track; taxi from Yusufeli if you have no car

properties.name: Yusufeli and the Çoruh Valley
properties.desc: Be clear about what changed: the 275 m Yusufeli dam closed in 2022 and the reservoir drowned the old town and the classic rafting reach of the Çoruh in 2023. A new town stands on the slope above the water. The side valleys — Barhal, Tekkale, Altıparmak — still run free and are why you come.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct; the gorge bakes above 35 °C in July–August
properties.tip: Do not plan a Çoruh rafting trip from the old descriptions — what is left is on the Barhal tributary above the reservoir, arranged locally in Yusufeli.
properties.rev: Reactions are mixed and often flat: people who knew the old valley describe the loss bluntly, while first-time visitors still rate the side gorges highly and complain about roadworks, dust and a soulless new town.
properties.onward: Erzurum (ERZ) airport, then 170 km north on the rebuilt D950, or Rize–Artvin (RZV) and south via Artvin; buses run from Erzurum and Artvin

properties.name: Borçka Karagöl
properties.desc: A landslide lake at 1,450 m in deep forest above Borçka, with a boardwalk around the shore and the reflection of the surrounding beech and spruce that made it famous. In late October the whole bowl turns copper. The last stretch of road is 25 km of climbing on a mostly unsurfaced surface.
properties.season: Late Oct for colour, Jun–Sep for the forest; snow closes the road Dec–Apr
properties.tip: Arrive before nine — the water only mirrors the trees while the air is still, and by mid-morning the breeze and the coaches both arrive.
properties.rev: Widely rated for the autumn reflections, and just as widely criticised for a rough 25 km climb, crowds and drone noise on October weekends, litter, and overpriced bungalows booked out months ahead.
properties.onward: Rize–Artvin (RZV) airport, then 90 km east via Hopa to Borçka, then 25 km of mountain road

properties.name: İşhan Church
properties.desc: A domed Georgian cathedral on a terrace 1,200 m above the Çoruh, with a carved arcade round the apse that is the best relief carving in the whole Tao-Klarjeti group. Parts of the dome fresco survive. The seven kilometres of hairpins up from the main road are steep, narrow and entirely worth it.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct; the access road is dangerous in ice and snow
properties.tip: Restoration scaffolding has come and gone here for years — check in Yusufeli whether the interior is currently open before committing to the climb.
properties.rev: Visitors call the carving world-class and the view extraordinary, while reporting long-running restoration works, scaffolding inside, a locked door on some days, and a nerve-testing single-track road up.
properties.onward: Erzurum (ERZ) airport, then the D950 towards Yusufeli and 7 km of hairpins from the İşhan junction; car only

properties.name: Kafkasör Plateau
properties.desc: A pine-shaded plateau at 1,300 m eight kilometres above Artvin, best known for the bull-wrestling festival in the last week of June, where paired bulls push each other around a natural arena until one walks away. Outside the festival it is a quiet forest picnic ground with a long view down the Çoruh gorge.
properties.season: Late Jun for the festival, Jul–Sep for quiet; cold and often snowed in Dec–Mar
properties.tip: If you come for the festival, sleep in Artvin and walk up — the single road is closed to traffic and the shuttle queues are long.
properties.rev: The festival is described as loud, chaotic and genuinely local rather than staged; complaints are severe congestion during festival week, almost nothing happening the rest of the year, and litter left behind.
properties.onward: Rize–Artvin (RZV) airport, then 110 km to Artvin, then 8 km up a steep paved road; taxis run from the town centre

properties.name: Camili (Macahel) Biosphere Reserve
properties.desc: Six villages in a valley that drains north into Georgia, cut off from the rest of Türkiye by a 1,800 m pass — the country's first UNESCO-recognised biosphere reserve, with primary forest that has never been logged and the protected Caucasian honeybee. Hay is still cut by scythe and stacked on wooden frames.
properties.season: Jun–Sep; the Çavuşlar pass is snow-blocked roughly Nov–May and the valley is then reachable only through Georgia
properties.tip: You need your passport even though you never leave Türkiye — there is a jandarma checkpoint at the pass because the valley sits inside the border zone.
properties.rev: Visitors describe an intact traditional landscape and outstanding honey, and warn about the exposed unpaved pass road, the border checkpoint, homestay-only accommodation, and no mobile signal in most of the valley.
properties.onward: Rize–Artvin (RZV) airport, then Hopa and Borçka, then 40 km over the Çavuşlar pass on a partly unsurfaced road; 4x4 preferable

properties.name: Ardanuç and the Cehennem Canyon
properties.desc: The road into Ardanuç threads a limestone slot barely wider than the car, with walls hundreds of metres high and a strip of sky above — locally the Cehennem, hell. Beyond it the valley opens into an orchard basin under the ruined citadel of Gevhernik, the old Georgian Artanuji.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct; the canyon floor is baking in July–August
properties.tip: Stop in the canyon itself rather than driving straight through — there is one lay-by halfway with room for two cars and it is the only place you can look up properly.
properties.rev: The canyon drive is the part everyone remembers; the complaints are that it lasts only two kilometres, there is nowhere safe to stop, rockfall is frequent, and the town itself has little to detain you.
properties.onward: Rize–Artvin (RZV) airport, then 110 km to Artvin and 35 km east; minibuses run from Artvin otogar

properties.name: Karagöl-Sahara National Park
properties.desc: Two separate pieces above Şavşat: a small black lake trapped in spruce forest at 1,500 m, and the Sahara yayla, a broad flower meadow higher up. The forest here is old, wet and dense, the sort where you hear woodpeckers and see nothing. Georgia is twenty kilometres away over the ridge.
properties.season: Jun–Sep; the park roads are snowbound Nov–May
properties.tip: The Karagöl lake and Sahara yayla are 25 km apart on different roads — do not assume one visit covers both, and do Karagöl first thing before the picnic parties arrive.
properties.rev: Visitors describe genuinely primeval forest and quiet lakes, then complain about picnic litter at Karagöl on summer weekends, a rough forest road, and very limited food or accommodation nearby.
properties.entry: ≈₺80 (€1.70) per vehicle at the park gate
properties.onward: Rize–Artvin (RZV) airport, then 130 km via Artvin to Şavşat, then 25 km on forest roads; car essential

properties.name: Yesemek Quarry
properties.desc: The largest known open-air sculpture workshop of the ancient Near East: several hundred half-finished Hittite lions, sphinxes and mountain gods lying on a hillside exactly where the carvers abandoned them nearly three thousand years ago.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct
properties.tip: Walk the whole upper slope, not just the marked path — the unfinished lions above the treeline are the ones that make the place.
properties.rev: Archaeology enthusiasts find it extraordinary and are usually alone there, though the site is exposed, poorly signposted, and a long detour from anywhere else.
properties.onward: Gaziantep (GZT), then about 1h30 southwest by car via İslahiye

properties.name: Kilis Old Town and Kitchen
properties.desc: A small border town with Ottoman stone houses, a good covered market and a cuisine that overlaps with Aleppo's — kilis tava, oruk, and a version of katmer worth the drive from Gaziantep on its own.
properties.season: Oct–May — summer is fierce
properties.tip: Eat kilis tava at lunchtime in a market lokanta, then take the long way back to Antep through the olive country rather than the highway.
properties.rev: Food-focused travellers find it a rewarding half-day from Gaziantep, though the town is otherwise quiet, hosts a large refugee population, and sits close enough to the border that some visitors feel uneasy.
properties.onward: Gaziantep (GZT), then 1h by car south; frequent buses from Antep otogar

properties.name: Oylum Höyük
properties.desc: One of the largest settlement mounds in the region, occupied more or less continuously from the Chalcolithic to the Iron Age, with a working excavation that has turned up Hittite and Mitanni layers. It is a mound rather than a monument, and reads as one.
properties.season: Mar–May and Oct–Nov · dig season is summer
properties.tip: Come during the summer dig season if you want it to mean anything — outside it there is little to see beyond the shape of the hill.
properties.rev: Of genuine interest to archaeology travellers, but casual visitors report a bare hill with no interpretation, and access to trenches depends entirely on the dig team being present.
properties.onward: Gaziantep (GZT), then about 1h by car to Kilis, then 15 min

properties.name: Dülük and Keber Tepe
properties.desc: Ancient Doliche, home of the cult of Jupiter Dolichenus that spread to every corner of the Roman empire, with rock-cut Mithraeum chambers and a quarried hillside just north of Gaziantep. Locals come for the pine woods and picnics rather than the archaeology.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Nov
properties.tip: The Mithraeum caves are the point and they are easy to walk past; ask for the Mithras mağarası, not the picnic area.
properties.rev: A pleasant short trip out of the city and free, but the ancient remains are scattered and unexplained, and weekends bring heavy picnic traffic.
properties.onward: Gaziantep (GZT), then 25 min north by car

properties.name: Bakırcılar Bazaar
properties.desc: The coppersmiths' quarter, where the sound arrives before the sight — dozens of workshops beating trays, coffee pots and cauldrons by hand. Around it sit spice stalls, the pistachio wholesalers and some of the best-value food in the country.
properties.season: Year-round — mornings, when the hammering starts
properties.tip: Buy a hand-hammered coffee pot here rather than in Istanbul; the same object costs a fraction and you can watch it being finished.
properties.rev: Food-minded travellers rate the whole quarter as the best market experience in Türkiye, though earthquake damage closed parts of the surrounding hans and some workshops have not returned.
properties.onward: Gaziantep (GZT), 25 min to the centre; the bazaar sits below the castle

properties.name: Emine Göğüş Culinary Museum
properties.desc: A restored 19th-century stone house explaining why Gaziantep is a UNESCO City of Gastronomy: the pepper varieties, the pistachio grades, the forty kinds of kebab and the correct way to layer baklava, laid out room by room.
properties.season: Year-round
properties.tip: Do it before you start eating your way round the city rather than after — it changes what you order for the rest of the trip.
properties.near: Emine Göğüş Mutfak Müzesi, Şahinbey, Gaziantep, Türkiye
properties.rev: Small but well judged, and cheap; the recurring criticism is that English labelling is thin and the whole visit takes barely half an hour.
properties.onward: Gaziantep (GZT), 25 min to the centre; a short walk from the castle

properties.name: Sof Mountain
properties.desc: The pine ridge above Gaziantep where the city goes to escape the heat, with a small ski lift in winter, cool picnic terraces in summer and long views over the plain toward Syria.
properties.season: Dec–Feb for snow, Jun–Sep as a heat escape
properties.tip: Drive up in the evening in high summer — it is reliably ten degrees cooler than the city and the lights of Antep spread out below.
properties.rev: Locals value it highly as a break from the heat and it is free, but there is little for a visitor beyond the view, and the winter facilities are modest by any standard.
properties.entry: Free · ski lift charged separately in season
properties.onward: Gaziantep (GZT), then 40 min by car northwest of the city

properties.name: Gaziantep Castle
properties.desc: A round Roman-then-Byzantine citadel on a mound in the middle of the city, damaged in the 2023 earthquake and partly under restoration. Even from the outside it anchors the old town, with the copper bazaar running off its skirts.
properties.season: Year-round — spring and autumn are pleasant, summer is not
properties.tip: Check whether the castle itself has reopened before planning around it; the circuit of the mound and the bazaar below are the real experience either way.
properties.rev: Visitors value it as the heart of the old city, but many arrive to find sections closed for post-earthquake restoration and note that the interior museum has been shut for extended periods.
properties.entry: Free to circle · interior fee when open, check locally
properties.onward: Gaziantep (GZT), 25 min into the centre; the old town is walkable from there

properties.name: Zeugma Mosaic Museum
properties.desc: The largest mosaic museum in the world, built to hold what was rescued from Zeugma before the Euphrates rose over it. The Gypsy Girl fragment — a pair of eyes that follow you across a darkened room — is the reason most people come, and it earns it.
properties.season: Year-round — indoors and air-conditioned, which matters here
properties.tip: Do the museum in the afternoon when the light outside is unbearable, and see the Gypsy Girl room last so it lands properly.
properties.near: Zeugma Mozaik Müzesi, Şehitkamil, Gaziantep, Türkiye
properties.rev: Almost universally praised as world-class and worth a trip to Gaziantep on its own, with the main complaint being that the Gypsy Girl room is small and gets congested with tour groups.
properties.onward: Gaziantep (GZT), 25 min by taxi or tram plus a short walk

properties.name: Rumkale
properties.desc: A fortress on a rock spur where the Merzimen stream meets the Euphrates, cut off on three sides by water since the dam rose. Armenian, Byzantine and Islamic layers pile on top of each other, reachable only by boat.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct
properties.tip: Boats leave from both Halfeti and Savaşan; the Savaşan side is cheaper and quieter, and you get the sunken-village view on the way.
properties.rev: The approach by water is the best part and reviewers agree it is worth the trip, though the site itself is unrestored, slippery, and boat operators sometimes allow only a short stop.
properties.onward: Gaziantep (GZT), then 1h30 by car to Halfeti or Savaşan, then boat

properties.name: Besni Old Town
properties.desc: An abandoned hillside town of stone houses and a ruined castle, evacuated after landslides and now slowly being consolidated as an open-air site. Empty streets, collapsed vaults and long views over the Besni plain.
properties.season: Mar–May and Sep–Nov
properties.tip: The new town below is where the famous Besni grapes and its pekmez come from — buy some at a roadside stall on the way out.
properties.rev: Atmospheric and completely uncommercial, but it is a genuine ruin field with unstable buildings, minimal signage and no facilities.
properties.onward: Adıyaman (ADF), then 50 min southwest by car

properties.name: Zeugma Ancient City
properties.desc: The Hellenistic bridgehead city on the Euphrates whose villas produced the mosaics now in Gaziantep. Much of it lies under the Birecik reservoir; what survives above water is a terraced site of house foundations looking down at the river that took the rest.
properties.season: Mar–May and Oct–Nov
properties.tip: See the museum in Gaziantep first — without it the site reads as bare foundations, and with it you can place every mosaic you saw.
properties.rev: Rewarding for people who care about the story of the rescue dig, but visitors expecting a standing ancient city are routinely underwhelmed by what is left.
properties.onward: Gaziantep (GZT), then 1h east by car via Nizip

properties.name: Halfeti
properties.desc: A stone town half-drowned by the Birecik dam, where boats glide over submerged streets and a minaret rises straight out of green water. The famous near-black roses grow in the surviving upper gardens.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct; the roses flower in spring
properties.tip: Take the boat from Halfeti rather than Rumkale side, go late afternoon, and ask the boatman to cut the engine over the sunken village.
properties.rev: The boat trip is widely called magical, but the village itself has become heavily commercialised, boatmen quote wildly different prices, and weekends bring domestic tour buses in numbers.
properties.entry: Free · boat trips ₺300–600 (≈€6–13) per person depending on route
properties.onward: Gaziantep (GZT) or Şanlıurfa GAP (GNY), each about 1h30 by car; buses run from Birecik

properties.name: Birecik and the Bald Ibis
properties.desc: The last semi-wild colony of northern bald ibis in the Middle East, a bird that nearly vanished entirely, kept going on cliffs above the Euphrates at Birecik. The town itself is a pistachio-and-tea river stop with a Crusader castle.
properties.season: Mar–Jul, when the birds are at the colony; they are penned over winter
properties.tip: Come in the morning when the birds are active on the cliff ledges, and ask at the station rather than trying to spot them from the road.
properties.rev: Birdwatchers rate the colony as unmissable, though casual visitors sometimes find the enclosure setting more zoo than wilderness, and the station keeps irregular hours.
properties.entry: Free or a nominal fee · check opening before travelling
properties.onward: Şanlıurfa GAP (GNY) or Gaziantep (GZT), each about 1h15 by car; frequent buses on the Antep–Urfa road

properties.name: Perre Ancient City
properties.desc: A Commagene and Roman necropolis cut straight into the rock at the edge of Adıyaman, with chamber tombs, a monumental fountain still running, and carved facades you can walk into. It sits within the modern town, which makes the scale of it stranger.
properties.season: Mar–Nov
properties.tip: Go early or late; the rock faces bake by mid-morning and the chambers are the only shade for a kilometre.
properties.rev: Good value and easy to reach from town, though the site is small and visitors note that some tombs are fenced off and the surroundings are built up.
properties.onward: Adıyaman (ADF), then 20 min by taxi — it is on the edge of the city

properties.name: Atatürk Dam
properties.desc: One of the largest dams on earth, holding back an inland sea of Euphrates water that turned the dry southeast green and drowned a good deal of history doing it. The scale from the viewing terrace is genuinely hard to process.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct
properties.tip: The best view is not the dam wall but the road along the reservoir toward Siverek, where the water fills whole valleys between bare hills.
properties.rev: Impressive as engineering and good for a break on a long drive, but there is little to actually do, security restricts photography near the wall, and summer heat off the water is fierce.
properties.entry: Free · photography restricted at the dam itself
properties.onward: Şanlıurfa GAP (GNY), then about 1h15 north by car on the Bozova road

properties.name: Karakuş Tumulus
properties.desc: A burial mound for the women of the Commagene royal house, marked by tall columns topped with an eagle, a lion and a relief of a handshake farewell. It stands alone above the Euphrates plain and catches extraordinary evening light.
properties.season: Apr–Oct
properties.tip: It is the best sunset spot on the Nemrut circuit and almost nobody stops — save it for last on the way back to Kahta.
properties.rev: Photographers rate it highly for the light and emptiness, but there is little to do beyond looking, and it is skipped by some tours.
properties.onward: Adıyaman (ADF), then 40 min by car toward Kahta

properties.name: Cendere Bridge
properties.desc: A Roman bridge from around AD 200 still carrying its single 30-metre arch over the Cendere gorge, with three of its four honorific columns standing. It served traffic until recently and looks barely touched.
properties.season: Apr–Oct
properties.tip: Walk down to the riverbed on the south side for the view that shows the whole arch — from the road you only see the deck.
properties.rev: A quick, free and photogenic stop that everyone on the Nemrut circuit enjoys, though it is genuinely a ten-minute visit and the riverbank collects litter.
properties.onward: Adıyaman (ADF), then about 1h by car on the Kahta–Nemrut road

properties.name: Arsameia on the Nymphaios
properties.desc: The Commagene summer capital below Nemrut, where a relief shows King Mithridates shaking hands with Heracles, and a long tunnel drops into the hillside toward a cult chamber nobody has fully explained.
properties.season: Apr–Oct
properties.tip: Bring a torch for the tunnel; it goes further than you expect and there is no lighting past the first few metres.
properties.rev: A strong companion to Nemrut and usually quiet, though it is a hot uphill walk with almost no shade and the tunnel is closed off after heavy rain.
properties.onward: Adıyaman (ADF), then 1h15 by car; every Nemrut tour from Kahta stops here

properties.name: Mount Nemrut
properties.desc: A first-century BC king built his own tomb on a 2,150 m summit and ringed it with colossal seated gods, then piled a cone of broken stone over the burial. Earthquakes toppled the heads, which now sit on the ground staring past you at the sunrise.
properties.season: Late May–mid Oct — the summit road is closed by snow the rest of the year
properties.tip: Sunrise means leaving Kahta around 03:00 and it is genuinely cold at the top even in August; sunset is warmer, emptier and lights the east terrace better.
properties.rev: Repeatedly described as one of the great sights of Türkiye, with the caveats that the final climb is a steep 600 m on loose stone, sunrise is crowded and freezing, and the road closes with early snow.
properties.onward: Adıyaman (ADF), then about 2h by car to the summit car park via Kahta; tours run from Kahta and Malatya

properties.name: Balıklıgöl
properties.desc: Two rectangular pools of sacred carp below the citadel rock, where tradition says Abraham was thrown into a fire that turned to water. Families feed the fish, pilgrims pray at the Halil-ür Rahman mosque, and the whole thing works as the city's living room.
properties.season: Year-round — evenings from Apr to Oct, when the courtyards fill
properties.tip: Climb the citadel steps at sunset for the view down over both pools, then come back through the rose garden when the lights come on.
properties.rev: Reviewers love the atmosphere and the free entry, though some find the commercial fish-food sellers pushy and the site far busier on Fridays and religious holidays.
properties.onward: Şanlıurfa GAP (GNY), 45 min by shuttle or taxi into the centre; everything old is then walkable

properties.name: Şanlıurfa Covered Bazaar
properties.desc: A working Ottoman bazaar rather than a souvenir one: felt-makers, coppersmiths hammering, sacks of isot pepper, and the Gümrük Han courtyard where old men play backgammon under a vine with tea coming every ten minutes.
properties.season: Year-round — mornings; closed Sunday in parts
properties.tip: Sit in Gümrük Han for a menengiç coffee, then buy isot pepper by weight from a spice seller rather than a pre-packed tourist box.
properties.rev: Consistently the highlight for people who came for the archaeology, though the alleys are confusing, and a few visitors report being steered toward a relative's shop by over-helpful guides.
properties.onward: Şanlıurfa GAP (GNY), 45 min to the centre; the bazaar is a five-minute walk from Balıklıgöl

properties.name: Göbekli Tepe
properties.desc: A hill of T-shaped limestone pillars carved with foxes, vultures and scorpions, raised by hunter-gatherers around 9600 BC — six thousand years before Stonehenge. It rewrote the story of when humans started building monuments, and it is still mostly underground.
properties.season: Apr–May and Oct–Nov — the shelter traps heat and July is punishing
properties.tip: Go at opening or in the last hour; the walkway is a fixed one-way loop and a tour group ahead of you means you see backs of heads for forty minutes.
properties.rev: Visitors call it genuinely moving once the age sinks in, but many arrive expecting a vast site and find a modest sheltered dig — going without reading up first is the commonest disappointment.
properties.onward: Şanlıurfa GAP (GNY), then 40 min by car; minibuses run from Urfa's Balıklıgöl in season

properties.name: Harran
properties.desc: Conical mud-brick beehive houses on a plain that has been farmed for five thousand years, beside the ruins of one of the world's oldest universities and a moon-god temple. The domes are built without timber and stay startlingly cool inside.
properties.season: Mar–May and Oct–Nov — the plain hits 45 °C in summer
properties.tip: The beehive houses in the village centre are a paid tourist set-up; walk five minutes out to see families still living in the real ones.
properties.rev: The architecture is genuinely unique and the setting stark and memorable, but visitors regularly mention children asking for money and an entrance experience that feels staged.
properties.entry: ₺100 (≈€2.20) for the house complex · ruins free
properties.onward: Şanlıurfa GAP (GNY), then 1h south by car; minibuses leave Urfa's otogar hourly

properties.name: Karahan Tepe
properties.desc: Göbekli Tepe's contemporary and, to many archaeologists, the more startling site: a room with eleven phallic pillars rising from bedrock and a human head carved into the rock wall, watching. It opened to visitors recently and still feels like a working dig rather than an attraction.
properties.season: Apr–May and Oct–Nov
properties.tip: Combine it with Göbekli Tepe in one day but do Karahan first — after the crowds and walkways of Göbekli it feels twice as raw.
properties.rev: Those who make the drive rate it above Göbekli Tepe for atmosphere, but the road is rough, there is almost no shade or infrastructure, and excavation can close sections without notice.
properties.onward: Şanlıurfa GAP (GNY), then about 1h15 east by car — there is no public transport, so hire or a driver

properties.name: Soğmatar
properties.desc: A hill sanctuary of the Sabians, who worshipped the sun, moon and five planets here in the second century. Rock-cut reliefs of robed figures stare out of a basalt outcrop above a village where nothing much has changed, and you will usually have it alone.
properties.season: Mar–May and Oct–Nov
properties.tip: Find the village muhtar or the boy with the key for the underground Pognon cave, which holds the best-preserved reliefs and is otherwise locked.
properties.rev: Travellers who reach it describe it as the most atmospheric site in the region, but there is no signage, no ticket office and no shade, and the last few kilometres of road are rough.
properties.entry: Free · a tip to whoever unlocks the cave is customary
properties.onward: Şanlıurfa GAP (GNY), then about 1h30 by car via Harran — you need your own vehicle

properties.name: Han el-Ba'rur
properties.desc: A square Ayyubid caravanserai from 1216 standing alone on the Tektek plateau, its stone arches and camel stalls intact enough that you can read the building at a glance. Nothing else is visible in any direction.
properties.season: Mar–May and Oct–Nov
properties.tip: It is unlocked and unstaffed — go in the last hour of light, when the low sun comes through the arches and the plateau turns orange.
properties.rev: A favourite of people doing the Tektek loop for its isolation and photogenic arches, though it takes about fifteen minutes to see and is not worth a dedicated trip.
properties.onward: Şanlıurfa GAP (GNY), then 1h20 by car on the Soğmatar–Şuayb loop

properties.name: Çermik Travertines
properties.desc: Terraces of white travertine built up by hot springs at Haydarhan, a smaller and almost unvisited cousin of Pamukkale, with thermal pools you can actually bathe in and no queue for anything.
properties.season: Oct–May — the thermal water is best when the air is cold
properties.tip: Go in winter, when steam rises off the terraces and the contrast with the cold air is the entire experience.
properties.rev: Those who find it enjoy having a Pamukkale-like landscape to themselves, but the facilities are dated, the pools are basic, and the terraces are smaller than photos imply.
properties.onward: Diyarbakır (DIY), then about 1h30 northwest by car

properties.name: Eğil
properties.desc: A castle rock and Assyrian royal reliefs above a turquoise arm of the Tigris reservoir, with rock-cut tombs and prophets' shrines in the cliffs. The water colour against the bare stone is the surprise.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct
properties.tip: Take the boat rather than only looking from the terrace — the cliff tombs and the reliefs only make sense from the water.
properties.rev: Visitors are struck by the colour and the emptiness, though facilities are basic, boat schedules are informal, and the site is far less developed than photographs suggest.
properties.entry: Free · boat trips around ₺250 (≈€5.50) per person
properties.onward: Diyarbakır (DIY), then about 1h north by car

properties.name: Ten-Eyed Bridge
properties.desc: A basalt bridge of 1065 carrying ten arches over the Tigris below the city walls, still standing on its original piers. Families picnic on the banks and the whole Hevsel garden belt spreads upstream.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct
properties.tip: Come at sunset and walk it from the far bank looking back — the walls, the bridge and the river line up only from that side.
properties.rev: A lovely free spot that locals clearly enjoy, though the riverbanks collect litter and the approach road from the old city is unpleasant on foot.
properties.onward: Diyarbakır (DIY), 30 min by taxi below the southern walls

properties.name: Diyarbakır Great Mosque
properties.desc: The oldest mosque in Anatolia, built in 1091 on the frame of a Byzantine church and before that a temple, with recycled Roman columns and a courtyard that reads more like a Damascus mosque than a Turkish one.
properties.season: Year-round
properties.tip: Sit in the courtyard for a while rather than going straight through — the two-storey arcades with their mismatched classical columns are the whole story of the city in one wall.
properties.rev: Architecturally remarkable and free, though it is an active mosque with the usual timing and dress requirements, and the surrounding bazaar streets can feel chaotic.
properties.entry: Free · closed to visitors during prayers
properties.onward: Diyarbakır (DIY), 25 min to Sur; the mosque is in the middle of the walled city

properties.name: Diyarbakır City Walls
properties.desc: Nearly six kilometres of black basalt wall, second in length only to the Great Wall, wrapped around the old city since Roman times and studded with inscriptions from every empire that held it. From the ramparts the Tigris and the green Hevsel gardens open out below.
properties.season: Mar–May and Oct–Nov — the basalt radiates heat in summer
properties.tip: Walk the stretch between Mardin Kapı and Yedi Kardeş bastion in the late afternoon for the Hevsel view; parts of the circuit are closed and it is not a continuous walk.
properties.rev: The scale impresses everyone, but access to the ramparts is patchy, some inner-city districts remain damaged and restricted since 2015–16, and it pays to ask locally which sections are open.
properties.entry: Free · some bastions have a small fee
properties.onward: Diyarbakır (DIY), 25 min into the old city by taxi

properties.name: Zerzevan Castle
properties.desc: A Roman garrison on the eastern frontier with a watchtower, rock-cut water channels, an underground church and — the reason it made headlines — an intact Mithraeum, one of the few in the world still bearing its cult niches.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct
properties.tip: The Mithraeum is entered by a narrow stair and is often only opened on request; ask at the gate rather than assuming it is included.
properties.rev: An excellent and still-quiet site that impresses almost everyone who makes the detour, though there is no shade, and excavation work regularly closes individual structures.
properties.onward: Diyarbakır (DIY), then 45 min south by car on the Mardin road

properties.name: Kasımiye Madrasa
properties.desc: A 15th-century madrasa whose courtyard pool is cut in the shape of a life: a channel that narrows and widens from birth to death. From its terrace the whole Mesopotamian plain opens out, which is the single best view in Mardin.
properties.season: Year-round — spring and autumn
properties.tip: Come 45 minutes before sunset, when the stone goes gold and the plain below turns purple; it is far less crowded than the Zinciriye.
properties.rev: Frequently rated better than the more famous Zinciriye for both architecture and calm, though it is a stiff walk up from the main street and closes earlier than people expect.
properties.onward: Mardin (MQM), 25 min by car, then a steep uphill walk from the main street

properties.name: Mardin Old Town
properties.desc: A city of honey-coloured limestone stacked in terraces down a hillside, with the Mesopotamian plain running flat to the horizon below. Arabic, Kurdish, Turkish and Syriac have all shaped it, and the stone carving on ordinary doorways is extraordinary.
properties.season: Apr–May and Sep–Nov — July and August are brutal
properties.tip: Stay in the old town, not the new city below, and walk the lower lane rather than the main street — the views under the arches are what people remember.
properties.rev: Widely called the most beautiful town in Türkiye, with the honest caveats that it is steep and hard on the knees, the main street is now solidly souvenir shops, and it is packed at holidays.
properties.onward: Mardin (MQM), then 25 min by car up to the old town; the airport is unusually close

properties.name: Deyrulzafaran Monastery
properties.desc: The Saffron Monastery, seat of the Syriac Orthodox patriarchate for six centuries, built over a temple where the sun was worshipped. Services are still held in Aramaic, and the underground chamber below the church is older than everything above it.
properties.season: Mar–Nov — closed to visitors during some services
properties.tip: Time your visit for a service if you can; hearing Aramaic sung in the church is worth more than the guided walk-through.
properties.rev: Visitors find it beautiful and still living rather than museum-like, though the compulsory guided format is rushed and photography is restricted inside the church.
properties.onward: Mardin (MQM), then 30 min by car — 6 km east of the old town

properties.name: Savur
properties.desc: A small stone town spilling down a bluff above a green river valley, often called a miniature Mardin but with orchards instead of a plain below. Almost no tourism, a castle ruin on top and very good breakfasts.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct
properties.tip: Walk down to the river gardens below the town in the late afternoon — the view back up at the stacked houses is the one worth having.
properties.rev: Loved by the few who detour for it and described as Mardin without the crowds, though there is little to actually do and accommodation is limited to a handful of guesthouses.
properties.onward: Mardin (MQM), then 45 min northeast by car; minibuses run from Mardin

properties.name: Dara Ancient City
properties.desc: A Byzantine frontier fortress town cut into and out of the rock: a vast pillared cistern, a necropolis of rock tombs, and a bone-filled burial chamber, with a modern village living among the ruins.
properties.season: Mar–May and Oct–Nov
properties.tip: The great cistern is the reason to come and it is easy to miss — it is down a lane behind the village, not on the main path.
properties.rev: Repeatedly named the surprise of a southeast trip, though signage is poor, the village dogs are assertive, and there is no shade at all.
properties.onward: Mardin (MQM), then 40 min southeast by car

properties.name: Hasuni Caves
properties.desc: A rock-cut settlement of several hundred chambers, churches and water channels carved into a valley wall outside Batman, used from Roman times onward and only recently opened up with paths and lighting.
properties.season: Mar–May and Oct–Nov
properties.tip: Ask for the church with the carved cross and the baptismal basin — it is the best-preserved chamber and easy to miss on the marked route.
properties.rev: An easy and rewarding side trip from Batman that few travellers know about, though interpretation is minimal and some chambers are gated off.
properties.onward: Batman (BAL), then 30 min by car from the city

properties.name: Malabadi Bridge
properties.desc: An Artuqid bridge of 1147 whose single pointed arch spans nearly 40 metres over the Batman river — for centuries the widest stone arch in the world. Small chambers inside the abutments once sheltered travellers overnight.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct
properties.tip: Pull off at the old road rather than the new highway bridge; from the riverbank below you get the arch reflected, which is the shot.
properties.rev: Engineering-minded visitors find the span genuinely impressive, though it is purely a roadside stop with no facilities and heavy traffic noise from the modern bridge alongside.
properties.onward: Batman (BAL), then 45 min northwest by car on the Diyarbakır road

properties.name: Nusaybin and Mor Yakup
properties.desc: Ancient Nisibis on the Syrian border, where the fourth-century church of Mor Yakup holds one of the oldest surviving Christian crypts anywhere, and a Roman bridge and city wall fragments surface between modern streets.
properties.season: Mar–May and Oct–Nov
properties.tip: The crypt and its carved capitals are the point; ask at the site office, as the lower chamber is often locked between visitors.
properties.rev: Historically significant and rarely visited, though the border-town setting is heavily policed, the site is fragmentary, and travellers should check current advisories before going.
properties.onward: Mardin (MQM), then 1h south by car; check border-region advisories before travelling

properties.name: Midyat
properties.desc: The stone heart of the Tur Abdin plateau, where Syriac silversmiths still make telkari filigree and the old quarter of Estel is a maze of carved limestone courtyards. Quieter and less polished than Mardin, and better for it.
properties.season: Apr–May and Sep–Nov
properties.tip: Sleep here rather than day-tripping — the guesthouses in old stone konaks are the whole point, and the town empties beautifully after dark.
properties.rev: Travellers consistently prefer Midyat's atmosphere to Mardin's commerce, though there is less to formally see, and a popular Turkish TV series has brought weekend crowds to one particular mansion.
properties.entry: Free · guesthouse courtyards usually welcome visitors for tea
properties.onward: Mardin (MQM), then 1h east by car; regular minibuses from Mardin otogar

properties.name: Hasankeyf
properties.desc: A twelve-thousand-year-old town on the Tigris, most of it flooded by the Ilısu dam in 2020. The cave city and the castle rock survive above the waterline, and several monuments were cut up and moved to a new park on the hillside.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct
properties.tip: Go knowing what it is now — the old bridge piers and the lower town are underwater, and the honest experience is the cave city plus the relocated monuments, not the town in the photographs.
properties.rev: Deeply mixed: some still find the setting extraordinary, many arrive expecting the pre-2020 town and leave saddened, and the relocated monuments in their landscaped park strike visitors as sterile.
properties.entry: ₺100 (≈€2.20) for the castle and cave city
properties.onward: Batman (BAL), then 45 min by car; minibuses run from Batman otogar

properties.name: Mor Gabriel Monastery
properties.desc: Founded in 397, the oldest working Syriac Orthodox monastery in the world, still home to a small community on the bare Tur Abdin plateau. The mosaic in the main church was a gift from a Byzantine emperor.
properties.season: Mar–Nov — visiting hours are limited and strictly kept
properties.tip: Check the visiting window before you drive out; it opens for only a couple of hours in the afternoon and turns people away outside it.
properties.near: Mor Gabriel Manastırı, Midyat, Mardin, Türkiye
properties.rev: A moving stop for anyone interested in early Christianity, but access is tightly controlled, the visit is short and guided, and modest dress is enforced.
properties.onward: Mardin (MQM), then about 1h15 by car past Midyat

properties.name: Botan Valley
properties.desc: A deep green canyon where the Botan river runs between limestone walls into the Tigris, now a national park with rafting in spring and swimming holes in summer. It is the wettest, greenest corner of a region people assume is all desert.
properties.season: Apr–Jun for water, Sep–Oct for walking
properties.tip: The Kasrik gorge stretch has the accessible viewpoints and picnic areas; the rest of the valley needs a boat or a guide.
properties.near: Botan Vadisi Milli Parkı, Siirt, Türkiye
properties.rev: A revelation for people who did not expect green canyons in the southeast, though infrastructure is thin, rafting operators are seasonal and informal, and roads into the valley are rough.
properties.onward: Siirt (SXZ), then 40 min by car east toward the Kasrik gorge

properties.name: Tillo
properties.desc: A hill village of scholars and mystics above Siirt, where a 17th-century astronomer built a tomb with a light channel that illuminates a specific point twice a year at the equinox. The stone lanes and the plain views are the rest of it.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct; the light event falls near the equinoxes
properties.tip: If you can time it to 21 March or 23 September, the light beam through İbrahim Hakkı's tomb is the reason the village is known at all.
properties.rev: A quiet and genuinely unusual stop, but outside the equinox days there is not much to see, and visitors note the village is a pilgrimage site with a devotional rather than touristic atmosphere.
properties.onward: Siirt (SXZ), then 25 min by car up from the city

properties.name: Siirt Büryan and the Old Bazaar
properties.desc: Lamb hung in a deep clay pit and cooked in its own steam overnight, served on flatbread in a handful of unchanged shops around Siirt's bazaar — a dish that basically does not exist outside this province and is eaten for breakfast.
properties.season: Year-round — go early, they sell out by mid-morning
properties.tip: Order büryan with perde pilavı alongside, and eat before ten; the good places cook one pit a day and close when it is gone.
properties.rev: Food travellers rate büryan among the best things they eat in Türkiye, with the caveat that the shops are plain, cash-only and crowded, and the fat content surprises people.
properties.onward: Siirt (SXZ), 25 min into the city; the bazaar shops are walkable from the centre

properties.name: Cizre and the Tigris
properties.desc: An old Tigris crossing with an Artuqid bridge, the Ulu Camii and the tomb traditionally held to be Noah's, on a plain that has been a frontier for three thousand years under the wall of Cudi mountain.
properties.season: Mar–May and Oct–Nov — summer here is among the hottest in the country
properties.tip: Check current travel advisories before planning this leg; conditions in Şırnak province change and local guidance is worth more than any guidebook.
properties.rev: Historically fascinating and almost never visited by foreigners, but this is a sensitive border area with checkpoints, and several governments advise against travel to parts of the province.
properties.onward: Şırnak Şerafettin Elçi (NKT), then about 1h by car; check advisories before travelling

properties.name: Mount Cudi
properties.desc: A 2,100 m limestone massif above the Tigris that Islamic and local tradition names as the landing place of Noah's ark, with Assyrian rock reliefs on its lower slopes and villages that still summer on its pastures.
properties.season: May–Oct for the high ground
properties.tip: This is not a casual hike — access depends on the security situation and permission, and it should only be attempted with local arrangement.
properties.rev: Of real interest to those drawn by the ark tradition, but access is frequently restricted, several governments advise against travel here, and independent hiking is not realistic.
properties.entry: Free · access subject to local permission and security conditions
properties.onward: Şırnak Şerafettin Elçi (NKT), then by road with local arrangement; check advisories first

properties.name: Darende and the Tohma Canyon
properties.desc: The Tohma cuts a narrow gorge through Darende, and a walkway is bolted to the rock a few metres above the water, running past the Somuncu Baba shrine complex and its pool of fat carp. Above the town the canyon opens out, with boat rides and a cable car that are pure Turkish weekend.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct; the shrine is busiest at weekends and religious holidays
properties.tip: Walk the canyon boardwalk early, before the pilgrim coaches arrive and the whole gorge fills with people throwing bread at the fish.
properties.rev: A genuinely pretty gorge with a well-made walkway, though the shrine end gets very crowded, the commercial add-ons feel bolted on, and parking in the town is chaos on Sundays.
properties.entry: Free · boat and cable car charged separately
properties.onward: Malatya Erhaç (MLX) airport, then 100 km west on the Kayseri road; Malatya–Darende buses run several times a day

properties.name: Levent Valley
properties.desc: A canyon cut into pale rock north of Akçadağ, with walls up to 200 m, a village of the same name on the rim, and rock-cut tombs and pigeon houses in the cliffs. Bolted sport-climbing routes have gone up on the best walls, and a path runs along the floor when the stream is low.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct; summer is too hot for the walls and the floor floods with the spring melt
properties.tip: Ask in Levent village for the way down to the canyon floor — the rim viewpoints are what everyone photographs, but the rock-cut chambers are all down at the bottom.
properties.rev: Climbers and walkers rate it well above its reputation, with the drawbacks being a rough approach road, no facilities in the village, and route information that circulates mostly by word of mouth.
properties.onward: Malatya Erhaç (MLX) airport, then 60 km west past Akçadağ; a car is essential and the final stretch is narrow

properties.name: Günpınar Waterfall
properties.desc: Spring water emerges from the hillside above Darende and falls in a broad fan of small cascades over travertine steps into a wooded basin, with tea tables built into the terraces. It runs at much the same volume all year, which is unusual here, and the water stays cold through August.
properties.season: May–Oct; the terraces ice over and the access road gets slippery in winter
properties.tip: Walk up past the last tea table to the head of the falls where the springs actually come out — most people stop at the first platform and photograph the same view as everyone else.
properties.rev: Praised as cool, green and cheap in a very hot province, with complaints about litter and loud music on summer weekends and a final access road that is narrow and badly surfaced.
properties.onward: Malatya Erhaç (MLX) airport, then 110 km west via Darende; a car is needed for the last 12 km

properties.name: Malatya Apricots and the Sire Pazarı
properties.desc: Malatya grows most of the world's dried apricots and nearly all of them pass through the Sire Pazarı, a covered hall where jute sacks are cut open, graded by hand and traded by shouting. In July the orchards are full of trays drying in the sun, and the unsulphured fruit comes out brown and tastes far better.
properties.season: Jul–Aug for the harvest and the drying trays; the market trades all year
properties.tip: Ask for kükürtsüz, the dark unsulphured fruit, and try the apricot kernels while you are there — the bright orange stuff is sulphured for export.
properties.rev: Food travellers rate the market as the real thing rather than a display, though it is dusty, loud, hard to photograph without asking, and much of the city around it is still rebuilding after the 2023 earthquakes.
properties.onward: Malatya Erhaç (MLX) airport, then 30 min into the city; the Sire Pazarı is near the old centre and easy by taxi

properties.name: Arslantepe Mound
properties.desc: A thirty-metre mound above the Malatya plain, occupied from the sixth millennium BC, where excavators found the earliest known palace complex and a hoard of early arsenical bronze swords. A canopy now covers the mud-brick palace and its wall paintings, which is the only reason the walls are still standing.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct; the plain reaches 40 °C in July and August with no shade on the mound
properties.tip: Come in the morning, when low sun still shows the paint on the mud brick — under a midday sun the whole site flattens into beige.
properties.rev: Archaeologically extraordinary and quiet enough that you may have it alone, though visitors regularly say it looks like a building site unless you read the boards first, and the best finds are in the Malatya and Ankara museums.
properties.entry: Small fee — check locally · covered by Museum Pass Türkiye
properties.onward: Malatya Erhaç (MLX) airport, then 30 km east to Orduzu on the Battalgazi road; a taxi from Malatya takes 20 min

properties.name: Battalgazi (Old Malatya)
properties.desc: Old Malatya was abandoned for the new town in the 19th century, so what remains sits among apricot orchards: a long circuit of brick and stone city wall with round towers, the 1224 Great Mosque with a blue-tiled Seljuk iwan, and the huge Silahtar Mustafa Paşa caravanserai.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct; blossom in early April, 40 °C in the July orchards
properties.tip: The tiled iwan of the Ulu Cami is behind a locked courtyard door much of the time — turn up at prayer time and find the muezzin rather than coming mid-morning.
properties.rev: Visitors like that a whole medieval town survives among the orchards, while noting that the 2023 earthquakes damaged several buildings, restoration hoarding is widespread, and opening hours are unpredictable.
properties.entry: Free · small fee at the han
properties.onward: Malatya Erhaç (MLX) airport, then 35 km northeast; city buses run out from Malatya through the day

properties.name: Kemaliye (Eğin)
properties.desc: Old Ottoman houses with carved wooden ceilings stacked on a shelf above the Euphrates, built with money sent home by emigrants. Above the town runs the Taş Yolu, a road hacked through cliff by hand over decades, running in and out of raw rock tunnels with the river a long way below.
properties.season: May–Oct; the Taş Yolu tunnels are unlit and the gorge road is grim in winter
properties.tip: Drive the Taş Yolu from the Kemaliye end towards Dutluca early in the morning — the tunnels are single-lane, and meeting a tractor in one is not fun.
properties.rev: Travellers describe it as the most spectacular road in Anatolia and the town as genuinely lived-in, but warn about no barriers, falling rock, and hotel beds that vanish entirely on summer weekends.
properties.onward: Erzincan (ERC) airport, then about 140 km southwest; the last stretch from İliç is slow and winding

properties.name: Keban Dam
properties.desc: The first of the big Euphrates dams, finished in the mid-1970s: a two-hundred-metre wall across a gorge that backed up a reservoir the size of a small sea. It drowned villages and the whole valley floor, and created the water that Pertek castle now stands in. The viewpoint above the crest looks down the length of the gorge.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct; the reservoir shore is dusty and low by late summer
properties.tip: Photographing the dam structure is restricted — shoot from the public viewpoint on the road above and keep the lens off the installations and the guard posts.
properties.rev: Engineering interest and sheer scale are the draw; visitors warn that access to the dam itself is controlled, security is touchy about cameras, and nothing at all is organised for tourists on site.
properties.entry: Free · no public access to the structure
properties.onward: Elazığ (EZS) airport, then 60 km northwest to Keban town; the viewpoints are on the road above the dam

properties.name: Munzur Springs
properties.desc: The Munzur comes out of the base of a mountain wall above Ovacık in a line of springs, full-sized from the first metre, ice cold and clear enough to read through. The site is sacred to local Alevis, who tie cloth to the trees and bring food, and there are tea tables in the shade beside the water.
properties.season: Jun–Sep; the road up is often blocked by snow outside that
properties.tip: This is a place of worship as much as a picnic ground — do not put beer on the table, and ask before photographing anyone at the water.
properties.rev: People find it genuinely beautiful and unusually charged with meaning; the complaints are weekend crowds, music from the picnic areas, and litter left around the pools by day-trippers.
properties.onward: Elazığ (EZS) airport, then 130 km to Tunceli, 60 km to Ovacık and 10 km more to the springs by car or village dolmuş

properties.name: Ovacık and the Munzur Pastures
properties.desc: Ovacık sits at 1,300 m in a bowl of high pasture under the Munzur range, with snow on the tops into July and thick honey coming off the meadows in August. The town itself is small and plain; the reason to come is the road beyond it toward the Munzur springs and the empty valleys on either side.
properties.season: Jun–Sep for the pastures; the district is snowbound and half-empty Dec–Mar
properties.tip: Buy Ovacık honey from a producer in the villages rather than a shop on the main road, and expect to be fed while you negotiate.
properties.rev: Visitors describe real hospitality and empty landscapes; the practical warnings are very limited accommodation, occasional road closures for military operations, and almost nothing open outside summer.
properties.onward: Elazığ (EZS) airport, then 130 km to Tunceli and 60 km further up the valley; minibuses run from Tunceli otogar

properties.name: Buzluk Cave
properties.desc: A limestone cave north of Harput that does everything backwards: it fills with ice through the summer and thaws in winter, because cold air sinks into the shaft and cannot get out again. In August there are ice columns on the floor while the hillside outside sits at 35 °C. Steps lead down about thirty metres.
properties.season: Jul–Aug for maximum ice, which is the opposite of what you would expect
properties.tip: Take a torch and a jacket — there is no lighting, the steps are wet, and the temperature drops thirty degrees in the first minute of the descent.
properties.rev: A memorable ten minutes and a real curiosity, but reports agree the access road is rough, the entrance is unsigned and sometimes gated, and there is no lighting or handrail inside.
properties.onward: Elazığ (EZS) airport, then about 25 km north beyond Harput on a minor road; a car and local directions are needed

properties.name: Harput
properties.desc: The old town of Elazığ sits on a rock plateau three hundred metres above it, half-abandoned when the population moved down in the 19th century. What is left is a big Artuqid-era castle, the 1156 Great Mosque with a leaning brick minaret, the Meryem Ana church, and a view across the plain to Hazar lake.
properties.season: May–Jun and Sep–Oct; the plateau is windy and cold from November onward
properties.tip: Go up in the evening for kürsübaşı music and orcik sweets at the cafes below the castle — daytime is coach parties, and the castle interior has been largely closed since the earthquakes.
properties.rev: Visitors rate the setting and the mosque highly, but note that the castle has been closed or half-closed for restoration for years, several churches are locked, and the plateau is bleak in wind.
properties.entry: Free · small fee at the castle when it is open
properties.onward: Elazığ (EZS) airport, then 15 km north up the escarpment; city buses and taxis run up from the centre

properties.name: Pertek Castle
properties.desc: A Seljuk-era castle that used to stand on a hill and now stands on an island, after the Keban reservoir flooded the valley around it in the 1970s. Walls and towers rise straight out of the water, and the small car ferry between the Elazığ and Tunceli banks passes close enough to photograph it from the deck.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct; the reservoir is at its lowest and least attractive in late summer
properties.tip: You do not need to land — take the Pertek car ferry across the reservoir and you get the castle from the water plus the crossing itself for the price of a ticket.
properties.rev: The setting is what people remember; the interior gets far less praise, landings depend on the water level and a willing boatman, and the ferry timetable is loose at the best of times.
properties.entry: Free from the water · small fee if a boatman lands you
properties.onward: Elazığ (EZS) airport, then 60 km north to the Pertek ferry pier; the crossing drops you on the Tunceli road

properties.name: Munzur Valley National Park
properties.desc: Türkiye's largest national park on paper: about 42,000 hectares of limestone gorge, black pine and clear river between Tunceli and Ovacık. The Munzur runs green over white stone the whole way, with wild goats on the crags and trout in the pools, and the road beside it is one long series of places to stop.
properties.season: May–Oct; the high country holds snow into June and the road can be cut in winter
properties.tip: The stretch above Ovacık is the wild part — most visitors stop at the first picnic spots ten minutes out of Tunceli and never see the gorge proper.
properties.rev: Tunceli people call it the finest valley in the country and outsiders usually agree, but the park has fought hydroelectric schemes for two decades, side valleys are still closed for military operations at times, and facilities are basic.
properties.onward: Elazığ (EZS) airport then 130 km north to Tunceli, or Erzincan (ERC) 180 km; the park road starts at the edge of town

properties.name: Halvori Springs
properties.desc: Twenty kilometres up the Munzur gorge from Tunceli, cold springs come out of the canyon foot straight into the river under willows, with wooden platforms built out over the water. People swim in the green pools, eat trout, and sit in the spray on the platforms all afternoon.
properties.season: Jun–Sep; the water is too cold and the road too rough outside summer
properties.tip: Swim upstream of the platforms rather than below them — those pools are deeper, colder and free of the frying-oil sheen off the restaurants.
properties.rev: A local favourite and cheap, though visitors mention rubbish along the bank at weekends, loud music from the restaurants, and river water cold enough to cramp your legs within a minute.
properties.entry: Free · platforms and meals charged by the restaurants
properties.onward: Elazığ (EZS) airport, then 130 km to Tunceli and 20 km up the Ovacık road; summer dolmuşes run from Tunceli otogar

properties.name: Lake Hazar and the Sunken City
properties.desc: A deep blue lake at 1,250 m in a trough of the East Anatolian Fault, with the walls of a drowned medieval settlement lying a few metres under the surface near the southern shore. When the water drops in late summer the tops of the walls break the surface and you can wade out to them.
properties.season: Jul–Sep for swimming and the lowest water; windy and cold the rest of the year
properties.tip: The ruins show best in September after the drawdown; dive clubs in Sivrice run trips over them, and from the shore you need a mask to see anything at all.
properties.rev: People are surprised how clear and cold the water is; the complaints are shoreline development at the Sivrice end, an underwhelming sunken city unless the level is low, and a strong wind most afternoons.
properties.entry: Free · dive trips charged by the club
properties.onward: Elazığ (EZS) airport, then 30 km southeast on the Diyarbakır road to Sivrice; minibuses run from Elazığ otogar

properties.name: Ergan Mountain
properties.desc: The ridge that hangs directly over Erzincan, with a gondola from the edge of town lifting you to about 2,600 m in a quarter of an hour. In winter it is a small, cheap ski hill with wide-open north-facing bowls; in summer the top is meadow, crocus and a view straight down onto the Erzincan plain.
properties.season: Jan–Mar for snow, Jun–Sep for the meadows and the ride up
properties.tip: Ride the gondola even without skis — the return ticket is trivial and the top station terrace is the best table in Erzincan on a clear evening.
properties.rev: Locals rate the value and the short transfer from town, but reviews mention that the gondola is often shut for wind or maintenance and that the resort has almost no infrastructure once you are up there.
properties.onward: Erzincan (ERC) airport, 10 km away; the gondola base is on the southern edge of the city

properties.name: Altıntepe
properties.desc: An Urartian hill fort on a low mound beside the Erzincan–Erzurum highway, excavated to reveal a temple, a columned audience hall and rock-cut tombs that gave up gold and bronze now in Ankara. What survives on site is foundations and a fine view, but it is one of the westernmost Urartian outposts and almost nobody stops.
properties.season: Apr–Oct; the mound is exposed and there is no shade or shelter
properties.tip: See the finds first in the Erzincan museum, otherwise the site reads as a field of stone outlines with no explanation.
properties.rev: Archaeology-minded visitors find it rewarding for its scale and isolation, but general reviews are lukewarm: little signage, an unstaffed gate, and everything portable removed to museums.
properties.onward: Erzincan (ERC) airport, then 20 km east on the D100 towards Üzümlü; the mound is signposted off the highway

properties.name: Girlevik Waterfall
properties.desc: Water spills over a wide travertine lip in dozens of separate threads rather than one column, dropping into a wooded gorge below Çağlayan village. In February the whole face freezes into a curtain of ice that draws climbers from across the region. In summer it is a picnic spot with tea gardens on the terraces.
properties.season: Apr–Jun at full flow; late Jan–Feb for the frozen face
properties.tip: Carry on 3 km past the falls to the Girlevik ice cave and the upper springs — nearly everyone stops at the first tea garden and turns around.
properties.rev: Consistently called worth the detour, though visitors complain the picnic area is littered on summer weekends and the loud music from the tea gardens carries right to the base of the falls.
properties.onward: Erzincan (ERC) airport, then roughly 30 km southeast via Çağlayan; minibuses run in summer only

properties.name: Pülümür Valley
properties.desc: The road from Erzincan down to Tunceli threads a red and ochre gorge for sixty kilometres, following the Pülümür stream past terraced hamlets and single-arch bridges. In late October the poplars along it turn yellow the whole length, and outside the summer months there is almost no traffic.
properties.season: May–Oct; the pass at the Erzincan end closes with snow in winter
properties.tip: Drive it north to south in the afternoon so the light is on the red rock, and stop in Pülümür town for trout, because there is nowhere else to eat on the entire road.
properties.rev: Drivers rate it among the best roads in the east; the honest notes are rockfall after rain, sparse fuel, and long stretches with no signal and no settlement.
properties.onward: Erzincan (ERC) airport, then south on the Tunceli road; Elazığ (EZS) works from the other end via Tunceli

properties.name: Palu
properties.desc: Old Palu stands abandoned on a cliff above the Murat river: an Urartian citadel with a cuneiform inscription of King Menua, a ruined Ottoman mosque and hamam, and the shell of an Armenian church, all in the same brown stone. The modern town sits on the flat a kilometre away.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct; the cliff is exposed and July is brutally hot
properties.tip: The Menua inscription is cut into the rock high on the citadel and is easy to walk past — look on the north face above the old cistern.
properties.rev: Rewarding for anyone who likes ruins nobody else visits, though the climb is steep and unshaded, there is no signage, and the 2023 earthquakes brought down more of the standing walls.
properties.onward: Elazığ (EZS) airport, then 75 km east on the Bingöl road; Elazığ–Palu minibuses stop in the new town below

properties.name: Kral Kızı Castle
properties.desc: A ruined fortress on a 1,400 m spur outside Genç, wrapped on three sides by streams so that only the eastern approach is walkable. What survives is broken wall lines and rubble rather than standing towers, and the local story gives it to a Persian king who shut his daughter away up there.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct; scrub and snakes in high summer, mud in winter
properties.tip: Treat it as a walk with a view rather than a monument — the spur above the stream junction is the real reward, and there is no path, so wear boots.
properties.rev: Honestly more legend than ruin — no signage, no path and little masonry left standing — but people who like empty hills and a good story find it worth an afternoon.
properties.onward: Bingöl (BGG) airport, then 35 km south to Genç, then about 3 km on foot or by farm track

properties.name: Bingöl Floating Islands
properties.desc: On a small lake in the hills above Solhan, mats of peat and root have broken free of the shore and drift with the wind, carrying grass and flowers with them. They are a registered natural monument, a few metres across, and they visibly change position over the course of a day.
properties.season: May–Sep; the lake freezes and the track is poor in winter
properties.tip: Go on a day with a light breeze — in dead calm the islands do not move at all, which is the entire point of the trip.
properties.rev: A genuinely odd natural phenomenon that people enjoy once they get there, with consistent complaints that the lake is small, the last kilometres are dirt track, and signposting from the main road is poor.
properties.onward: Bingöl (BGG) airport, then 60 km east to Solhan and a short climb on a rough track; a car is needed

properties.name: Yakutiye Medrese
properties.desc: Built in 1310 under Ilkhanid rule, this one is roofed rather than open, which matters in Erzurum. The surviving minaret is sheathed in turquoise and dark blue tile, and the facade carries palm trees, lions and a double-headed eagle. Inside is the city's Turkish-Islamic arts museum, with local kilims and silver oltu-stone work.
properties.season: Year-round — it is one of the few Erzurum sights that works in a January blizzard
properties.tip: The oltu-stone workshops in the covered bazaar behind it cut the black jet into rosaries while you wait, and prices drop sharply once you leave the street facing the medrese.
properties.rev: Reviewers like that it is warm, compact and genuinely museum-like, but several note the collection is thin for the ticket and that the second minaret has been missing for centuries despite the name.
properties.entry: Small fee — check locally · covered by Museum Pass Türkiye
properties.onward: Erzurum (ERZ) airport, then any city bus or a 15-minute taxi to Cumhuriyet Caddesi

properties.name: Cağ Kebabı
properties.desc: Lamb stacked on a horizontal spit over wood embers, cut into skewers as the outside crisps, then handed to you to slide onto flatbread with raw onion and sumac. It started in Oltu and Erzurum turned it into a lunchtime institution. Ordering is by the skewer and the counter keeps a running count.
properties.season: Year-round; a plate of it after a January morning outside is the point
properties.tip: Eat it before two in the afternoon — the good places carve one spit a day and simply close when the meat runs out.
properties.rev: Almost universally praised as the best lamb in Türkiye, with the caveats that the per-skewer bill climbs faster than people expect and that the famous places are cramped, smoky and cash-preferred.
properties.onward: Erzurum (ERZ) airport, then a short taxi to the centre; the cluster of grills is around Cumhuriyet Caddesi

properties.name: Çifte Minareli Medrese
properties.desc: A 13th-century Seljuk college whose brick twin minarets and deeply undercut stone portal face straight down Erzurum's main street. The courtyard is open to the sky, so snow sits in it half the year, and the domed Hatuniye tomb at the back is the quietest corner. Three conical Saltuqid tombs stand two minutes south.
properties.season: May–Oct; Dec–Mar the courtyard is under snow and the stone is punishing to touch
properties.tip: Walk two minutes south to the Üç Kümbetler — three conical tombs on a patch of grass that almost every coach party skips.
properties.rev: Visitors call the portal carving the finest Seljuk stonework outside Divriği, while grumbling that half the building is usually behind restoration hoarding and there is almost no signage in English.
properties.entry: Small fee — check locally · covered by Museum Pass Türkiye
properties.onward: Erzurum (ERZ) airport, 12 km out; the medrese sits on Cumhuriyet Caddesi and everything downtown is walkable

properties.name: Palandöken
properties.desc: A bare, treeless ridge rising straight off the southern edge of Erzurum, with the top station above 3,100 m and long fall-line runs that drop back towards the city lights. The snow is dry and cold because of the altitude, and the Ejder run is one of the longest continuous descents in the country.
properties.season: Dec–Mar for skiing; summer is dull grassy slopes and an empty gondola
properties.tip: Stay in the city rather than the slope hotels — a taxi to the lifts costs less than a single resort dinner and you get to eat in real kebab houses.
properties.rev: Skiers rate the snow quality and near-empty pistes highly, but the recurring complaints are old lifts, brutal wind that shuts the upper chairs, and very little après-ski beyond hotel lobbies.
properties.onward: Erzurum (ERZ) airport, then 20 minutes by road to the lift base; free hotel shuttles run in season

properties.name: Muş Old Town and Castle
properties.desc: The old quarter climbs the hill behind modern Muş in terraces of cut stone houses, with ruined castle walls on the crest and the 18th-century Alaeddin Bey mosque halfway up. From the top the whole plain opens out, flat to the horizon, with the Bingöl mountains white on the far side.
properties.season: May–Jun and Sep–Oct; the plain bakes in July and the hill is snowbound in winter
properties.tip: Walk up late in the afternoon and come down through the Kale mahallesi alleys, where the houses still have carved lintels — a few more are lost to concrete every year.
properties.rev: Visitors like the view and the feeling of an unvisited provincial town, while pointing out that the castle is little more than foundations, the climb is steep, and much of the old fabric is derelict.
properties.onward: Muş (MSR) airport, then 20 min into town; the old quarter begins directly behind the main street

properties.name: Öşkvank (Oshki) Monastery
properties.desc: The largest of the Tao-Klarjeti churches, built in the 960s, with a colonnaded south porch, monumental relief figures of its founders and column capitals carved like Romanesque work three centuries early. It stands in the village of Çamlıyamaç, technically in Erzurum province, but everyone visits it on the Yusufeli church circuit.
properties.season: Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct; the Tortum valley is hot in midsummer and icy in winter
properties.tip: Combine it with İşhan and Tortum waterfall in one day — they are strung along the same road and separately are each a long detour.
properties.rev: Described as the most architecturally ambitious church in the region; complaints are decades of stop-start restoration, propped walls, a collapsed section of roof, and modern village building right against the apse.
properties.onward: Erzurum (ERZ) airport, then 110 km north on the Tortum–Yusufeli road, turning off at Çamlıyamaç; car or a Yusufeli-based tour

properties.name: Muş Plain Tulips
properties.desc: For about three weeks in spring the slopes above the Muş plain turn red with wild tulips — small, sharp-petalled, growing straight out of grazing land rather than beds. Families drive out at weekends to sit among them, and the fields move year to year with the grazing, so you ask rather than navigate.
properties.season: Late Apr to mid-May only, and the exact fortnight shifts with the winter
